# REENTRY HOUSING ASSISTANCE GRANT APPLICATION
## FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope)
### EIN: 33-2640449 | Texas Statewide Service Area

---

> **COMPLIANCE NOTICE — REQUIRED PRIOR TO SUBMISSION:**
> Before submitting this application, FAITH Foundation must confirm the following federal compliance items are current and documented:
> - **SAM.gov Active Registration** — Must be active and current. A lapsed registration will disqualify the award. Renew annually. (2 CFR § 200.206)
> - **Unique Entity Identifier (UEI)** — Required on all federal grant applications. Confirm your UEI is assigned through SAM.gov. [NEEDS INPUT: Confirm UEI number for inclusion on application cover sheet]
> - **Single Audit / OMB A-133** — If FAITH Foundation will expend $750,000 or more in federal awards in the fiscal year, a Single Audit conducted by an independent auditor is required and must be submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end. (2 CFR § 200.501). At present budget levels ($75,000 annual budget), this threshold is unlikely to be triggered, but must be monitored as funding grows.
> - **Indirect Cost Rate (NICRA)** — FAITH Foundation should document its intent to use the de minimis rate of 10% of modified total direct costs (MTDC) if it has never had a negotiated indirect cost rate agreement. (2 CFR § 200.414)
> - **Financial Management System** — FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks. Confirm that the system is configured to separately track source and application of federal funds, compare outlays to budget amounts, and support written procedures for cost allowability determinations. (2 CFR § 200.302)
> - **Property Management Standards** — Any equipment or real property acquired with federal funds (including modular housing units) must be inventoried, depreciated per federal standards, and managed per 2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316.
> - **Procurement Standards** — All purchases under this federal award must follow documented, competitive procurement procedures. Cornerstone Communities construction must proceed through competitive open-bid processes. Conflicts of interest must be documented and avoided. (2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327)
> - **Federal Cost Principles** — All costs charged to this award must be allowable, allocable, and reasonable per 2 CFR Subpart E. Unallowable costs include lobbying, entertainment, and alcohol.

---

## SECTION I: STATEMENT OF NEED

### The Housing Crisis Facing Returning Citizens in Texas Is Not Theoretical — It Is Documented, Acute, and Statistically Predictable

The United States faces a housing crisis of historic proportions, and no population bears its consequences more severely than individuals returning from correctional institutions. For formerly incarcerated individuals in Texas, housing instability is not merely a hardship — it is a structural barrier that statistical evidence consistently links to unemployment, supervision violations, and reincarceration. FAITH Foundation exists precisely to break this cycle, and the data below establishes that this crisis is both urgent and addressable through the targeted housing intervention this application describes.

#### The National Reentry Housing Emergency

Formerly incarcerated people are approximately **10 times more likely to experience homelessness** than the general population. (National Low Income Housing Coalition, 2018; Prison Policy Initiative.) Between **23.1% and 47.8%** of annual homeless shelter admissions nationally are individuals with incarceration histories — meaning that at any given moment, nearly half the population in emergency shelter has experienced incarceration. (Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019.) These are not outliers. They are the predictable outcomes of releasing individuals into a housing market that systemically excludes them.

The scale of release is staggering: **nearly 450,000 individuals** were released from state and federal prisons in 2021 alone. On average, a formerly incarcerated individual spends more than six months unemployed post-release. (UNLV Reentry Research Brief.) Without stable housing, employment becomes nearly impossible to obtain and maintain. Without employment, housing costs cannot be covered. The cycle is self-reinforcing and, without intervention, nearly self-sealing.

The consequences of housing instability after release are severe and documented: **82% of individuals released from prison** across 24 states were re-arrested within 10 years of release. (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024.) Research from the CSG Justice Center (2025) confirms that people experiencing homelessness after release are at increased risk of reincarceration due to more frequent law enforcement contact and supervision violations directly related to their housing status — violations that have nothing to do with new criminal conduct and everything to do with the absence of a stable address.

Private housing markets offer little refuge. Landlord criminal background screening, damaged credit histories, and legal restrictions on federally subsidized housing combine to eliminate most market-rate options. The nation simultaneously faces a shortage of **7.3 million rental units** affordable and available to extremely low-income households — the population category in which most returning citizens fall. (National Low Income Housing Coalition.) The market gap is not marginal. It is structural.

#### Texas: A State at the Center of the Reentry Housing Crisis

Texas sits at the center of this national crisis. Nearly **28,000 Texans** were experiencing homelessness in the 2024 Point-in-Time count, with **44% living unsheltered** — meaning they lacked access even to emergency shelter, let alone transitional or permanent housing. (HUD 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, cited in Texas HB 158.) Texas ranks among the seven states that together account for **64% of all people experiencing homelessness** in the United States. (HUD 2024 AHAR.)

Chronic homelessness in Texas is accelerating. The Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network documented **2,594 chronically homeless individuals** in 2023, up sharply from 1,949 in 2022 — a 33% increase in a single year. For formerly incarcerated individuals attempting reentry, this environment means that even the floor of housing stability — access to emergency shelter — is increasingly unavailable.

Rural South and Central Texas, where FAITH Foundation concentrates its work, faces compounding barriers: limited nonprofit housing infrastructure, constrained public transportation, insufficient transitional housing inventory, and geographic isolation that makes accessing services in urban centers impractical for individuals under supervision or without transportation.

#### The Rural South Texas Gap

Rural South Texas communities where FAITH Foundation operates face acute housing shortages with limited nonprofit infrastructure to address them. Individuals released from correctional institutions in or near these communities confront a near-total absence of transitional housing options. Without placement into stable housing immediately upon release — or within the narrow window before supervision violations accumulate — the statistical outcome is predictable: return to homelessness, return to criminal justice system contact, and reincarceration at public cost.

FAITH Foundation was established specifically because this gap existed and no organization was addressing it through the combination of immediate transitional placement and structured pathway to permanent housing that the evidence base identifies as most effective.

#### Why Stable Housing Is the Essential First Intervention

FAITH Foundation's theory of change is grounded in evidence: **stable housing is the prerequisite** for sustained recovery, successful reentry, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. Without it, every other intervention — employment services, substance use treatment, family reunification — operates on an unstable foundation. With it, the data shows that individuals can and do rebuild. The research on Housing First models and transitional housing with wraparound services consistently demonstrates that when housing is secured first, outcomes across all other domains improve measurably.

This application requests support to directly provide that first intervention — transitional housing placement, case management, and a structured pathway to permanent housing — for formerly incarcerated individuals returning to communities across Texas.

---

## SECTION II: PROGRAM DESIGN AND HOUSING STRATEGY

### Second Chance Reentry: A Structured Pathway from Release to Permanent Housing

FAITH Foundation's **Second Chance Reentry program** is the targeted vehicle through which this grant will be deployed. It is embedded within and supported by the Foundation's broader integrated housing ecosystem, ensuring that reentry participants do not receive an isolated service but rather access a complete continuum from transitional placement through permanent homeownership.

#### Program Overview and Logic Model

The Second Chance Reentry program provides formerly incarcerated individuals with three interconnected services upon or shortly after release from correctional institutions in Texas:

**1. Transitional Housing Placement**
Participants are placed into stable transitional housing units — either within FAITH Foundation's developing Cornerstone Communities network or through coordinated placement with partner transitional housing providers — upon or immediately following release. Housing placement is the first and non-negotiable priority, consistent with the evidence base showing that the window immediately following release is the highest-risk period for the reentry-to-homelessness pipeline.

Transitional housing units are modular and manufactured units deployed on acquired or donated land in rural South Texas communities. Through the Foundation's strategic partnership with **Bright Box Homes**, modular units are supplied at below-market cost, allowing charitable contributions to be converted directly into durable, move-in-ready housing. Units range from **$30,000 to $60,000** per unit, making them significantly more cost-effective than traditional construction in rural settings where contractor access and material delivery costs inflate conventional development budgets.

Transitional housing placement is available for **up to 24 months**, providing the stabilization runway that research identifies as necessary for formerly incarcerated individuals to achieve employment, rebuild credit, and qualify for permanent housing.

**2. Case Management and Wraparound Services**
Each participant is assigned a case manager who maintains a **maximum 15-to-1 client ratio**, ensuring sufficient individual attention for complex reentry needs. Case management services include:
- Employment services coordination and employer referral through FAITH Foundation's network of local employer partners
- Legal aid referral for record expungement, supervision compliance, and civil legal matters
- Benefits enrollment coordination with county social services agencies
- Family reunification support
- Transportation assistance for rural case management outreach
- Connection to peer mentorship through FAITH Foundation's trained volunteer mentor network

**3. Financial Literacy and Housing Stability Education**
Case-managed participants are enrolled in FAITH Foundation's **Financial Literacy program**, providing hands-on budgeting, credit-building, and debt management education. For formerly incarcerated individuals who frequently have no credit history, damaged credit, or outstanding legal financial obligations, this education is not supplementary — it is prerequisite to qualifying for permanent housing. Participants complete modules on budgeting on a single income, understanding credit reports and disputing errors, managing legal financial obligations and payment plans, and saving toward housing deposits and eventual down payments.

#### The Cornerstone Communities Model: Addressing Housing Supply

FAITH Foundation recognizes that case management and employment support cannot produce stable housing outcomes if no affordable housing units exist to place participants into. This is the supply-side failure that most reentry programs do not address. **Cornerstone Communities** is FAITH Foundation's answer to that failure.

FAITH Foundation acquires or accepts donation of land parcels in rural South Texas communities, then develops purpose-built transitional micro-communities through competitive open-bid construction processes using modular and manufactured housing units supplied through the Bright Box Homes partnership. Each Cornerstone Community includes:

- Individual housing units (modular/manufactured, $30,000–$60,000 per unit)
- Shared community spaces for programming, meals, and fellowship
- On-site case management offices
- Recovery programming spaces
- Remote work and learning center access
- Community laundry facilities
- Shuttle transportation for rural access to employment, court appearances, and services

Participants enter Cornerstone Communities as transitional residents. As they stabilize — securing employment, completing financial literacy programming, rebuilding credit — they progress toward permanent housing. When a participant graduates to permanent housing, their unit becomes available for the next returning citizen, creating a **rotating asset model** that generates ongoing capacity rather than consuming it.

[NEEDS INPUT: Site control documentation — confirm whether FAITH Foundation has identified or secured a specific land parcel for the first Cornerstone Community, and provide parcel address, acreage, and acquisition status (donated, under option, etc.) for inclusion in this section. If no parcel is yet secured, note expected timeline for first parcel acquisition.]

[NEEDS INPUT: Current unit count — confirm the number of transitional housing units FAITH Foundation currently has deployed or under development, and the number this grant funding would directly support. If no units are yet deployed, confirm the target number of units to be developed with this grant funding.]

#### Participant Intake and Eligibility

Reentry program participants are recruited through coordinated referrals from FAITH Foundation's **reentry service partners**, who coordinate with the Foundation to place formerly incarcerated individuals upon release. Referral partners connect participants with employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support. Eligibility criteria include:

- Release from a Texas state or federal correctional institution within the preceding 90 days, OR anticipated release within 30 days (pre-release enrollment)
- Willingness to participate in case management and financial literacy programming
- Absence of active sex offender registration requirements incompatible with community housing placement
- Income at or below area median income thresholds consistent with low-to-moderate income (LMI) requirements

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirm the specific income eligibility threshold used by this program (e.g., 80% AMI, 50% AMI) and the specific Texas counties or geographic area served under this grant for CDBG LMI documentation purposes.]

#### Fair Housing, ADA Compliance, and Affirmative Marketing

FAITH Foundation is committed to full compliance with the Fair Housing Act and all applicable state and local fair housing laws. The Foundation does not discriminate in program enrollment or housing placement on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, or disability. All programs maintain open enrollment regardless of faith background, consistent with the Foundation's mission to serve all people regardless of religious affiliation.

FAITH Foundation affirmatively markets its Second Chance Reentry program to populations with the greatest documented unmet need, including African American returning citizens — who are disproportionately represented in both the incarcerated and homeless populations — and Hispanic residents of rural South Texas communities. Outreach materials are distributed through reentry partner organizations, county social services offices, and faith communities serving these populations.

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirm whether Cornerstone Communities units are designed or will be designed to meet ADA accessibility standards for individuals with mobility impairments or other disabilities. If accessible units are planned, specify the percentage or number of accessible units. If this has not yet been addressed, note it for architectural planning.]

---

## SECTION III: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY AND EXPERIENCE

### Leadership With Lived Experience, Construction Expertise, and Governance Strength

FAITH Foundation brings to this grant an unusual and powerful combination: a founder with nearly two decades of lived experience navigating incarceration and reentry in Texas, board leadership with 15 years of construction industry expertise, and pastoral governance accountability grounded in decades of community ministry. Together, these leaders bring the credibility, technical capacity, and mission alignment this work demands.

#### Reid Whitesides — Founder & President

Reid Whitesides founded FAITH Foundation from a position of deep personal knowledge. During a long struggle with addiction, Reid spent **nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas** — giving him firsthand, unmediated understanding of the challenges formerly incarcerated individuals face when attempting to rebuild their lives. Today, he has been **sober for more than fifteen years** and leads the Foundation with the conviction that what worked for his own transformation — stable housing as a foundation, faith as motivation, and practical support as a mechanism — can work for others.

Beyond his personal experience, Reid brings more than **20 years of professional experience** in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries. This practical expertise is directly applicable to the Foundation's Cornerstone Communities development work — he understands construction timelines, contractor management, material costs, and the specific challenges of rural housing development in South Texas. He also brings technology skills in website development, software applications, and automation tools that support the Foundation's administrative and reporting infrastructure.

Reid's combination of lived reentry experience and housing industry expertise is rare in the nonprofit sector and positions FAITH Foundation to design and deliver reentry housing programming that is simultaneously credible to participants, technically sound in execution, and operationally efficient.

#### Scott Ellis — Treasurer & Board Chair

Scott Ellis is the owner of **E4 Roofing & Construction**, a Georgetown, Texas-based company he has led for more than **15 years**. His experience in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems provides FAITH Foundation with the financial oversight and construction industry knowledge essential to responsible housing development. Scott's 15 years of business ownership demonstrate sustained organizational leadership and financial stewardship — exactly the governance discipline required of a nonprofit managing federal housing funds.

As Board Chair, Scott ensures that FAITH Foundation maintains rigorous financial controls, responsible budget management, and accountability to funders. The Foundation uses **QuickBooks** for financial management, with financial oversight exercised directly by Scott as Treasurer, providing an internal control structure appropriate to the Foundation's current operating scale.

#### Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary & Protector

Pastor Juan Valdez brings more than **40 years of Christian faith** and **nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience** to the Foundation's governance. His ministry has extended across the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. As Secretary and Protector, Pastor Valdez provides spiritual oversight, governance accountability, and mission stewardship — ensuring the Foundation remains faithful to its core purpose as it grows. Beyond ministry, Pastor Valdez and his wife Martha operated a successful business in San Antonio for **34 years**, demonstrating the consistency and reliability that characterize effective organizational leadership. He currently serves as Associate Pastor at Temple of Praise in Texas.

#### Organizational History and Mission Alignment

FAITH Foundation was established by Reid Whitesides to address the critical shortage of affordable and transitional housing in rural South Texas communities — a gap he experienced personally and observed professionally. The Foundation was built on the conviction that **stable housing is the essential foundation for recovery from addiction, successful reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency.** This conviction is not theoretical; it is the organizing principle of every program the Foundation has designed.

FAITH Foundation is a newly established 501(c)(3) organization in its inaugural funding cycle, with initial operations supported through founder investment and church community support. While the organization does not yet have a multi-year track record of completed program outcomes, its founding leadership brings the specific expertise — construction industry knowledge, lived reentry experience, and pastoral governance — that is most directly relevant to the delivery of reentry housing services in rural Texas. The Foundation's program model is evidence-informed, drawing on HUD, VA, and peer organization documentation of best practices in transitional housing and reentry support.

#### Partnerships That Extend Organizational Reach

FAITH Foundation's service capacity is significantly extended through its active partnership network:

- **Reentry service partners** coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals upon release, connecting them to employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support
- **Recovery program partners** refer individuals completing treatment who need stable transitional housing, providing ongoing support services for dual-diagnosis participants
- **County social services agencies and local housing authorities** refer eligible families, coordinate benefits enrollment, and collaborate on case management
- **Church partners** provide volunteer labor, mentorship volunteers, congregational fundraising, and programming space at no cost to the Foundation
- **Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers** provide discounted or donated materials and units for Cornerstone Communities development
- **Land owners in rural South Texas** donate or sell land at reduced cost for community development sites
- **Bright Box Homes** supplies modular and manufactured housing units for deployment in Cornerstone Communities, with a $2,500 donation to FAITH Foundation for every home sold — creating a renewable funding mechanism tied directly to housing production

FAITH Foundation also actively accepts in-kind donations of land, building materials, modular and manufactured housing units, construction equipment and labor, furnishings, appliances, household goods, and professional services including legal, architectural, surveying, and construction management — all documented at fair market value for matching fund and audit purposes.

---

## SECTION IV: BUDGET JUSTIFICATION AND COST EFFECTIVENESS

### A Cost-Effective Model Designed for Rural Housing Markets

FAITH Foundation's budget strategy prioritizes **direct program delivery over administrative overhead**, with indirect costs maintained below **15% of total program budget**. The modular and manufactured housing deployment model — the core of the Cornerstone Communities initiative — is selected specifically because it is cost-effective in rural Texas markets where traditional construction is prohibitively expensive.

#### Cost Per Unit

Modular and manufactured housing units are deployed at **$30,000 to $60,000 per unit**, inclusive of site preparation and utility infrastructure installation. This cost structure is significantly below the per-unit cost of traditional affordable housing construction in Texas, where community development financial institutions and HUD programs routinely report per-unit costs of $150,000 to $300,000 or more for new construction. The modular approach delivers move-in-ready, durable housing at a fraction of conventional cost — a critical advantage in rural markets where construction labor is limited and material delivery costs inflate traditional budgets.

#### Budget Allocation Framework

| Category | Allocation Approach |
|---|---|
| Transitional housing unit acquisition | $30,000–$60,000 per unit; competitive open-bid procurement |
| Site preparation and utility infrastructure | Variable by site; competitively bid |
| Community common space construction | Competitively bid; in-kind labor reduction where available |
| Case management personnel | Maximum 15:1 client ratio; sliding-scale program fees partially offset |
| Housing navigator | Coordinates placement across transitional and permanent housing options |
| Transportation (rural outreach) | Program vehicles for rural case management |
| Program supplies and participant support | Direct service delivery costs |
| Financial literacy programming | Volunteer instructor model; materials cost |
| Administrative and indirect costs | Below 15% of total program budget |

#### Leveraged Funding and Cost Reduction

FAITH Foundation significantly reduces cash outlays through multiple leveraging mechanisms:

- **In-kind donations** of building materials, volunteer construction labor, and professional services (legal, architectural, surveying) reduce capital costs and are documented at fair market value
- **Donated or below-market land** from private owners, churches, and municipalities eliminates or dramatically reduces land acquisition costs
- **Bright Box Homes partnership** provides modular housing units and generates $2,500 per unit sold toward Foundation voucher funding — a renewable, self-sustaining contribution mechanism
- **Church partner volunteer labor** reduces programming delivery costs
- **Sliding-scale program fees** assessed on participant income provide partial cost recovery while maintaining affordability

**Financial Management:** All grant expenditures are tracked through QuickBooks, with quarterly financial reporting to the Board of Directors. Scott Ellis serves as Treasurer with direct oversight of financial controls. The Foundation maintains documented procedures for determining cost allowability in compliance with federal cost principles (2 CFR Subpart E), and all costs charged to this award will be allowable, allocable, and reasonable. Unallowable costs — including lobbying, entertainment, and alcohol — are excluded from all program budgets.

**Procurement Compliance:** All construction and capital purchases under this federal award will follow documented competitive procurement procedures consistent with 2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327, including open-bid construction processes for Cornerstone Communities development. Conflicts of interest are documented and avoided.

**Property Management:** Equipment and real property — including modular housing units — acquired with federal funds will be inventoried, managed, and disposed of in compliance with 2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316, including physical inventory, depreciation calculations, and federal agency approval for disposal.

[NEEDS INPUT: Provide a line-item budget for this specific grant request, including the total amount requested, allocation by budget category, and identification of any matching or leveraged funds confirmed for this grant period. The narrative framework above cannot substitute for a completed line-item budget.]

---

## SECTION V: SUSTAINABILITY AND LONG-TERM IMPACT

### A Rotating Asset Model Built for the Long Term

FAITH Foundation's sustainability is not dependent on any single grant, program fee, or donor relationship. It is built into the **rotating housing asset model** at the core of the Cornerstone Communities initiative — a structural mechanism that generates ongoing program capacity as a natural consequence of the program doing its job.

When a Cornerstone Community resident stabilizes and transitions to permanent housing — the intended outcome for every participant — their unit does not sit empty. It becomes immediately available for the next returning citizen who needs it. Each successful transition simultaneously honors a departing resident's achievement and creates capacity for the next person. The asset does not depreciate with use in program terms; it multiplies impact.

#### Diversified Revenue Architecture

FAITH Foundation actively pursues diversified funding across multiple streams to avoid dependency on any single source:

- **Program fees** assessed on a sliding scale based on participant income, ensuring affordability while generating partial cost recovery
- **Rental income** from stabilized housing units during the transitional period
- **Recurring grant funding** from federal, state, and private sources
- **Corporate sponsorships and in-kind donations**, anchored by the Bright Box Homes partnership that generates $2,500 per home sold toward Foundation voucher funding
- **Church partnerships and congregational giving** from FAITH Foundation's faith community partner network
- **Individual donor cultivation** through ongoing relationship development

Physical assets — land parcels and modular housing units — appreciate over time and reduce ongoing capital expenditure requirements. As the Cornerstone Communities portfolio grows, the Foundation's balance sheet strengthens, reducing dependence on annual grant cycles for capital costs.

#### Long-Term Affordability

FAITH Foundation is committed to maintaining the affordability and transitional housing purpose of its Cornerstone Communities units for populations in need. [NEEDS INPUT: If this grant requires a formal long-term affordability restriction or covenant on housing units funded by the award (e.g., CDBG affordability period), confirm FAITH Foundation's ability and willingness to execute such a restriction and provide specifics on the proposed covenant duration and terms.]

#### Partner Network as Sustainability Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation's sustainability is further protected by its partner network, which delivers services and capacity at reduced cost:

- Church partners contribute volunteer labor, programming space, and congregational fundraising that reduce operating overhead
- Reentry and recovery service partners maintain active referral pipelines, reducing the cost of participant recruitment and intake
- County social services agencies coordinate benefits enrollment, reducing Foundation staff time on benefits navigation
- Land donors and below-market sellers reduce capital acquisition costs for new Cornerstone Communities sites

This partner ecosystem means that FAITH Foundation's program delivery capacity is not solely a function of its cash budget — volunteer labor, donated space, in-kind materials, and partner-funded referrals extend the effective program reach well beyond what grant dollars alone would purchase.

#### Measurement and Accountability Beyond the Grant Period

FAITH Foundation measures long-term impact across five documented domains:

1. **Housing Placement** — Number of individuals transitioned from homelessness or unstable housing into transitional units and permanent housing, tracked at 30/60/90-day retention intervals
2. **Financial Stability** — Down payment assistance awards disbursed, average award amount, and percentage of recipients maintaining housing at 12 months
3. **Reentry Success** — Formerly incarcerated individuals housed, employment placement rates, and recidivism reduction compared to regional averages
4. **Recovery Outcomes** — Individuals in active recovery housed, sobriety milestones maintained, and connection rates to ongoing treatment
5. **Community Development** — Cornerstone Communities sites developed, modular units acquired and placed, occupancy rates, and successful transitions from transitional to permanent housing

All outcomes are tracked longitudinally with quarterly reporting to the Board of Directors and annual program evaluation. FAITH Foundation is committed to transparency in financial stewardship and program outcomes and will pursue third-party outcome verification as the organization scales. Annual impact reports will be published and made available to all funders, donors, and stakeholders.

---

## SECTION VI: INTENDED IMPACT

### From Release to Stability to Permanence — A Measurable Arc of Change

FAITH Foundation's Second Chance Reentry program is designed to produce measurable, sustained change in the lives of formerly incarcerated individuals and the communities to which they return. The intended impact of this grant is not counted in bed-nights or service contacts. It is counted in stable addresses, maintained employment, avoided reincarceration, and — ultimately — homes that participants own.

#### Year 1 Reentry-Specific Targets (Grant Period)

- Place formerly incarcerated individuals into stable transitional housing upon or within 90 days of release
- Achieve a **90-day housing retention rate** of 85% or higher among reentry program participants
- Connect **100% of placed participants** to case management and financial literacy programming within 30 days of placement
- Establish confirmed employer partnerships for **reentry employment referrals** within the grant period
- Achieve employment placement for **reentry participants within 90 days** of program enrollment
- Track and report on **recidivism prevention** — the percentage of reentry participants who avoid reincarceration within 24 months of program completion

[NEEDS INPUT: Insert specific participant count targets for this grant (e.g., number of formerly incarcerated individuals to be housed, number of case management slots, number of employment placements targeted) based on the grant amount requested and program capacity confirmed for this funding period.]

#### The Broader Trajectory

FAITH Foundation's long-term vision for its reentry participants extends beyond transitional stability. Within **24 months of program enrollment**, participants who complete the financial literacy curriculum, achieve sustained employment, and maintain stable transitional housing are positioned to qualify for FAITH Foundation's **Down Payment and Housing Voucher** program — transitioning from transitional tenant to permanent homeowner. This is the arc the Second Chance Reentry program is designed to produce: not temporary relief, but permanent stability.

The evidence supports this ambition. When formerly incarcerated individuals secure stable housing, the statistical probability of reincarceration decreases materially. When they build credit and savings, the probability of permanent homeownership increases. When they achieve homeownership, the probability of intergenerational stability for their children increases. FAITH Foundation's model is designed to produce each of these outcomes in sequence, and to measure each one.

#### Why This Investment Matters Beyond the Individual

Every formerly incarcerated individual who achieves stable housing and avoids reincarceration represents a measurable public benefit: reduced correctional system costs, reduced emergency services utilization, increased tax contributions from employment, and reduced law enforcement burden. The CSG Justice Center documents that housing instability directly drives reincarceration through supervision violations — meaning that housing investment is, in part, public safety investment. FAITH Foundation's Second Chance Reentry program is a cost-effective intervention at the precise point where housing, public safety, and community reintegration intersect.

A world where every individual — regardless of reentry status, economic hardship, or recovery journey — has a stable path to permanent housing is not an abstraction for FAITH Foundation. It is the operational goal behind every modular unit placed, every case management hour logged, and every financial literacy curriculum completed. This grant is an investment in that world, one participant and one stable address at a time.

---

*FAITH Foundation is a 501(c)(3) public charity, EIN 33-2640449, incorporated in Texas and serving communities across South and Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast region. All program services are available to all individuals regardless of faith background, race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status, or other protected characteristic.*

# FAITH Foundation
## Neighborhood Stabilization Program (NSP) Grant Application
### Full Project Narrative

---

**Applicant Organization:** FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope)
**EIN:** 33-2640449
**Tax Status:** 501(c)(3) Public Charity
**Service Area:** South and Central Texas; Texas Gulf Coast region, with primary focus on rural and underserved communities

**Contact:** 209 Surecast Drive, Suite 105, Burnet, Texas 78611 | (888) 497-6620

> - **[REQUIRED] Financial Management System Standards:** Confirm your financial management system (QuickBooks) produces accurate, current, and complete disclosures of financial results with effective internal controls and written cost-allowability procedures. *(2 CFR § 200.302)*
> - **[RECOMMENDED] Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA):** If recovering indirect costs on this award, confirm you have either a negotiated NICRA with your cognizant federal agency or are applying the de minimis 10% MTDC rate. *(2 CFR § 200.414)*
> - **[REQUIRED] Property Management Standards:** Confirm written procedures are in place for managing real property and equipment acquired with federal funds, including inventory and disposal requirements. *(2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316)*
> - **[REQUIRED] Federal Procurement Standards:** Confirm documented procurement procedures providing full and open competition are in place for all NSP-funded acquisitions. *(2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327)*
> - **[REQUIRED] Single Audit / OMB A-133 Threshold:** If federal expenditures reach or exceed $750,000 in any fiscal year, a Single Audit is required within 9 months of fiscal year end. *(2 CFR § 200.501)*

---

## SECTION I: STATEMENT OF COMMUNITY NEED

### The Housing Crisis in Texas: A Compounding Emergency

Texas communities — particularly rural and underserved communities across South and Central Texas and the Gulf Coast region — are experiencing a housing destabilization crisis of measurable and documented severity. FAITH Foundation exists precisely to address this crisis. The data below, drawn from federal and peer-reviewed sources, establishes the urgent need for Neighborhood Stabilization Program investment in our service area.

**Homelessness and Housing Instability in Texas**

Texas is among the states with the most acute homelessness and housing instability challenges in the nation. According to the HUD 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, nearly 28,000 Texans were experiencing homelessness during the 2024 Point-in-Time count — including 1,837 veterans. Critically, 44% of Texans experiencing homelessness were entirely unsheltered, meaning they had no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing of any kind. This unsheltered rate reflects a catastrophic shortage of affordable housing inventory in the communities FAITH Foundation serves.

Chronic homelessness in Texas is accelerating rather than declining. The Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network documents 2,594 individuals identified as chronically homeless in Texas in 2023, up from 1,949 in 2022 — an increase of 33% in a single year. Meanwhile, 4,085 veterans were served by Texas Continuums of Care as of December 2023, reflecting persistent demand that outpaces available housing capacity. Texas is among just seven states that collectively account for 64% of all people experiencing homelessness in the United States. *(HUD 2024 AHAR)*

**The Foreclosure and Vacancy Dimension**

The abandonment and foreclosure crisis intersects directly with homelessness in Texas communities. Nationally, the shortage of affordable rental units affordable and available to extremely low-income households has reached 7.3 million units. *(National Low Income Housing Coalition)* In Texas, the median home price increased over 40% since 2020, pricing out the populations FAITH Foundation serves while simultaneously reducing the pool of affordable inventory available for acquisition and rehabilitation under NSP. Vacant, abandoned, and foreclosed properties in rural South Texas communities represent both a community blight problem and an underutilized asset that, with NSP investment, can be converted into permanent affordable housing.

Formerly incarcerated individuals — a core population served by FAITH Foundation — are approximately 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population, and they make up between 23.1% and 47.8% of annual homeless shelter admissions nationally. *(Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019)* This population is almost universally excluded from private market rental housing due to criminal background screening, driving them toward informal, unstable, or unsheltered arrangements — or directly into vacant and abandoned properties — when no structured transitional housing exists.

**Veteran Housing Instability**

Texas has one of the highest concentrations of homeless veterans in the nation. Nationally, 32,882 veterans were experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2024, including 13,851 who were entirely unsheltered. *(VA 2024 PIT Count)* In Texas, veteran homelessness decreased 9.7% between 2023 and 2024 — progress that is directly attributable to targeted housing interventions. However, 1,837 Texas veterans remain without stable housing, and the system capacity to serve them is insufficient. FAITH Foundation's Veterans Path Home program addresses this gap directly within our service area.

**Single-Parent Housing Instability**

Single-parent families — particularly single mothers — face a structural homeownership gap that drives cyclical housing instability. The homeownership rate among single mothers is approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples without children. *(U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024)* Single-parent households face estimated home prices approaching five times their income, reflecting severe and persistent housing cost burden. *(NAHB Eye on Housing, 2024)* In Texas communities where affordable inventory is limited and foreclosed properties sit vacant, single-parent families are disproportionately destabilized by the same market conditions that NSP is designed to address.

**The Down Payment Barrier and the Wealth Gap**

The down payment barrier is the single most documented obstacle to homeownership for the populations FAITH Foundation serves. First-time homebuyers now represent just 21% of the market — the lowest share since NAR began tracking in 1981 — and the median age of first-time buyers has climbed to a record 40 years old. *(NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers)* Sixty-seven percent of millennials have no savings for a home down payment. *(REsimpli 2025 Market Survey)* The racial homeownership gap remains severe: the Black homeownership rate stands at 46.6% and the Hispanic homeownership rate at 49.9%, compared to 74.0% for white households. *(Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University, Q1 2024)*

For the populations FAITH Foundation serves — veterans, formerly incarcerated individuals, people in addiction recovery, and single-parent families — these barriers are compounded by criminal records, credit damage, service-connected disabilities, addiction histories, and single-income limitations. These families are not failing to achieve homeownership because of lack of aspiration. They are failing because the system was not designed to include them.

**The Gap FAITH Foundation Fills**

The data reveals two interconnected failures in the Texas housing market. First, there is insufficient affordable housing inventory — particularly in rural South and Central Texas communities where traditional construction is cost-prohibitive and foreclosed or abandoned properties sit vacant. Second, there is insufficient financial assistance to bridge the gap between housing crisis and permanent stability. Most existing programs address one side of this equation. FAITH Foundation's integrated model addresses both: the demand side through direct down payment assistance vouchers and housing counseling, and the supply side through our Cornerstone Communities land acquisition and modular housing development initiative. NSP investment directly enables FAITH Foundation to convert blighted, vacant, and foreclosed properties into permanent affordable housing — stabilizing neighborhoods while permanently housing the families most affected by those conditions.

---

## SECTION II: PROJECT DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGY

### Theory of Change

Stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery from addiction, successful community reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. FAITH Foundation's model addresses the root cause of cyclical homelessness — the absence of affordable transitional and permanent housing in rural communities. By deploying modular housing units in purpose-built Cornerstone Communities, paired with case management, peer mentorship, financial literacy instruction, and down payment assistance, individuals progress through a structured pathway from crisis to stability to permanent housing. Each successful transition frees capacity for the next participant, creating a self-sustaining cycle of community impact.

### Integrated Program Model

FAITH Foundation operates three interconnected housing programs that together deliver a complete pathway from housing instability to permanent ownership. Under this NSP application, all three programs are engaged in the acquisition, rehabilitation, and long-term stewardship of housing units in targeted Texas communities.

**Program 1: Down Payment Assistance Voucher Program**

FAITH Foundation provides direct financial assistance of up to $2,500 per qualifying family toward down payment costs on affordable housing units. The program pathway is structured as follows:

1. **Application and Eligibility Screening** — Applicants are screened for income eligibility targeting low- to moderate-income households consistent with NSP income requirements. Enrollment is prioritized for veterans, formerly incarcerated individuals, people in addiction recovery, single-parent families, and individuals experiencing or at risk of homelessness.
2. **Mandatory Financial Literacy and Credit Repair Education** — All voucher recipients must complete FAITH Foundation's financial literacy curriculum covering budgeting, credit reports, credit repair strategies, mortgage preparation, loan terms, homeownership financial planning, and avoidance of predatory lending. Courses are offered in-person and virtually. Completion is a prerequisite for voucher issuance.
3. **Housing Unit Matching** — Qualified participants are matched with available affordable housing inventory, including modular and manufactured units available through the Foundation's partnership with Bright Box Homes, as well as units acquired and rehabilitated through NSP-funded activities.
4. **Voucher Issuance and Closing Assistance** — Vouchers are issued directly at closing, with Foundation housing navigators providing support through the purchase process.

**Program 2: Transitional Housing Program**

The Transitional Housing Program places individuals exiting homelessness, incarceration, or addiction treatment into stable transitional units with case management support, financial literacy training, and peer mentorship for up to 24 months. NSP-funded acquisition and rehabilitation activities directly expand the pool of transitional units available for program participants. Case managers maintain a maximum 15-to-1 client ratio, ensuring individualized support and consistent contact with each participant throughout their housing journey.

**Program 3: Cornerstone Communities Initiative**

The Cornerstone Communities Initiative is FAITH Foundation's flagship development program and the core vehicle through which NSP investment is deployed. FAITH Foundation acquires land and deploys modular and manufactured housing units to create purpose-built micro-communities specifically designed for transitional residents in rural and underserved Texas communities.

Each Cornerstone Community includes:
- Individual residential housing units (modular and manufactured)
- Shared community spaces for programming and peer support
- On-site case management and wraparound services including recovery programming, financial literacy instruction, remote work and learning centers, community laundry facilities, and shuttle transportation
- A structured resident pathway from transitional housing through permanent homeownership

As residents stabilize and transition to permanent housing, their units become available for new participants — creating a rotating, self-sustaining cycle of community impact. NSP funding accelerates this model by enabling FAITH Foundation to acquire foreclosed and abandoned properties, rehabilitate them to habitable condition, and deploy them as Cornerstone Community units.

### NSP Activity Design

FAITH Foundation proposes to deploy NSP funding across the following eligible activities, structured in alignment with NSP program requirements:

**Activity A: Property Acquisition**
FAITH Foundation will identify, evaluate, and acquire foreclosed, abandoned, and vacant residential properties in targeted Texas communities. Property selection will prioritize parcels in neighborhoods with documented concentrations of foreclosure and abandonment, consistent with NSP area targeting requirements. All acquisitions will comply with the Uniform Relocation Act and applicable environmental review requirements prior to commitment of NSP funds. Competitive open-bid procurement will govern all real estate transactions and contractor engagements. *(2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327)*

Acquisition costs for modular and manufactured housing units range from $30,000 to $60,000 per unit based on size and configuration. Site preparation and utility infrastructure represent additional capital requirements, budgeted on a per-site basis following geotechnical and utility assessment.

**Activity B: Rehabilitation and Stabilization**
Acquired properties will be rehabilitated to habitable condition consistent with applicable local building codes, HUD housing quality standards, and accessibility requirements. Rehabilitation scopes will be determined by licensed inspection and bid through a competitive contractor selection process. Board Chair and Treasurer Scott Ellis, owner of E4 Roofing & Construction with more than 15 years of construction industry leadership, provides the Foundation with direct expertise in residential construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems — a material organizational asset for responsible rehabilitation project management.

**Activity C: Affordable Housing Placement**
Rehabilitated units will be made available to income-eligible households consistent with NSP beneficiary targeting requirements. FAITH Foundation will implement affordability covenants and deed restrictions as required by NSP regulations to ensure long-term affordability. All beneficiary households will be screened against NSP income limits. [NEEDS INPUT: Specific income targeting tier (e.g., at or below 50% AMI, 80% AMI, 120% AMI) to be confirmed against applicable NSP Notice of Funding and local area median income data.]

**Activity D: Demolition (as applicable)**
Where acquired properties are determined to be beyond cost-effective rehabilitation, FAITH Foundation will pursue clearance and site preparation for new affordable construction, consistent with NSP eligible use provisions and following required environmental review.

### Implementation Timeline

| Phase | Activity | Timeline |
|---|---|---|
| Months 1–2 | Post-award mobilization; SAM.gov compliance verification; environmental review process initiation; community needs assessment and NSP target area finalization | Months 1–2 |
| Months 2–4 | Property identification and due diligence; environmental review completion; acquisition negotiations | Months 2–4 |
| Months 3–6 | First property acquisitions; rehabilitation scope development; contractor procurement | Months 3–6 |
| Months 4–9 | Rehabilitation construction; beneficiary outreach and eligibility screening; financial literacy enrollment | Months 4–9 |
| Months 6–12 | First unit occupancy by income-eligible households; case management enrollment; voucher program activation | Months 6–12 |
| Months 10–18 | Ongoing rehabilitation and occupancy pipeline; 6-month housing retention measurement; quarterly HUD reporting | Months 10–18 |
| Month 18–24 | 12-month housing retention measurement; program evaluation; Year 1 impact report; pipeline for Phase 2 | Months 18–24 |

### Roles and Responsibilities

- **Reid Whitesides, Founder and Executive Director:** Overall program leadership, community partnerships, donor and partner relationship management, program strategy.
- **Scott Ellis, Treasurer and Board Chair:** Construction oversight, contractor procurement, budget management, financial compliance, and fiscal reporting.
- **Pastor Juan Valdez, Secretary and Protector:** Governance accountability, ethics oversight, community and church partnership coordination, mission stewardship.
- **Case Management Staff:** Participant intake and eligibility screening, case planning, housing placement coordination, 30/60/90-day and 12-month retention tracking.
- **Housing Navigator:** Coordinates placement across transitional and permanent housing options; manages voucher issuance and closing assistance.
- **Bright Box Homes (Strategic Partner):** Supplies modular and manufactured housing units at discounted rates; donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold, providing a self-reinforcing funding mechanism for the voucher program.
- **Church, Recovery, and Reentry Partners:** Referral pipeline, wraparound service coordination, volunteer labor, and community programming.

### Contingency Planning

FAITH Foundation's modular housing model provides inherent contingency flexibility. Because units are manufactured off-site, rehabilitation and installation timelines are significantly less susceptible to weather delays and on-site construction complications than traditional construction. In the event of acquisition delays due to title complications or environmental findings, FAITH Foundation will maintain a pipeline of identified alternative properties to sustain program momentum. Program vehicles for rural case management outreach ensure that case managers can maintain participant contact regardless of geographic barriers.

---

## SECTION III: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY AND EXPERIENCE

### Leadership and Qualifications

FAITH Foundation's leadership team brings together direct lived experience with housing instability, more than two decades of construction and project management expertise, and nearly 30 years of nonprofit governance and community stewardship. This combination is rare among housing nonprofits and directly relevant to NSP program requirements.

**Reid Whitesides — Founder, President, and Executive Director**

Reid Whitesides brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries. His expertise in residential construction and housing systems is directly applicable to FAITH Foundation's property acquisition, rehabilitation, and community development activities. His commitment to this work is irreducibly personal: during a long struggle with addiction, Reid spent nearly 20 years incarcerated in the State of Texas. Those experiences gave him firsthand insight into the barriers that formerly incarcerated individuals, people in recovery, and homeless individuals face when attempting to access stable housing. Today, sober for more than 15 years, Reid leads FAITH Foundation with the conviction that stable housing is the first step toward lasting change — and the operational knowledge to deliver it. He also brings technology development expertise, having built websites, software applications, and automation tools that support the Foundation's administrative infrastructure.

**Scott Ellis — Treasurer and Board Chair**

Scott Ellis is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based company he has led for more than 15 years. His experience in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems makes him uniquely qualified to oversee FAITH Foundation's NSP-funded acquisition and rehabilitation activities. Scott's understanding of construction costs, building practices, property improvement, and long-term asset stewardship ensures that NSP-funded projects are executed responsibly, efficiently, and with maximum community impact. As Treasurer and Board Chair, he provides the Foundation with financial oversight, strategic guidance, and the accountability infrastructure required for federal award compliance.

**Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary and Protector**

Pastor Juan Valdez brings nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience and a lifetime of community stewardship. His 34-year track record as a small business owner in San Antonio — operating a hair studio in the same location for three decades — reflects the consistency, reliability, and fiduciary stewardship that characterize his role in Foundation governance. As Secretary and Protector, Pastor Valdez provides governance accountability, ethics oversight, and mission stewardship that safeguard the organization's charitable purpose.

### Administrative Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation maintains its financial management through QuickBooks, providing accurate, current, and complete disclosures of financial results consistent with the financial management system standards required under 2 CFR § 200.302. The Foundation has deployed the Benavora grant management platform to support grant application tracking, reporting, and compliance management. All program data is collected through the Foundation's case management system and reported quarterly to the board of directors. Annual impact reports will be published and made available to all funders, donors, and stakeholders.

FAITH Foundation accepts and documents in-kind donations of land, building materials, modular and manufactured housing units, construction equipment, labor, furnishings, appliances, and professional services at fair market value, consistent with federal matching fund documentation requirements.

### Organizational History and Stage

FAITH Foundation was established by Reid Whitesides to address the critical shortage of affordable and transitional housing options in rural South Texas communities. The Foundation is in its inaugural funding cycle, with initial operations funded through founder investment and church community support. As a newly established 501(c)(3), FAITH Foundation has not yet produced measurable program outcomes — and this narrative is transparent about that reality. However, the Foundation has established the organizational infrastructure, leadership capacity, strategic partnerships, and program model required to responsibly deploy NSP funds and deliver measurable community impact.

The Foundation's Cornerstone Communities model represents an evidence-informed approach to rural affordable housing development that directly addresses the NSP program's core objective: stabilizing communities suffering from high levels of abandoned and foreclosed homes by converting those properties into permanent, affordable housing for income-eligible households.

**Important Note on Organizational Stage:** Reviewers should note that FAITH Foundation is a founding-stage organization with a current annual budget of $75,000. We present this information transparently and invite the funder to consider the following: our leadership brings direct construction, project management, and housing development expertise; our strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes provides a renewable, self-sustaining funding mechanism; and our modular housing model is specifically designed to deploy affordable housing at scale in rural communities where traditional development is cost-prohibitive. We are committed to the administrative compliance infrastructure required of federal award recipients and will prioritize all compliance requirements identified in this application.

---

## SECTION IV: BUDGET REASONABLENESS AND LEVERAGE

### Budget Framework

FAITH Foundation's budget allocation prioritizes direct program delivery over administrative overhead, with indirect costs maintained below 15% of total program budget. The following framework governs NSP fund deployment:

| Budget Category | Description | Estimated Cost Range |
|---|---|---|
| **Property Acquisition** | Purchase of foreclosed, abandoned, and vacant residential properties in NSP target areas | [NEEDS INPUT: Total acquisition budget based on grant award amount and target unit count] |
| **Rehabilitation and Construction** | Rehabilitation of acquired properties to habitable condition; site preparation and utility infrastructure | $30,000–$60,000 per unit (modular); site prep costs vary by parcel |
| **Down Payment Assistance Vouchers** | Direct financial assistance of up to $2,500 per qualifying household | $2,500 per voucher |
| **Case Management and Supportive Services** | Personnel costs for case managers (15:1 client ratio maximum) and housing navigator | [NEEDS INPUT: Personnel cost detail based on grant award amount] |
| **Financial Literacy Programming** | Instructor costs, materials, venue, and virtual platform costs | [NEEDS INPUT: Per-cohort cost detail] |
| **Program Vehicles** | Transportation for rural case management outreach | [NEEDS INPUT: Vehicle cost or lease detail] |
| **Indirect / Administrative** | Accounting (QuickBooks), reporting, legal, compliance — capped below 15% of total program budget | ≤15% of total program costs |

### Cost Effectiveness

FAITH Foundation's modular housing model is specifically designed to reduce per-unit costs below those of traditional construction — an important factor in demonstrating NSP budget reasonableness. Modular and manufactured housing units from Bright Box Homes and comparable suppliers range from $30,000 to $60,000 per unit, compared to typical new construction costs that are substantially higher in Texas markets. This cost advantage means more units can be produced per NSP dollar invested, maximizing the number of households stabilized per award.

In-kind donations of building materials, volunteer construction labor, and professional services are documented at fair market value and reduce cash outlays significantly. Land donations from private owners, churches, municipalities, and developers eliminate land acquisition costs entirely for Cornerstone Communities development, freeing NSP funds for rehabilitation and housing unit deployment.

### Leverage and Matching Funds

FAITH Foundation's Bright Box Homes partnership provides a self-sustaining, renewable funding mechanism: Bright Box Homes donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold through any channel. This private sector partnership constitutes a recurring non-federal revenue stream that supplements NSP investment and demonstrates the Foundation's commitment to leveraged, diversified funding.

Additional leverage sources include:
- Church partner congregational fundraising and in-kind labor
- Building material supplier discounts and donations
- Land owner donations and below-market-rate land sales
- Sliding-scale program fees from participants with income
- Rental income from stabilized housing units

[NEEDS INPUT: Specific dollar amounts for confirmed matching funds, in-kind contributions, or other leveraged resources available to apply to this NSP application. A 1:1 or greater local match, even when not required, significantly strengthens the application's competitiveness on federal reviewer rubrics.]

---

## SECTION V: BENEFICIARY TARGETING AND AFFORDABILITY

### Income Eligibility and Targeting

FAITH Foundation's programs are designed to serve economically disadvantaged individuals and families who are systematically excluded from market-rate housing. All NSP-funded housing units will be made available to income-eligible households consistent with NSP program requirements. Beneficiary targeting prioritizes:

- **Military veterans** experiencing or at risk of homelessness
- **Formerly incarcerated individuals** reentering society
- **Individuals in addiction recovery** transitioning from treatment programs
- **Single-parent families**, particularly single mothers with dependent children
- **Individuals experiencing homelessness** or at imminent risk of homelessness

These populations are concentrated among extremely low-income and very low-income households — precisely the households NSP affordability requirements are designed to serve. The homeownership rate among single mothers is approximately 34%; formerly incarcerated individuals face a homelessness rate 10 times higher than the general population; and veteran homelessness, while declining, remains a documented crisis in Texas communities.

[NEEDS INPUT: Specific AMI targeting tier (e.g., at or below 50% AMI, 80% AMI, 120% AMI) to be confirmed against the applicable NSP Notice of Funding and the local area median income for targeted Texas counties. This must be explicitly stated in the final application to satisfy NSP beneficiary targeting requirements.]

### Affordability Covenants and Long-Term Stewardship

FAITH Foundation is committed to ensuring that all NSP-funded units remain affordable and accessible to income-eligible households over the long term. Affordability covenants and deed restrictions will be recorded on all acquired and rehabilitated properties consistent with NSP regulatory requirements. FAITH Foundation's rotating housing asset model — in which units occupied by transitioning residents become available for new participants as those residents achieve permanent housing stability — is inherently aligned with the long-term affordability stewardship that NSP requires.

[NEEDS INPUT: Specific affordability period (e.g., 5, 10, 15, or 20 years depending on activity type and NSP requirements) to be confirmed against applicable NSP regulations and included in the final application.]

### Beneficiary Projections

Based on FAITH Foundation's Year 1 program targets and the housing unit capacity described in this application:

- **Year 1:** 15 households placed in transitional or permanent NSP-funded housing; 10 down payment assistance vouchers distributed ($25,000 in direct assistance); 25 households enrolled in financial literacy and homeownership counseling
- **Year 2:** 40 housing vouchers distributed ($100,000 in direct assistance); 20 families graduated from homeownership counseling into active homebuyers; 90% housing retention rate target at 12 months

## SECTION VI: COMPLIANCE AND REGULATORY ADHERENCE

FAITH Foundation is committed to full compliance with all NSP regulatory requirements and applicable federal standards. The following compliance commitments are incorporated into our program design:

### Environmental Review

Prior to commitment of NSP funds for any specific property acquisition or rehabilitation, FAITH Foundation will complete the required environmental review process in accordance with 24 CFR Part 58 (or Part 50, as applicable). No NSP funds will be committed to or expended on a specific property until the environmental review record is complete and an Authority to Use Grant Funds (AUGF) has been issued. Environmental review documentation will be maintained in the project file for each property.

### Fair Housing

FAITH Foundation affirms its commitment to full compliance with the Fair Housing Act, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and all other applicable civil rights laws. Our programs are designed to affirmatively further fair housing by specifically targeting populations — including Black veterans, Hispanic families, formerly incarcerated individuals, and single mothers — who face documented disparate impacts from housing discrimination and market exclusion. All marketing and outreach for NSP-funded housing opportunities will be conducted in a manner consistent with Affirmative Fair Housing Marketing Plan requirements.

### Davis-Bacon Act

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirm whether NSP-funded rehabilitation activities will trigger Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements (applicable to construction contracts over $2,000 for NSP-assisted properties). If triggered, document your plan for wage rate compliance, certified payroll submission, and contractor certification.]

### HUD Reporting and Data Management

FAITH Foundation will comply with all HUD reporting requirements for NSP-funded activities, including quarterly financial and performance reporting through the Disaster Recovery Grant Reporting (DRGR) system or applicable reporting platform. All program data will be collected through the Foundation's case management system. Financial management is maintained through QuickBooks, consistent with 2 CFR § 200.302 financial management system standards.

### Federal Cost Principles (2 CFR 200 Subpart E)

All costs charged to this NSP award will be allowable, allocable, and reasonable, consistently applied, and fully documented. Unallowable costs — including lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties — will not be charged to this award. Indirect costs will be maintained below 15% of total program budget and applied consistently across all funding sources.

### Administrative Requirements (2 CFR 200 Subpart D)

FAITH Foundation will maintain internal controls, comply with all federal statutes and regulations, and adhere to all terms and conditions of this award. Performance and financial reports will be submitted on schedule. All records will be retained for a minimum of three years following the close of the award period, consistent with 2 CFR § 200.333. Any budget modifications requiring prior approval will be submitted to the awarding agency before implementation.

### Property Management (2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316)

Real property and equipment acquired with NSP funds will be managed according to federal property management standards. FAITH Foundation will maintain a written property inventory, conduct physical inventories at least every two years, and obtain federal approval prior to any disposition of NSP-funded assets. Depreciation will be calculated and applied as required.

### Procurement (2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327)

All procurements under this NSP award will be conducted through documented procedures providing full and open competition. Construction and rehabilitation contracts will be competitively bid. Potential conflicts of interest will be disclosed and documented. FAITH Foundation's Treasurer and Board Chair, Scott Ellis, will recuse himself from any procurement decisions involving E4 Roofing & Construction or any entity in which he holds a financial interest, consistent with conflict-of-interest requirements. [NEEDS INPUT: Confirm written conflict-of-interest policy exists and is on file with the board.]

### SAM.gov and UEI

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirm active SAM.gov registration and provide UEI number for inclusion on the application. Confirm annual renewal is current.]

### Single Audit

FAITH Foundation's current annual operating budget of $75,000 is substantially below the $750,000 federal expenditure threshold that triggers Single Audit requirements under 2 CFR § 200.501. Should NSP award funding cause total federal expenditures to reach or exceed $750,000 in any fiscal year, FAITH Foundation will engage an independent auditor and submit the required Single Audit to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end.

---

## SECTION VII: SUSTAINABILITY

FAITH Foundation's long-term sustainability is built on a rotating housing asset model that is structurally aligned with the NSP program's community stabilization objectives. As residents transition from Cornerstone Communities into permanent housing, their units become available for new participants — creating continuous housing capacity without requiring continuous capital investment at the same scale.

The Foundation's Bright Box Homes partnership provides the renewable, private-sector funding engine that drives this model. Bright Box Homes donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold through any channel, funding the vouchers that help the next family into a home — a self-reinforcing cycle of community investment directly tied to new home construction activity in the market.

Additional sustainability mechanisms include:
- Sliding-scale program fees based on participant income
- Rental income from stabilized housing units
- Recurring grant funding from federal, state, and private sources
- Corporate sponsorships and in-kind donations
- Church partnerships and congregational giving
- Individual donor cultivation

Physical assets — land parcels and modular housing units — appreciate over time and reduce ongoing capital expenditure requirements. The Foundation actively pursues diversified funding across government grants, private foundations, corporate giving programs, faith-based funders, and community development financial institutions to avoid dependency on any single source. Operational costs are controlled through volunteer labor, donated materials, and shared administrative infrastructure across program sites.

Within five years, FAITH Foundation intends to publish independently verified annual impact reports, establish a second Bright Box Homes-style corporate partnership generating recurring voucher funding, expand the Cornerstone Communities model beyond initial Texas communities, and achieve a 30% homeownership conversion rate among participants enrolled in Year 1. These outcomes will establish the evidence base for continued federal, state, and private investment in the Foundation's model.

---
