# FAITH Foundation
## Homeless Veterans Reintegration Program (HVRP)
### Grant Narrative — Full Proposal

**Organization:** FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope)
**EIN:** 33-2640449
**Service Area:** South & Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast Region
**Contact:** 888-497-6620 | 209 Surecast Drive, Suite 105, Burnet, Texas 78611

---

> **Compliance Notice to Applicant — Review Before Submission**
> The following federal compliance items require attention prior to submitting this application or accepting any federal award. These are flagged throughout the narrative where relevant and summarized here for immediate action:
> - **[REQUIRED] Unique Entity Identifier (UEI):** Confirm UEI is assigned and active through SAM.gov. The UEI replaced the DUNS number in April 2022 and is required on all federal grant applications. (2 CFR § 200.1)
> - **[REQUIRED] SAM.gov Active Registration:** Verify registration is current and will not lapse during the award period. Lapsed registration can delay or disqualify an award. (2 CFR § 200.206)
> - **[REQUIRED] Financial Management System Standards:** FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks for accounting. Confirm the system provides accurate, current, and complete disclosure of financial results; identifies sources and application of funds; and supports written procedures for cost allowability determinations. (2 CFR § 200.302)
> - **[RECOMMENDED] Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA):** If no negotiated rate exists, FAITH Foundation may apply the de minimis rate of 10% of modified total direct costs (MTDC). Document this election in the budget narrative. (2 CFR § 200.414)
> - **[REQUIRED] Single Audit / OMB A-133 Threshold:** If federal expenditures reach or exceed $750,000 in any fiscal year, an independent single audit must be submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end. (2 CFR § 200.501)
> - **[REQUIRED] Federal Cost Principles (2 CFR 200 Subpart E):** All costs charged to this award must be allowable, allocable, and reasonable. Unallowable costs include lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties.
> - **[REQUIRED] Administrative Requirements (2 CFR 200 Subpart D):** Maintain records for a minimum of 3 years; submit required performance and financial reports; obtain prior approval for significant budget modifications.
> - **[REQUIRED] Property Management Standards:** Any equipment or real property acquired with federal funds must be inventoried, tracked, and disposed of in accordance with federal standards. (2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316)
> - **[REQUIRED] Federal Procurement Standards:** All procurements under this award must follow documented, competitive procedures. (2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327)

---

## SECTION 1: STATEMENT OF NEED

### The Scale of Veteran Homelessness in Texas

Veteran homelessness is not a historical artifact — it is an ongoing crisis demanding urgent, targeted response. On a single night in January 2024, **32,882 veterans were experiencing homelessness across the United States**, including **13,851 sleeping unsheltered** — without access to emergency shelter, safe haven, or transitional housing. (VA 2024 Point-in-Time Count) While this figure represents the lowest count since federal measurement began in 2009, it nonetheless reflects tens of thousands of men and women who answered their nation's call and returned home to find no stable place to land.

Texas stands at the center of this crisis. **In the 2024 Point-in-Time count, 1,837 veterans were experiencing homelessness in Texas**, a 9.7% decrease from 2,036 in 2023 — progress that is real but insufficient. (VA/HUD 2024 PIT Count) Texas Continuums of Care served **4,085 veterans** as of December 2023, up from 3,962 in 2022, indicating that demand is growing even as point-in-time counts fluctuate. (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network) Of the nearly 28,000 Texans experiencing homelessness overall, **44% were unsheltered** — meaning they had no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing of any kind. (HUD 2024 AHAR, cited in Texas HB 158)

Texas, California, and Florida carry the highest concentrations of homeless veterans in the nation. (Mission Roll Call, 2024) The rural and underserved communities of South and Central Texas — FAITH Foundation's primary service area — face compounded challenges: fewer shelter beds, fewer VA-affiliated service providers, greater distances to medical and employment resources, and a near-total absence of affordable transitional housing inventory purpose-built for veterans exiting homelessness.

### Who These Veterans Are: Subpopulations and Distinct Barriers

Not all homeless veterans face identical circumstances, and effective reintegration requires understanding the specific barriers each subpopulation encounters.

**Chronically homeless veterans** represent a population with the most severe and longest-duration housing instability. Texas documented **2,594 chronically homeless individuals in 2023, up from 1,949 in 2022** — a 33% single-year increase. (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network) Veterans experiencing chronic homelessness often carry co-occurring mental health conditions, substance use disorders, and service-connected disabilities that compound standard barriers to housing access.

**Black veterans** are dramatically overrepresented in the homeless veteran population. While Black Americans comprise 14% of the overall veteran population, they represent **31% of homeless veterans nationally**. (Mission Roll Call, 2024) Systemic inequities in wealth accumulation, homeownership history, and access to VA benefits compound the standard reintegration barriers these veterans face.

**Veterans with service-connected disabilities** face compounding barriers: limited physical mobility affecting employment options, medical appointment demands that conflict with work schedules, and housing stock that frequently fails to meet accessibility requirements.

**Veterans transitioning from incarceration** face a dual barrier. Formerly incarcerated individuals are approximately **10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population**. (National Low Income Housing Coalition; Prison Policy Initiative) For veterans who have served time, this risk is compounded by the loss of VA benefits during incarceration and the challenge of rebuilding eligibility and access upon release.

**Female veterans**, while not separately enumerated in the provided Texas data, represent a growing share of the homeless veteran population nationally and face gender-specific barriers including domestic violence history, childcare obligations, and shelter environments that can be unsafe or inaccessible. [NEEDS INPUT: Local or state data on female veteran homelessness rates in the Texas service area, if available from VA regional office or Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network]

### Why Standard Homeless Programs Fall Short for Veterans

Veterans are not simply civilians who happen to be homeless. Their pathways into housing instability are shaped by military service, and their pathways out must account for the same. Standard homeless programs typically lack:

- **VA benefits navigation expertise** — HUD-VASH vouchers, VA Supportive Services for Veteran Families (SSVF) grants, and service-connected disability compensation are underutilized by veterans who do not have a skilled navigator helping them access what they have earned.
- **Military culture competency** — Veterans often resist help framed as charity. Programs structured around mutual accountability, peer mentorship from fellow veterans, and clear milestones align with military culture and produce better engagement and retention.
- **Employment bridges from military to civilian** — Military occupational specialties do not map neatly onto civilian credentialing systems. Veterans need translators — literally and professionally — who can convert military experience into civilian employment credentials.
- **Rural-accessible housing** — Most permanent supportive housing and HUD-VASH placements are concentrated in urban centers. Veterans in rural South and Central Texas have no equivalent infrastructure.

FAITH Foundation's Veterans Path Home program was designed to address each of these gaps directly, within an integrated continuum that moves veterans from crisis to stable, permanent housing.

### The Affordable Housing Gap Underneath the Crisis

The veteran homelessness crisis does not exist in isolation from the broader housing affordability emergency. The United States faces a shortage of **7.3 million rental units** affordable and available to extremely low-income households. (National Low Income Housing Coalition) First-time homebuyers now account for just **21% of the housing market** — the lowest share since tracking began in 1981. (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers) The median age of a first-time homebuyer has reached a record **40 years old**. (NAR 2025 Profile)

For veterans who have lost years to service, deployment, disability, or incarceration, this market does not wait. The down payment gap, compounded by criminal record screening, disability income limitations, and credit damage from periods of instability, makes homeownership functionally inaccessible without direct intervention. **74.2% of homeowner households with incomes below $30,000 are cost-burdened**, paying more than 30% of income on housing — the highest rate in over 20 years. (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University)

This is the gap FAITH Foundation exists to close — not just for the duration of a crisis, but permanently, through a structured pathway from emergency shelter to transitional housing to permanent homeownership.

---

## SECTION 2: PROGRAM DESIGN — VETERANS PATH HOME

### Overview and Theory of Change

FAITH Foundation's Homeless Veterans Reintegration Program (HVRP) is delivered through our **Veterans Path Home** program, an integrated continuum of services that addresses veteran homelessness at every stage — from initial crisis contact through permanent housing placement and long-term stability.

Our theory of change is grounded in the evidence base and the lived experience of our leadership: **stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery from addiction, successful community reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency.** Veterans experiencing homelessness cannot hold jobs they cannot get to, cannot attend VA appointments they have no address for, and cannot rebuild relationships without a stable, private space to call home. Every intervention FAITH Foundation delivers is designed to establish and maintain that foundation — and then build upon it toward permanent ownership.

The model operates through five sequential but flexible stages:

**Stage 1 — Outreach and Intake**
FAITH Foundation staff and volunteers conduct direct outreach to veterans in unsheltered locations, VA medical facilities, county jails, and partner referral networks. Veterans are assessed for housing need, VA benefits status, employment history, substance use and mental health history, and legal barriers to housing. Intake is conducted in a trauma-informed, culturally competent manner designed to meet veterans where they are — not where a program assumes they should be.

**Stage 2 — Emergency Bridge Housing**
Veterans in immediate crisis are connected to emergency bridge housing assistance — rapid rental and deposit assistance that prevents the immediate, acute harm of unsheltered homelessness while the longer-term reintegration plan is developed. This stage is intentionally brief and action-oriented, designed to create the stability necessary for a veteran to engage meaningfully with employment and housing navigation services.

**Stage 3 — Transitional Housing with Wraparound Services**
Veterans are placed into FAITH Foundation's transitional housing units — including purpose-built Cornerstone Communities units — for up to 24 months. During this period, participants receive:

- **Individualized case management** with a dedicated case manager maintaining a maximum 15-to-1 client ratio
- **VA benefits navigation** — enrollment or re-enrollment in VA healthcare, service-connected disability claims support, HUD-VASH voucher application assistance, and SSVF coordination
- **Employment services** (detailed in Section 3)
- **Financial literacy and credit-building education** — hands-on budgeting, credit report review, credit repair strategies, mortgage preparation, and homeownership financial planning, offered in-person and virtually
- **Peer mentorship** from trained veteran mentors who have completed the program or bring relevant lived experience
- **Recovery support** for veterans with co-occurring substance use disorders, including connection to sober living resources, on-site support groups where available, and recovery stability tracking
- **Mental health and trauma-informed care referrals** coordinated with VA mental health services and community behavioral health partners

[NEEDS INPUT: Names of specific VA medical centers, Vet Centers, or VA Regional Offices with which FAITH Foundation has or is pursuing formal partnership MOUs — reviewers will award higher marks for documented VA coordination]

**Stage 4 — Permanent Housing Linkage and Down Payment Assistance**
Veterans who have stabilized in transitional housing and achieved the financial readiness milestones defined in their individualized plan become eligible for FAITH Foundation's **Down Payment and Housing Voucher** program. Through our strategic partnership with **Bright Box Homes**, FAITH Foundation provides $2,500 vouchers toward down payment costs on affordable modular and manufactured housing units. This mechanism converts charitable giving directly into permanent housing assets and creates a self-reinforcing funding cycle: every Bright Box Homes unit sold generates a $2,500 contribution to FAITH Foundation, funding the next family's voucher.

Veterans who are not yet ready for homeownership are linked to permanent rental housing through landlord partnerships, HUD-VASH vouchers, and housing navigation services, with an ongoing relationship maintained to support future homeownership preparation.

**Stage 5 — Long-Term Stability and Follow-Up**
Housing retention is tracked at 30, 60, 90 days, 6 months, and 12 months post-placement. Case managers conduct follow-up contacts at each interval. Veterans who experience instability triggers — job loss, health crisis, relationship breakdown — receive rapid re-engagement through FAITH Foundation's case management system before those triggers cascade into housing loss.

### Cornerstone Communities: The Supply-Side Solution

HVRP participants in FAITH Foundation's service area benefit from the Cornerstone Communities initiative — purpose-built transitional micro-communities sited on donated or acquired rural land, developed using modular and manufactured housing units. Each Cornerstone Community includes individual residential units, shared community spaces, on-site case management access, recovery programming, remote work and learning resources, and shuttle transportation for rural access.

The Cornerstone Communities model is uniquely suited to rural South and Central Texas, where the affordable housing inventory available to homeless veterans is functionally nonexistent. Modular units can be sited on donated land without the delays and costs of traditional construction, bringing housing solutions directly to underserved communities rather than concentrating resources in urban centers where many veterans do not want to or cannot relocate.

As veterans transition to permanent housing, their Cornerstone units become available for incoming participants — creating a rotating capacity model that extends the impact of each unit indefinitely.

### Logic Model Summary

| **Inputs** | **Activities** | **Outputs** | **Short-Term Outcomes** | **Long-Term Impact** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grant funding | Veteran outreach and intake | Veterans screened and enrolled | Veterans stably housed within 30 days | Veterans in permanent housing |
| Bright Box Homes partnership | Emergency bridge housing | Bridge housing placements | VA benefits accessed | Veterans achieving homeownership |
| Modular housing units | Transitional housing placement | Transitional units occupied | Employment secured | Long-term housing retention |
| Case management staff | VA benefits navigation | Benefits enrolled | Financial readiness improved | Reduced veteran homelessness in service area |
| Volunteer mentors | Employment services | Jobs placed | Peer mentorship relationships active | Reduced recidivism and recovery relapse |
| Church and VSO partnerships | Financial literacy education | Graduates of financial literacy | Credit scores improved | Self-sustaining Cornerstone Communities |
| QuickBooks financial system | Down payment voucher issuance | Vouchers disbursed | Permanent housing secured | Replicable model for rural Texas |

---

## SECTION 3: EMPLOYMENT AND REINTEGRATION SERVICES

### Veteran-Centered Employment Strategy

Employment is not a standalone service in FAITH Foundation's HVRP — it is an integrated component of every veteran's individualized reintegration plan, developed at intake and updated throughout the transitional housing period. The Foundation's approach to veteran employment recognizes that **military occupational experience is an asset that civilian employers frequently fail to recognize**, and that the role of the employment services provider is to bridge that translation gap.

**Individualized Employment Plans (IEPs)** are developed for each enrolled veteran within the first 30 days of program participation. Each IEP documents the veteran's military occupational specialty (MOS) or rate, prior civilian employment history, documented skills and certifications, employment barriers (criminal record, disability, gaps in employment history, geographic limitations), target employment sector, credential or training needs, and realistic 90-day employment placement milestones.

**Military-to-Civilian Skills Translation** is a core component of IEP development. Founder Reid Whitesides brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, and housing-related industries — sectors that absorb a significant share of veteran job-seekers and where military skills in logistics, operations, equipment operation, and team leadership translate directly. The Foundation's board also includes Scott Ellis, owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based firm he has operated for more than 15 years. Scott's direct industry access creates a natural pipeline between veteran job-seekers with construction and skilled trades backgrounds and an employer who understands military culture.

**Employer Partnerships:** FAITH Foundation's Year 1 targets include establishing partnerships with a minimum of 3 local employers specifically for reentry and recovery program participants, including veterans. These partnerships are structured to provide:
- Committed job interview slots for program completers
- On-the-job mentorship from veteran employees where available
- Accommodation awareness for veterans with service-connected disabilities
- Feedback loops to FAITH Foundation case managers supporting 90-day employment retention

[NEEDS INPUT: Letters of commitment or MOUs from employer partners for HVRP — reviewers assign significantly higher employment services scores when employer partnerships are documented with signed letters. E4 Roofing & Construction (Scott Ellis) should be approached as a founding employer partner and their commitment documented prior to submission.]

**Vocational Training and Credentialing:** For veterans whose target employment requires additional credentialing, FAITH Foundation connects participants with community college workforce programs, Texas Workforce Commission resources, and VA Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (VR&E) services. Case managers are responsible for identifying and removing barriers to enrollment, including transportation (addressed through program vehicles for rural outreach) and documentation.

[NEEDS INPUT: Specific vocational training partners or community college partnerships in the South/Central Texas service area — if any exist or are in development, document them here to strengthen this section]

**Veterans with Disabilities:** Veterans with service-connected disabilities receive employment planning that specifically accounts for their documented limitations and accommodations needs. Case managers coordinate with VA Vocational Rehabilitation counselors and, where applicable, with employers willing to provide reasonable accommodations. FAITH Foundation's commitment to serving all veterans regardless of disability status is non-negotiable.

**90-Day Employment Retention:** Employment placement is not the finish line. FAITH Foundation tracks employed veterans at 30, 60, and 90 days post-placement. Case managers maintain contact with both the veteran and, with consent, the employer during this window. Veterans who lose employment during this period receive immediate re-engagement and a revised IEP.

**Year 2 Target:** Place 15 reentry and recovery participants — including veterans — into stable employment within 90 days of program enrollment, as documented in FAITH Foundation's impact framework.

---

## SECTION 4: HOUSING STABILITY PLAN

### A Complete Continuum — Not a Single Intervention

FAITH Foundation's housing stability plan for HVRP participants is not a single program component — it is a complete continuum from the night of crisis contact through permanent homeownership. Each stage is designed to connect to the next, with no gaps in case management or service access between transitions.

**Emergency Bridge Housing (Days 1–30)**
Veterans identified as homeless or at immediate risk of homelessness receive rapid rental and deposit assistance. This intervention is designed to be deployed within 48–72 hours of enrollment, creating immediate housing stability that allows the veteran to engage with longer-term services. Emergency bridge assistance is funded through FAITH Foundation's direct assistance budget and is not contingent on employment status, VA enrollment, or any other qualifying criterion beyond verified veteran status and housing need.

**Transitional Housing (Months 1–24)**
Veterans transition from emergency placement into FAITH Foundation's transitional housing units, including Cornerstone Communities modular units in South and Central Texas. Transitional housing participants:
- Maintain a lease or occupancy agreement with FAITH Foundation
- Pay program fees on a sliding scale based on income, ensuring no veteran is excluded for inability to pay while creating a contribution to long-term sustainability
- Receive on-site or proximate case management
- Participate in financial literacy education, employment services, and peer mentorship
- Develop a individualized housing stability plan with target milestones for permanent housing transition

**Coordination with VA Resources**
FAITH Foundation's case managers assist veterans in accessing the full menu of VA housing resources available to eligible participants:
- **HUD-VASH (HUD-VA Supportive Housing):** Case managers support veterans in applying for HUD-VASH vouchers and connect them with local Public Housing Authorities managing the program.
- **SSVF (Supportive Services for Veteran Families):** Coordination with SSVF grantees operating in FAITH Foundation's service area for eligible veterans.
- **VA Healthcare Enrollment:** Many veterans experiencing homelessness have allowed their VA healthcare enrollment to lapse. FAITH Foundation's intake process includes healthcare enrollment as a standard component.

[NEEDS INPUT: Names of specific SSVF grantees operating in FAITH Foundation's service area (South/Central Texas and Gulf Coast) with whom coordination exists or is being established — reviewers look for named coordination partners]

**Veterans Service Organization (VSO) Partnerships**
FAITH Foundation maintains active relationships with veterans service organizations that provide referral, peer support, and VA benefits navigation. These partnerships extend FAITH Foundation's reach into the veteran community and ensure that veterans who may not self-identify as homeless or housing-insecure are connected to services.

[NEEDS INPUT: Names of specific VSOs with which FAITH Foundation has formal or informal referral relationships — e.g., American Legion posts, VFW posts, DAV chapters, or Texas Veterans Commission contacts in the service area]

**Permanent Housing Linkage**
Veterans completing the transitional housing phase are connected to permanent housing through one of two pathways:
1. **Homeownership via Down Payment Voucher:** Veterans who have achieved financial readiness milestones — improved credit, documented income, completed financial literacy curriculum — receive FAITH Foundation's $2,500 down payment assistance voucher for use toward an affordable modular housing unit through Bright Box Homes. This pathway moves veterans from renter to owner and begins the process of wealth accumulation that makes permanent stability self-sustaining.
2. **Permanent Rental Placement:** Veterans not yet ready for ownership are connected to permanent rental housing through landlord partnerships and HUD-VASH voucher placement, with an active ongoing relationship to support future homeownership preparation.

**12-Month Housing Retention**
FAITH Foundation tracks housing retention at 90 days, 6 months, and 12 months post-permanent-placement. Year 2 targets include achieving a **90% housing retention rate among voucher recipients at the 12-month mark.** Case managers maintain contact at each interval and deploy rapid re-engagement for veterans at risk of losing housing before loss occurs.

---

## SECTION 5: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY

### Leadership and Lived Experience

FAITH Foundation's capacity to serve homeless veterans is rooted in the leadership team's direct, personal understanding of the barriers veterans and marginalized populations face — not as observers, but as individuals who have lived through addiction, incarceration, and housing instability and come out the other side into stable, productive lives.

**Reid Whitesides — Founder, President, and Executive Director** brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries. His commitment to this mission is deeply personal: during a long struggle with addiction, Reid spent nearly 20 years incarcerated in the State of Texas. Today, he has been sober for more than 15 years. His firsthand experience navigating the barriers to housing, employment, and community reintegration after incarceration and addiction gives him an insight into program design that no credential can replicate. Reid also brings a passion for technology, having developed websites, software applications, and automation tools that support the Foundation's operational infrastructure, including the Benavora grant management platform.

**Scott Ellis — Treasurer and Board Chair** is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based company with more than 15 years of operation under his leadership. His experience in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems provides the Foundation with direct industry expertise for evaluating housing-related opportunities, managing modular housing development costs, and ensuring that capital projects are executed responsibly. Scott has been a resident of Georgetown, Texas for more than 24 years and brings deep community rootedness to the Foundation's governance.

**Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary and Protector** provides spiritual oversight, governance accountability, and mission stewardship. With more than 40 years of Christian faith and nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience, Pastor Valdez brings governance integrity and ethical leadership. His ministry has extended across the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. Together with his wife Martha, he operated a successful business in San Antonio for 34 years — a record of consistency, reliability, and community investment that characterizes his service to the Foundation. He currently serves as an Associate Pastor at Temple of Praise in Texas.

### Veteran-Centered Program Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation's Veterans Path Home program is specifically designed around the distinct needs of veterans experiencing homelessness. While FAITH Foundation is in its inaugural funding cycle, the program model is built on evidence-based frameworks documented by HUD, the VA, and peer organizations operating comparable veteran housing and reintegration programs.

[NEEDS INPUT: If any current staff members are veterans or have military service history, this should be stated explicitly here — veteran peer specialist models are heavily weighted in HVRP scoring. If a veteran peer specialist role is planned, describe it.]

**Case Management Infrastructure:** FAITH Foundation's budget framework supports case managers operating at a maximum **15-to-1 client ratio**, ensuring that each veteran in the program receives individualized, consistent attention. A dedicated housing navigator coordinates placement across transitional and permanent housing options. All program data is collected through FAITH Foundation's case management system and reported quarterly to the board of directors.

**Financial Management:** FAITH Foundation uses **QuickBooks** for financial management and accounting, providing accurate, current, and complete disclosure of financial results and source-and-application-of-funds tracking as required by 2 CFR § 200.302. The Foundation maintains indirect costs below 15% of total program budget. Scott Ellis's 15+ years of business financial leadership provides oversight integrity.

**Technology Infrastructure:** FAITH Foundation has deployed the **Benavora grant management platform** for grant application tracking and reporting. Supabase is used for data management. These systems support the performance reporting requirements associated with federal awards.

**Peer Mentorship:** FAITH Foundation recruits and trains volunteers for mentorship, financial literacy instruction, and community outreach. Year 1 targets include recruiting and training **20 volunteers** in these roles. Peer mentorship by individuals with shared lived experience — including veterans who have completed reintegration successfully — is a structural component of the program model.

**Faith-Based, Inclusive Service Model:** FAITH Foundation is rooted in Christian principles of grace, redemption, and service. All programs are open to all individuals regardless of religious affiliation. Faith-based programming is offered as an available resource, not a requirement for participation. The Foundation serves all veterans regardless of race, gender, religion, disability status, or background.

### Founding Stage Transparency

FAITH Foundation is in its inaugural funding cycle, with initial operations funded through founder investment and church community support. The organization has not yet produced measurable program outcomes. All projected outcomes in this narrative are based on evidence-based models documented by HUD, the VA, and peer organizations operating similar programs, and represent the targets FAITH Foundation commits to pursuing with the support of this award. FAITH Foundation will pursue third-party outcome verification beginning in Year 2 of operations.

**[COMPLIANCE NOTE]:** As a new organization in its inaugural funding cycle, FAITH Foundation's current annual budget is $75,000. If awarded federal funding under this HVRP application, the organization must confirm SAM.gov active registration and UEI assignment prior to award. If total federal expenditures reach or exceed $750,000 in any fiscal year, a single audit will be required. (2 CFR § 200.501) FAITH Foundation should also confirm or elect an indirect cost rate approach (de minimis 10% of MTDC or negotiated NICRA) prior to budget finalization.

---

## SECTION 6: INTENDED IMPACT AND PERFORMANCE METRICS

### HVRP-Aligned Performance Targets

FAITH Foundation's performance framework for this HVRP award is aligned with the standard HVRP performance measures established by the Department of Labor and VA:

[NEEDS INPUT: The specific number of veterans FAITH Foundation commits to serve under this HVRP award — this is the single most critical quantitative target in the application and must be based on the award amount requested and the cost-per-veteran-served calculation in the budget. Insert the specific served figure here.]

|---|---|---|
| Veterans enrolled in HVRP services | [NEEDS INPUT: Total # based on budget] | Program year |

**Note to Applicant:** HVRP applications are scored heavily on specific, quantifiable performance targets aligned with DOL HVRP performance standards. The targets marked [NEEDS INPUT] above are essential to a competitive application and must be populated with realistic figures derived from the requested budget amount and cost-per-veteran-served calculation. A general benchmark: competitive HVRP grantees typically target an entered employment rate of 60% or higher and a 90-day employment retention rate above 75%.

### How FAITH Foundation Measures Impact

FAITH Foundation tracks and reports impact across five domains, measured longitudinally with quarterly reporting:

1. **Housing Placement:** Number of veterans transitioned from homelessness or unstable housing into transitional and permanent housing, tracked by 30/60/90-day retention rates.

2. **Financial Stability:** Number of down payment assistance awards disbursed, average award amount, and percentage of recipients maintaining housing at 12 months.

3. **Employment Outcomes:** Employment placement rates, 90-day retention rates, and average wage at placement for veterans served.

4. **VA Benefits Access:** Number and percentage of enrolled veterans successfully accessing VA healthcare, disability compensation, and housing vouchers.

5. **Recovery and Reentry Outcomes:** For veterans with co-occurring substance use disorders or reentry backgrounds — sobriety milestone maintenance, connection rates to ongoing treatment, and recidivism reduction compared to regional averages.

All program data is collected through FAITH Foundation's case management system and reported quarterly to the board of directors. Annual impact reports are published and made available to all funders, donors, and stakeholders. Third-party outcome verification is planned beginning in Year 2.

# FAITH Foundation
## Reentry Housing Assistance Grant — Program Narrative

**Organization:** FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope)
**EIN:** 33-2640449
**Service Area:** South & Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast Region
**Annual Operating Budget:** $75,000

---

## SECTION 1: STATEMENT OF NEED

### The Reentry Housing Crisis in Texas

Stable housing is the single most powerful predictor of successful community reintegration after incarceration. Without it, formerly incarcerated individuals face a cascading series of failures — supervision violations, reincarceration, unemployment, and homelessness — that cost communities far more than the investment required to prevent them. The data is unambiguous, and the need in Texas is acute.

**The National Scope**

Formerly incarcerated people are approximately 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population. (National Low Income Housing Coalition, 2018; Prison Policy Initiative.) Formerly incarcerated individuals account for between 23.1% and 47.8% of annual homeless shelter admissions nationally. (Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019.) In states where tracking is available, the numbers are alarming: 28% of individuals released from state prisons in 2024 were released directly into homelessness. (NC Reentry Housing Assessment, 2025.) Nationally, 82% of individuals released from prison across 24 states were re-arrested within 10 years of release. (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024.) Nearly 450,000 individuals were released from state and federal prisons in 2021 alone, and on average, a formerly incarcerated individual spends more than six months unemployed post-release. (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024.) People who are unhoused after release face sharply elevated reincarceration risk due to increased law enforcement contact and supervision violations directly tied to their housing status. (CSG Justice Center, 2025.)

The structural barrier compounding this crisis is a national shortage of 7.3 million rental units affordable and available to extremely low-income households — and that shortage is deepened for individuals with criminal records, who are systematically screened out of private rental markets regardless of their individual circumstances. (National Low Income Housing Coalition.)

**The Texas Context**

Texas is among the states with the highest concentrations of individuals experiencing homelessness and housing instability. Nearly 28,000 Texans were experiencing homelessness in the 2024 Point-in-Time count, including 1,837 veterans. (HUD 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, cited in Texas HB 158.) Of those, 44% were unsheltered — meaning they had no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing whatsoever. (HUD 2024 AHAR.) Chronic homelessness in Texas rose to 2,594 individuals in 2023, up sharply from 1,949 the previous year. (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network.) The permanent housing system has capacity for only 9.5% of people in need, and shelter capacity can house only 16% of households currently in the system. (National Alliance to End Homelessness, 2025.)

For individuals reentering Texas communities from state correctional facilities, the absence of affordable transitional housing options — particularly in rural and underserved areas — creates an immediate crisis at the moment of release. Without a stable address, reentry participants cannot maintain parole or probation conditions, cannot secure employment, and cannot access the benefits and services that support recovery and stability. The result is a predictable cycle of recidivism that harms individuals, families, and communities alike.

Research estimates that reentry participants who complete structured housing and support programs show a 43% lower recidivism rate compared to those without stable housing supports. (Projected Community Impact data, FAITH Foundation Knowledge Base.) Every dollar invested in stable reentry housing generates an estimated $16 in downstream economic activity through reduced justice system costs, increased employment, and tax base contributions. (FAITH Foundation Projected Community Impact.)

**The Rural Gap**

In rural South and Central Texas — FAITH Foundation's primary service area — the housing gap for reentry populations is especially severe. Limited nonprofit infrastructure, dispersed geography, and a near-total absence of purpose-built transitional housing means that individuals released from correctional facilities in these regions frequently have no structured options available to them at all. Traditional urban-focused shelter and transitional housing programs are inaccessible to individuals without transportation, further isolating this population and increasing the probability of failure.

FAITH Foundation was established specifically to address this gap. Our Cornerstone Communities model — deploying modular and manufactured housing units on acquired or donated land in rural communities — brings transitional housing solutions directly to the places where they are most needed, rather than concentrating resources in urban centers while rural communities remain unserved.

---

## SECTION 2: PROGRAM DESIGN AND EVIDENCE-BASED APPROACH

### Second Chance Reentry Program: From Release to Stable Housing to Permanent Home

FAITH Foundation's **Second Chance Reentry Program** is a structured, evidence-informed continuum of housing assistance and wraparound support services designed to move formerly incarcerated individuals from the moment of release through transitional stability and into permanent housing. The program operates on a foundational theory of change: *stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery, successful reentry, and long-term economic self-sufficiency.* Every program element is designed to support that progression.

The program is not a single intervention. It is an integrated pathway with defined stages, clear milestones, and wraparound services aligned to the evidence base on what works for reentry populations.

### Theory of Change

FAITH Foundation's model addresses the root cause of cyclical reincarceration for housing-unstable individuals: the absence of affordable transitional housing in rural and underserved communities. By deploying modular housing units in purpose-built Cornerstone Communities, paired with case management, peer mentorship, financial literacy education, and direct down payment assistance, reentry participants progress through a structured pathway from crisis to stability to permanent housing. Each successful transition frees a unit for the next participant, creating a self-sustaining cycle of community impact.

### Program Pathway: Five Defined Stages

**Stage 1 — Pre-Release Coordination and Intake (30–60 Days Before Release)**

Where coordination is permitted, FAITH Foundation's housing navigator engages with reentry service partners to identify individuals preparing for release who will need transitional housing placement. Pre-release intake includes eligibility screening, needs assessment, and preliminary case planning. Upon release, participants complete a formal intake assessment covering housing history, employment history, substance use history, mental health needs, legal obligations (parole/probation conditions), family support resources, and financial status. This intake assessment drives individualized case planning and determines the appropriate starting point in the program continuum.

**Stage 2 — Transitional Housing Placement (Day 1 Through Month 6)**

Participants are placed into transitional housing units within the Cornerstone Communities network. Units are modular and manufactured homes sited on acquired or donated land in South and Central Texas communities, providing private, dignified living space rather than congregate shelter. Placement is immediate upon intake completion, eliminating the housing gap at the moment of release that drives early supervision failures.

During this stage, participants work with an assigned case manager (maximum 15-to-1 caseload ratio) to stabilize identification documents, enroll in eligible benefits, connect with parole or probation supervision requirements, and establish an employment search or job placement plan. Case management contacts occur at minimum weekly during the first 90 days.

**Stage 3 — Wraparound Services Engagement (Months 1–12)**

Simultaneous with housing placement, participants are connected to a coordinated suite of wraparound services addressing the full range of barriers to reintegration. Services are delivered both on-site at Cornerstone Communities and through referral partnerships across the service area:

- **Employment Support:** Coordination with reentry service partners for job placement, vocational training referrals, and employer engagement. Program target: employment placement within 90 days of enrollment.
- **Financial Literacy Education:** Mandatory enrollment in FAITH Foundation's Financial Literacy and Credit Repair Education Seminars, covering budgeting, credit reports, credit repair strategies, debt management, and homeownership preparation. Offered in-person and virtually to accommodate rural participants without transportation.
- **Legal Aid and Benefits Navigation:** Referral to legal aid partners for record expungement eligibility review, driver's license restoration, child support navigation, and civil legal needs. Coordination with county social services for SNAP, Medicaid, and other benefits enrollment.
- **Substance Use and Recovery Support:** On-site peer support groups and referral to recovery program partners for participants in active recovery. Accountability structures are integrated into the case management relationship without serving as conditions of housing.
- **Peer Mentorship:** Each participant is matched with a trained volunteer mentor — where possible, an individual with lived reentry experience — for accountability, encouragement, and practical guidance.
- **Family Reunification Support:** Case managers facilitate connection with family services partners where participants are working to restore relationships with children or family members.

**Stage 4 — Housing Stabilization and Financial Readiness (Months 6–18)**

As participants stabilize in transitional housing, the program shifts emphasis toward financial readiness and permanent housing preparation. Participants who complete the Financial Literacy program and demonstrate housing stability at the six-month milestone are enrolled in homeownership counseling — FAITH Foundation's pre-purchase counseling curriculum covering mortgage readiness, buyer education, and down payment planning.

Participants who reach employment stability and financial readiness milestones become eligible for FAITH Foundation's Down Payment and Housing Vouchers — $2,500 direct assistance awards funded through the Foundation's partnership with Bright Box Homes, applied toward rental deposits or down payments on permanent housing. This voucher mechanism converts the participant's transitional housing stability into a direct pathway to permanent housing without requiring them to save the full cost of housing entry on their own.

**Stage 5 — Permanent Housing Transition and 12-Month Follow-Up (Month 18–24)**

Upon transitioning to permanent housing — whether through voucher-assisted rental placement or homeownership — participants graduate from the active program into a 12-month follow-up track. Case managers conduct check-ins at 30, 60, 90, 180, and 365 days post-transition to monitor housing retention, employment status, and recovery stability. Housing retention at 12 months is a primary program outcome metric.

Vacated transitional units immediately become available for the next intake participant, sustaining the program's capacity without requiring new capital expenditure.

### Evidence Base

FAITH Foundation's program design is grounded in evidence-based models documented across the reentry housing research base:

- **Housing First principles:** Immediate, unconditional housing placement as the foundation for all other intervention, consistent with HUD-supported models showing improved outcomes relative to treatment-first approaches for housing-unstable populations.
- **Case management intensity in the first 90 days:** Research supports high-contact case management in the immediate post-release period as the highest-leverage point for preventing early recidivism.
- **Financial literacy and credit-building as workforce and housing stability tools:** Financial literacy education has demonstrated 50–80 point credit score improvements over 12 months in comparable programs. (FAITH Foundation Knowledge Base.)
- **Peer mentorship:** Lived-experience mentorship has demonstrated significant impact on reentry outcomes across multiple evidence reviews.
- **Employment as stabilization:** Placement in employment within 90 days of release is among the strongest predictors of sustained housing retention and recidivism reduction.

---

## SECTION 3: TARGET POPULATION AND COMMUNITY NEED

FAITH Foundation's Second Chance Reentry Program serves **formerly incarcerated adults reentering communities in South and Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast region**, with particular focus on individuals released into rural and underserved communities where transitional housing resources are absent or severely limited.

**Primary Population Served**

- Adults released from state or federal correctional facilities in Texas
- Individuals on parole or probation requiring stable housing as a condition of supervision
- Individuals released without a stable housing destination ("released to the street")
- Individuals with co-occurring substance use histories whose reentry is complicated by the intersection of criminal record and recovery status
- Veterans involved in the justice system, who face compounded barriers of criminal record, potential service-connected disability, and housing instability

**Why This Population in This Place**

Rural South and Central Texas communities face a unique configuration of need: high concentrations of individuals released from correctional facilities, near-zero purpose-built transitional housing infrastructure, limited public transportation that would allow access to urban shelter resources, and landlord markets in which criminal records represent near-absolute barriers to rental housing. The gap between what exists and what is needed is not marginal — it is nearly total in many of the communities FAITH Foundation serves.

FAITH Foundation's founder, Reid Whitesides, brings direct lived experience to this understanding. During a long struggle with addiction, Mr. Whitesides spent nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas. His firsthand knowledge of the barriers faced at the moment of release — no stable housing, no employment, no financial foundation — drives the design of every element of the Second Chance Reentry Program. He has been sober for more than fifteen years and leads the Foundation with a conviction forged in personal experience: that lives are transformed when people are given access to hope, opportunity, and a stable foundation.

**Gap in Existing Services**

Existing reentry service infrastructure in the Foundation's service area is concentrated in urban centers and largely unavailable to individuals releasing into rural communities. Transitional housing programs with available units are oversubscribed, and most do not provide the integrated continuum — from immediate placement through financial readiness to permanent housing — that FAITH Foundation's model delivers. Most programs address one element of the reentry housing challenge; FAITH Foundation addresses the full continuum from release to permanent homeownership.

---

## SECTION 4: HOUSING AND WRAPAROUND SERVICES

### Housing Model: Cornerstone Communities

FAITH Foundation's primary housing infrastructure for reentry participants is the **Cornerstone Communities Initiative** — purpose-built micro-communities of modular and manufactured housing units deployed on acquired or donated land in rural and underserved Texas communities.

Each Cornerstone Community includes:
- **Individual residential units:** Modular and manufactured housing units providing private, dignified living spaces for transitional residents. Units are sourced through FAITH Foundation's strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes and other building material suppliers at reduced cost or through donation.
- **Community common spaces:** Shared facilities supporting programming, peer community, and daily living.
- **On-site wraparound services access:** Case management, recovery programming, financial literacy education, remote work and learning center access, community laundry facilities, and shuttle transportation for rural mobility.

Units are sized and configured to be deployable on donated or acquired rural land parcels without the delays and costs of traditional construction — bringing housing solutions directly to underserved communities rather than requiring participants to travel to urban resources they cannot access.

**Housing Units Available to Reentry Participants**

Through the Bright Box Homes partnership, FAITH Foundation has access to a range of modular housing options including 20x20 and 20x40 expandable container homes, Apple cabins, and space capsule units — each providing self-contained, move-in-ready residential spaces suitable for transitional occupancy and eventual permanent placement.

Participants in transitional housing are not in congregate shelter. They occupy individual units, preserving dignity and privacy while building the stability and daily structure that reintegration requires.

### Wraparound Services Architecture

FAITH Foundation does not deliver wraparound services in isolation. Services are integrated into a coherent case management framework in which the participant's assigned case manager coordinates across all service domains:

| Service Domain | Delivery Model | Partner Type |
|---|---|---|
| Housing Placement | Direct — Cornerstone Communities | FAITH Foundation |
| Case Management | Direct — 15:1 ratio, weekly contact | FAITH Foundation |
| Financial Literacy | Direct — in-person and virtual seminars | FAITH Foundation |
| Employment Support | Referral and coordination | Reentry service partners |
| Legal Aid & Benefits | Referral | Legal aid partners, county social services |
| Recovery Support | On-site peer groups + referral | Recovery program partners |
| Peer Mentorship | Direct — trained volunteer mentors | FAITH Foundation / church partners |
| VA Benefits Navigation | Referral (for veteran participants) | Veterans service organizations |

FAITH Foundation maintains active partnerships across these service domains with church partners, recovery program partners, reentry service providers, county social services agencies, local housing authorities, and veterans service organizations throughout South and Central Texas. Reentry service partners specifically coordinate to place formerly incarcerated individuals into transitional housing upon release, connecting them with employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support.

**Continuum of Care**

The program delivers a genuine continuum — not a collection of disconnected services. Participants enter at the point of crisis (release), move through stabilization (transitional housing and wraparound services), progress to financial readiness (financial literacy, employment, credit-building), and graduate to permanent housing (voucher-assisted rental or homeownership). The case management relationship persists across all stages and through the 12-month post-transition follow-up period, ensuring that early warning signs of housing instability are identified and addressed before they result in loss of housing or reincarceration.

---

## SECTION 5: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY AND PARTNERSHIPS

### Leadership and Governance

FAITH Foundation is governed by a committed board of directors whose combined experience in construction, housing, finance, ministry, and — critically — lived reentry experience uniquely qualifies the organization to execute this program.

**Reid Whitesides, Founder and President** brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries, and personally spent nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas. His lived experience of reentry, now anchored by more than fifteen years of sobriety, is not a biographical footnote — it is the operating intelligence behind every element of the Second Chance Reentry Program. Mr. Whitesides also brings technology expertise, developing websites, software applications, and automation tools that support the Foundation's program data and grant management infrastructure.

**Scott Ellis, Treasurer and Board Chair,** is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction in Georgetown, Texas, with more than 15 years of business leadership experience in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems. His practical expertise in construction costs, building practices, and long-term asset stewardship directly supports the Cornerstone Communities development model and ensures that housing assets are acquired and maintained with sound financial discipline.

**Pastor Juan Valdez, Secretary and Protector,** brings more than 40 years of Christian faith and nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience, with leadership extending across the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. In addition to his ministry leadership, Pastor Valdez and his wife Martha operated a successful business in San Antonio for 34 years — a record of sustained operational commitment that reflects the consistency and stewardship he brings to governance oversight. He currently serves as Associate Pastor at Temple of Praise and provides mission accountability and ethical governance to the Foundation.

Together, this leadership team combines hands-on construction and housing expertise, rigorous financial oversight, deep community and ministry relationships, and direct personal knowledge of the reentry experience — a rare combination that positions FAITH Foundation credibly and effectively to serve this population.

### Staffing Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation's program operations are supported by case managers maintaining a maximum 15-to-1 client ratio and a housing navigator who coordinates placement across transitional and permanent housing options. Financial management is conducted through QuickBooks, and program data is managed through the organization's Supabase data management system and Benavora grant platform.

[NEEDS INPUT: Names and credentials of current case management staff, housing navigator, and any licensed clinical or social work staff should be listed here if available to strengthen this section.]

### Partnerships

FAITH Foundation's partnership network is deliberately constructed to fill every service gap in the reentry continuum:

- **Church partners** provide volunteer labor, mentorship volunteers, meeting space for participant programming, and congregational fundraising support.
- **Recovery program partners** refer individuals completing treatment who need stable transitional housing and provide ongoing support services for residents in active recovery.
- **Reentry service partners** coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals upon release, connecting them with employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support.
- **County social services agencies and local housing authorities** refer eligible individuals, coordinate benefits enrollment, and collaborate on case management.
- **Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers** provide discounted or donated materials and units for Cornerstone Communities development.
- **Bright Box Homes** provides modular housing units at discounted rates and donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold — creating a renewable funding stream tied directly to housing production.
- **Veterans service organizations** refer military veterans experiencing housing instability and coordinate VA benefits enrollment for dual-eligible participants.

[NEEDS INPUT: Formal letters of support or memoranda of understanding from named partner organizations — particularly reentry service partners and county social services agencies — should be attached to strengthen the partnerships section for scoring purposes.]

### Organizational History and Stage

FAITH Foundation was established by Reid Whitesides to address the critical shortage of affordable and transitional housing options in rural South Texas communities. The organization is in its founding period of operations, with initial activities funded through founder investment and church community support. As a newly established 501(c)(3), FAITH Foundation has not yet produced multi-year program outcome data; however, the organization's evidence-based program design, leadership qualifications, strategic partnerships, and documented model provide a strong foundation for the work this grant will support.

The Foundation actively pursues diversified funding to build toward long-term sustainability and has deployed the Benavora grant management platform to support competitive grant applications across federal, state, and private funding sources.

---

## SECTION 6: BUDGET JUSTIFICATION AND COST-EFFECTIVENESS

FAITH Foundation's budget allocates resources with a consistent priority: maximum dollars reaching program participants and housing assets, with administrative overhead maintained below 15% of total program budget.

**Budget Allocation Framework**

| Category | Description |
|---|---|
| **Direct Housing Assistance** | Down payment and transitional housing vouchers ($2,500 per qualifying participant), rental deposit assistance, and emergency bridge housing for individuals released without stable placement. Voucher funding flows entirely to participants. |
| **Housing Infrastructure** | Modular housing unit acquisition ($30,000–$60,000 per unit), site preparation and utility infrastructure installation, and community common space construction for Cornerstone Communities. These expenditures create appreciating physical assets that reduce per-unit costs over time. |
| **Case Management and Staffing** | Personnel costs for case managers (15:1 ratio) and housing navigator. Case management is the highest-leverage operational investment in the reentry housing model — the evidence base is clear that intensive case management in the first 90 days post-release is the primary driver of housing retention and recidivism reduction. |
| **Program Services** | Financial literacy instruction, materials, and virtual platform access; peer mentorship program coordination; transportation for rural case management outreach. |
| **Operations and Administration** | Accounting (QuickBooks), insurance, legal and compliance, property maintenance, program supplies, and organizational administration — maintained below 15% of total program budget. |

**Cost-Effectiveness**

[NEEDS INPUT: Total grant amount requested and resulting cost-per-client calculation should be inserted here once the funding request amount is determined. The narrative should specify: (a) number of reentry participants to be served with these funds, (b) total direct assistance dollars, and (c) cost per participant including case management and housing services.]

In-kind donations of building materials, volunteer labor, and professional services significantly reduce cash outlays and are documented at fair market value for matching fund requirements. The rotating Cornerstone Communities model — in which transitional units become available for new participants as residents transition to permanent housing — generates ongoing program capacity from each capital investment, improving cost-effectiveness over time.

**Indirect Cost Rate**

FAITH Foundation maintains indirect costs below 15% of total program budget. [NEEDS INPUT: If FAITH Foundation has an established Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA) with a cognizant federal agency, it should be cited here. If not, the organization should confirm use of the de minimis 10% rate per 2 CFR § 200.414 for federal awards.]

---

## SECTION 7: EVALUATION AND OUTCOMES MEASUREMENT

### Measurable Outcomes

FAITH Foundation defines success for the Second Chance Reentry Program across five measurable outcome domains, tracked longitudinally with quarterly reporting:

**1. Housing Placement and Retention**
- Number of reentry participants placed in transitional housing within 72 hours of program enrollment
- Housing retention rates at 30, 60, 90, 180, and 365 days
- *Target:* 90% housing retention among program participants at the 12-month mark (Year 2)

**2. Recidivism Prevention**
- Percentage of reentry participants who avoid reincarceration within 24 months of program enrollment
- *Target:* Measurable reduction versus regional recidivism baseline, tracked against available Texas Department of Criminal Justice data

**3. Employment Attainment**
- Number of participants placed in employment within 90 days of program enrollment
- *Target:* 15 reentry participants placed in stable employment within 90 days (Year 2)

**4. Financial Stability**
- Number of down payment assistance vouchers disbursed to program graduates
- Average improvement in credit score among financial literacy program completers
- *Target:* 50–80 point credit score improvement within 12 months for financial literacy completers

**5. Permanent Housing Transition**
- Number of participants transitioning from transitional to permanent housing
- Percentage of transitional housing units successfully turned over to new intake participants
- *Target:* 30% homeownership conversion rate among Year 1 participants by Year 3

### Data Collection and Reporting

All participant data is collected through FAITH Foundation's case management system (Supabase data management platform) and reported quarterly to the board of directors. Annual impact reports will be published and made available to all funders, donors, and stakeholders. FAITH Foundation is committed to transparency in both financial stewardship and program outcomes, and will pursue third-party outcome verification beginning in Year 2.

Outcome tracking tools include intake and exit assessments, 30/60/90/180/365-day follow-up protocols, housing retention verification, employment verification, and credit score tracking for financial literacy participants.

---

## SECTION 8: SUSTAINABILITY

FAITH Foundation's long-term sustainability is built on a rotating housing asset model that generates ongoing capacity without recurring capital expenditure. As reentry participants transition to permanent housing, their transitional units become available for new participants — creating a self-sustaining cycle of impact from each initial investment.

**Diversified Revenue Streams**
- Recurring grant funding from federal, state, and private sources
- Corporate sponsorships and in-kind donations
- Program fees on a sliding scale based on participant income
- Rental income from stabilized housing units
- Church partnerships and congregational giving
- Individual donor cultivation
- Bright Box Homes partnership: $2,500 donation per home sold, creating a renewable funding stream tied directly to housing production

**Physical Asset Appreciation**

Land parcels and modular housing units acquired for Cornerstone Communities represent appreciating assets that reduce ongoing capital expenditure requirements and improve per-unit economics over time.

**Funding Diversification**

The Foundation actively pursues diversified funding across government grants, private foundations, corporate giving programs, faith-based funders, and community development financial institutions to avoid dependency on any single source. This grant, if awarded, would represent one component of a deliberately diversified funding portfolio.

---

## COMPLIANCE NOTICES

The following compliance requirements under 2 CFR Part 200 (Uniform Guidance) apply to this application and require the applicant's attention prior to award:

> **[REQUIRED] SAM.gov Active Registration:** All organizations applying for or receiving federal financial assistance must maintain an active registration in SAM.gov, renewed annually. A lapsed registration can delay or disqualify an award. FAITH Foundation should confirm its SAM.gov registration is current before submission. (2 CFR § 200.206)

> **[REQUIRED] Unique Entity Identifier (UEI):** All applicants must have a UEI assigned through SAM.gov (replaced DUNS number in April 2022). The UEI is required on all federal grant applications. FAITH Foundation should confirm its UEI is active and included on all application documents. (2 CFR § 200.1; GSA UEI transition policy, April 4, 2022)

> **[REQUIRED] Financial Management System Standards:** Recipients must maintain a financial management system providing accurate, current, and complete disclosures of financial results; adequate source and application of funds identification; effective internal controls; and written procedures for determining cost allowability. FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks for financial management. (2 CFR § 200.302) — Confirm that QuickBooks implementation meets 2 CFR § 200.302 standards for grant financial tracking and segregation.

> **[REQUIRED] Federal Cost Principles Compliance (2 CFR 200 Subpart E):** All costs charged to federal awards must be allowable, allocable, and reasonable. Unallowable costs include lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties. FAITH Foundation should ensure all budget line items comply with Subpart E prior to submission.

> **[REQUIRED] Administrative Requirements (2 CFR 200 Subpart D):** Recipients must maintain internal controls, comply with federal statutes, follow award terms and conditions, and meet performance and financial reporting requirements. Records must be retained for a minimum of three years. Budget modifications may require prior approval.

> **[REQUIRED] Property Management Standards:** Equipment and real property — including modular housing units — acquired with federal funds must be managed per federal standards, including property inventory, physical inventory at least every two years, depreciation calculations, federal approval for disposal, and residual inventory return at closeout. (2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316)

> **[REQUIRED] Federal Procurement Standards:** Procurements under federal awards must follow documented procedures providing full and open competition. FAITH Foundation's use of competitive open-bid construction for Cornerstone Communities development is consistent with these requirements. (2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327)

> **[REQUIRED] Single Audit / OMB A-133 Threshold:** If FAITH Foundation expends $750,000 or more in federal awards in a fiscal year, a Single Audit by an independent auditor is required, submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end. Given the current $75,000 annual budget, this threshold is not immediately applicable but should be monitored as the organization grows. (2 CFR § 200.501)

> **[RECOMMENDED] Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA):** FAITH Foundation should determine whether it will use the de minimis indirect cost rate of 10% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC) per 2 CFR § 200.414, or negotiate a rate with its cognizant federal agency. This determination should be documented prior to award. (2 CFR §§ 200.414, 200.68)
