# FAITH Foundation
## Rural Housing Preservation Grant Program
### Pre-Application Narrative

**Applicant Organization:** FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope)
**EIN:** 33-2640449
**Tax Status:** 501(c)(3) Public Charity
**Service Area:** South & Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast region, with primary focus on rural and underserved communities
**Contact:** Reid Whitesides, Founder & President

---

> **⚠ COMPLIANCE NOTICES — ACTION REQUIRED BEFORE SUBMISSION**
>
> The following federal compliance items require resolution prior to submitting this application. Failure to address these items may delay or disqualify an award.
>
> - **SAM.gov Active Registration (2 CFR § 200.206):** Confirm that FAITH Foundation's SAM.gov registration is active and current. Registration must be renewed annually. A lapsed registration will disqualify the application.
> - **Unique Entity Identifier / UEI (2 CFR § 200.1):** [NEEDS INPUT: Confirm UEI number assigned through SAM.gov. The UEI replaced the DUNS number in April 2022 and is required on all federal grant applications.]
> - **Single Audit / OMB A-133 Threshold (2 CFR § 200.501):** FAITH Foundation's current annual budget is $75,000. If this award or combined federal expenditures in any fiscal year equal or exceed $750,000, a single audit performed by an independent auditor and submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end will be required. Plan accordingly.
> - **Indirect Cost Rate (2 CFR §§ 200.414, 200.68):** As a newly established organization without a Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA), FAITH Foundation may elect the de minimis rate of 10% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC). This election must be consistently applied and documented. Confirm this election in the budget narrative.
> - **Federal Cost Principles (2 CFR Subpart E):** All costs charged to this award must be allowable, allocable, and reasonable. Unallowable costs include lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties. All expenditures must be fully documented.
> - **Administrative Requirements (2 CFR Subpart D):** FAITH Foundation must maintain internal controls, comply with all federal statutes and award terms, retain financial records for a minimum of three years, and follow prior-approval procedures for budget modifications.
> - **Financial Management System (2 CFR § 200.302):** FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks as its financial management system. Confirm that the system is configured to separately identify and track federal award expenditures by grant, funding source, and budget line item.
> - **Property Management Standards (2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316):** Any equipment or real property — including modular housing units — acquired with HPG funds must be inventoried, tracked, and managed in accordance with federal property management standards, including physical inventories at minimum every two years.
> - **Federal Procurement Standards (2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327):** All procurements under this award must follow documented procedures providing for full and open competition. Construction contracts and housing unit acquisitions must comply with applicable thresholds: micro-purchases under $10,000 require no bid; small purchases between $10,000 and $250,000 require price/rate quotes; larger procurements require sealed bids or competitive proposals. Conflicts of interest must be avoided and documented.

---

## SECTION I: STATEMENT OF NEED

### The Rural Housing Crisis in South and Central Texas

Rural South Texas communities face a housing preservation and rehabilitation crisis that is both chronic and accelerating. The populations FAITH Foundation serves — military veterans, individuals in addiction recovery, formerly incarcerated citizens reentering society, single-parent families, and individuals experiencing or at risk of homelessness — are concentrated precisely in the rural communities where affordable housing inventory is most critically depleted and where the physical condition of existing housing stock is most severely deteriorated.

The national evidence base is unambiguous. According to the HUD 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, 745,652 people were experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2025, including 266,320 living unsheltered. Texas is among the seven states accounting for 64% of the nation's total homeless population (HUD 2024 AHAR). The 2024 Point-in-Time count identified nearly 28,000 Texans experiencing homelessness, including 1,837 veterans — with 44% of that population unsheltered, meaning they had no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing of any kind (HUD 2024 AHAR, cited in Texas HB 158).

These figures reflect not only the failure of emergency response systems, but the collapse of the housing preservation infrastructure that keeps very low- and low-income homeowners in safe, stable dwellings in rural communities. When deteriorating homes become uninhabitable, the families inside them enter the homelessness pipeline. When landlords in rural areas allow rental stock to deteriorate below habitability standards, very low-income tenants have nowhere to turn in communities where emergency shelter may be hours away.

### Who Is Left Behind in Rural Texas

The populations most harmed by the rural housing preservation gap are precisely those the HPG program is designed to serve:

**Veterans:** In Texas, 1,837 veterans were experiencing homelessness as of the 2024 Point-in-Time count, with veteran homelessness among the highest concentrations nationally (VA/HUD 2024 PIT Count). Veterans in rural South Texas frequently lack access to VA services available in urban centers, and their housing — often older owner-occupied stock — deteriorates without access to affordable repair resources.

**Formerly Incarcerated Individuals:** Formerly incarcerated people are approximately 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population (National Low Income Housing Coalition / Prison Policy Initiative). Between 23.1% and 47.8% of annual homeless shelter admissions nationally are formerly incarcerated individuals (Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019). In rural Texas communities, the absence of safe, affordable housing upon release drives recidivism: 82% of individuals released from prison across 24 states were re-arrested within 10 years (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024), a cycle that stable housing directly interrupts.

**People in Recovery:** Individuals exiting addiction treatment require stable, safe housing as the biological and psychological prerequisite for sustained sobriety. Rural South Texas communities lack the transitional and rehabilitated housing stock that urban recovery communities can access. Without safe housing, recovery fails — and the cycle of addiction, incarceration, and homelessness repeats.

**Single-Parent Families:** The homeownership rate among single mothers is approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples without children (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024). Single-parent households face estimated home prices approaching five times their income (NAHB Eye on Housing, 2024). In rural Texas, single parents often occupy aging, deteriorating housing stock they cannot afford to repair, placing their children at risk and their housing tenure in jeopardy.

**Low-Income Homeowners:** 74.2% of homeowner households with incomes below $30,000 are cost-burdened, paying more than 30% of income on housing — the highest rate in over 20 years (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University). In rural communities, these households frequently cannot access home repair financing and cannot afford contractor-market repair costs, resulting in progressive deterioration of owner-occupied homes that represent families' only wealth-building asset.

### The Rural Deficit: Why Standard Solutions Fail

Rural South Texas faces a compounding structural problem that urban-focused housing programs cannot address. Traditional construction is cost-prohibitive in rural areas due to contractor scarcity, material transportation costs, and limited subcontractor availability. Conventional home repair financing requires credit scores and income documentation that very low-income rural homeowners frequently cannot provide. And the nonprofit housing infrastructure that exists in San Antonio, Austin, or Houston has minimal reach into the rural communities of South Texas, where transportation barriers, geographic isolation, and the absence of local service providers leave very low-income residents without recourse.

FAITH Foundation was established specifically to fill this gap. Our model — deploying modular and manufactured housing solutions in purpose-built Cornerstone Communities on acquired or donated rural land — addresses the structural barriers that make traditional housing development cost-prohibitive in rural areas. The same modular approach that enables us to place new units in rural communities also enables us to approach housing rehabilitation and preservation with scalable, cost-efficient solutions tailored to the geographic realities of South and Central Texas.

The Rural Housing Service's Housing Preservation Grant program is the precise mechanism through which FAITH Foundation can extend this model to serve very low- and low-income homeowners and rural rental property owners whose existing housing stock requires repair and rehabilitation to remain safe, stable, and livable.

---

## SECTION II: PROGRAM DESIGN

### Overview: The HPG-Funded Housing Preservation Program

FAITH Foundation proposes to deploy Rural Housing Service Housing Preservation Grant funds to assist very low- and low-income homeowners in repairing and rehabilitating their homes in eligible rural areas of South and Central Texas, and to assist rural rental property owners in repairing and rehabilitating units that will be made available to low- and very low-income persons. This program directly implements the purposes of the HPG program as authorized under 7 CFR Part 1944, Subpart N.

### Theory of Change

Stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery from addiction, successful community reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. FAITH Foundation's model addresses the root cause of cyclical homelessness — the absence of affordable, safe, and preserved housing in rural communities. By providing direct repair and rehabilitation assistance to very low- and low-income homeowners and qualifying rental property owners, paired with case management, financial literacy education, and connection to wraparound support services, individuals and families are stabilized in their existing homes rather than displaced into homelessness. Each preserved home maintains one family's foundation of stability, prevents the downstream costs of homelessness, and keeps rural community housing stock viable for future occupancy.

### Target Population and Eligibility

FAITH Foundation will prioritize HPG assistance for:

- **Very low-income homeowners** (at or below 50% of Area Median Income) in eligible rural Texas communities, with particular focus on veterans, individuals in recovery, formerly incarcerated individuals, and single-parent households
- **Low-income homeowners** (at or below 80% of AMI) in eligible rural communities whose homes present health, safety, or habitability concerns
- **Rental property owners** in eligible rural communities who agree, as a condition of assistance, to make rehabilitated units available to low- and very low-income persons at rents affordable to those income levels

All assisted areas will meet the RHS definition of rural areas as defined under 7 CFR 1944.656. Income eligibility determinations will follow the definitions and procedures established in 7 CFR Part 1944, Subpart N.

### Program Components

**Component 1: Homeowner Assessment and Intake**

FAITH Foundation will conduct outreach to eligible rural communities through our existing network of church partners, county social services agencies, local housing authorities, veterans service organizations, recovery program partners, and reentry service providers. Potential applicants will be identified through referrals from these partners, as well as through direct community outreach in eligible rural areas.

Each applicant household will undergo:
- Income verification and eligibility determination per HPG income standards
- Property assessment by qualified personnel with construction expertise
- Prioritization scoring based on health and safety risk, income level, household vulnerability, and property preservation urgency
- Development of an individualized repair and rehabilitation scope of work

**Component 2: Repair and Rehabilitation Delivery**

Approved homeowners and qualifying rental property owners will receive direct repair and rehabilitation assistance. Eligible repair categories include:

- Structural repairs necessary to ensure habitability and safety
- Roof repair and replacement
- Plumbing, electrical, and HVAC system repair and upgrade
- Accessibility modifications for residents with disabilities
- Weatherization and energy efficiency improvements
- Repair or replacement of deteriorated floors, walls, and insulation
- Remediation of health hazards including mold, lead-based paint, and pest infestation

All repair and rehabilitation work will be procured through FAITH Foundation's documented competitive procurement procedures in compliance with 2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327. Contracts above $10,000 will require competitive bidding; contracts above $250,000 will require sealed bids or competitive proposals. Conflicts of interest will be identified and documented at all stages of procurement. FAITH Foundation's Treasurer, Scott Ellis — owner of E4 Roofing & Construction with more than 15 years of construction industry experience — will provide technical oversight to ensure contractor compliance, quality of work, and appropriate use of funds.

**Component 3: Wraparound Support Services**

FAITH Foundation's HPG program is not a stand-alone repair program. Consistent with our integrated service model, assisted homeowners and residents of rehabilitated rental units will be connected to:

- Financial literacy and budgeting education to support long-term housing retention
- Down payment assistance voucher pipeline for renters seeking to transition to homeownership
- Case management through our Transitional Housing Program for residents in recovery, reentry, or other vulnerable circumstances
- Connection to veterans service organizations and VA benefits navigation for veteran homeowners
- Referrals to employment services, childcare navigation, and public benefits enrollment as appropriate

**Component 4: Rental Unit Rehabilitation and Affordability Agreements**

For rental property owners receiving HPG assistance, FAITH Foundation will execute written affordability agreements as required under 7 CFR Part 1944, Subpart N, ensuring that rehabilitated units are made available to low- and very low-income tenants at rents affordable to those income levels for the period required by program regulations. Compliance with affordability commitments will be monitored by FAITH Foundation through annual certification and periodic site visits.

### Participant Recruitment and Enrollment Timeline

FAITH Foundation proposes the following enrollment and implementation schedule:

| Milestone | Timeline |
|---|---|
| Award notification and post-award mobilization | Months 1–2 |
| Staff onboarding and procurement system activation | Month 2 |
| Partner network activation and referral pipeline launch | Month 2–3 |
| Community outreach and intake initiation | Month 3 |
| First applicant eligibility determinations completed | Month 3–4 |
| First repair scopes of work approved and contractors procured | Month 4–5 |
| First repair and rehabilitation projects initiated | Month 5 |
| Ongoing intake, assessment, and repair delivery | Months 5–18 |
| Final project completions and closeout documentation | Months 19–24 |

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirm the proposed grant period length. This timeline assumes a 24-month performance period. If RHS specifies a different performance period in the final Notice of Funding Availability, the timeline should be adjusted accordingly.]

Recruitment will prioritize rural communities with the highest concentrations of very low-income homeowners and deteriorated housing stock in FAITH Foundation's service area of South and Central Texas. Outreach will be conducted in English and Spanish to ensure accessibility to the predominantly bilingual communities we serve.

### Geographic Focus and Rural Eligibility

FAITH Foundation's primary service area encompasses South and Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast region, with concentrated focus on rural and underserved communities. All assisted properties will be located in areas meeting the RHS definition of "rural" under applicable regulations. FAITH Foundation will confirm the rural eligibility status of each assisted property prior to approving assistance.

[NEEDS INPUT: Identify the specific Texas counties or communities targeted for HPG assistance. Explicitly citing communities with populations below 20,000 and median household incomes below the Texas non-metro median will strengthen alignment with USDA Rural Development eligibility priorities.]

---

## SECTION III: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY

### About FAITH Foundation

FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization established in Texas to address the critical shortage of affordable and preserved housing options in rural South Texas communities. The organization was founded on the conviction that stable housing is the essential foundation for recovery from addiction, successful reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. FAITH Foundation is also recognized as a faith-based and community organization, making it fully eligible under the HPG program's explicit inclusion of Faith-Based and Community Organizations as qualified applicants.

FAITH Foundation's current annual budget is $75,000, with operations funded through founder investment and church community support during this inaugural funding cycle. The organization is actively pursuing diversified federal, state, and private funding to scale its programs to meet documented community need.

### Leadership Team

**Reid Whitesides — Founder & President**

Reid Whitesides brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries directly to FAITH Foundation's mission. His practical expertise in construction and property improvement is not academic — it is built from two decades of hands-on industry experience that directly informs the Foundation's approach to housing preservation and rehabilitation.

Reid's commitment to this work is also deeply personal. During a long struggle with addiction, he spent nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas. Those experiences gave him firsthand insight into the barriers that very low-income individuals face when rebuilding their lives after addiction, incarceration, and homelessness. Today, sober for more than fifteen years, Reid leads FAITH Foundation with the conviction that every person deserves the opportunity to build a better future, regardless of their past. His combination of construction industry expertise, technology skills, and lived experience with the populations FAITH Foundation serves makes him uniquely qualified to lead this program.

**Scott Ellis — Treasurer & Board Chair**

Scott Ellis provides FAITH Foundation with exceptional financial oversight and construction industry expertise. As owner of E4 Roofing & Construction — a Georgetown, Texas-based company he has led for more than 15 years — Scott brings direct, current experience in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems. His understanding of construction costs, building practices, property improvement, and long-term asset stewardship ensures that HPG-funded repair and rehabilitation projects are approached responsibly, efficiently, and with a focus on maximizing community impact.

As Treasurer, Scott oversees FAITH Foundation's financial management, ensuring proper stewardship of organizational and grant resources. FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks as its financial management system, maintained in compliance with the financial management standards of 2 CFR § 200.302, with separate tracking of federal award expenditures by grant and budget line item.

**Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary & Protector**

Pastor Juan Valdez provides FAITH Foundation with nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience and a lifetime of community service. His ministry has extended across the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. Beyond ministry, he and his wife Martha operated a successful business in the same San Antonio location for 34 years — a testament to the consistency, reliability, and stewardship that characterize his governance role at FAITH Foundation. Pastor Valdez provides governance accountability, ethical oversight, and mission stewardship, helping to ensure that the Foundation remains a faithful and transparent steward of the public and private resources entrusted to it.

### Relevant Experience and Programmatic Capacity

FAITH Foundation operates three interconnected housing programs across South Texas: the Down Payment Assistance Program, the Transitional Housing Program, and the Cornerstone Communities Initiative. These programs collectively demonstrate the organizational infrastructure, partnerships, and operational experience necessary to administer a housing preservation and rehabilitation program for very low- and low-income homeowners and rural rental property owners.

The Cornerstone Communities Initiative is particularly relevant to HPG program administration. This initiative involves land acquisition, deployment of modular and manufactured housing units, site preparation, utility infrastructure installation, contractor procurement, and ongoing property management — all operational activities directly transferable to the management of a repair and rehabilitation grant program. The Foundation's existing procurement practices, financial management systems, and construction oversight capacity are the same systems that will govern HPG fund deployment.

### Partnership Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation's existing partner network provides the referral infrastructure, service coordination, and community reach necessary to identify eligible homeowners and connect assisted residents to wraparound support services:

- **Church partners** provide volunteer labor, community outreach access, and meeting space for program orientation and financial literacy education
- **County social services agencies and local housing authorities** refer eligible very low- and low-income families, coordinate benefits enrollment, and provide case management collaboration
- **Recovery program partners** refer individuals completing treatment who need stable housing and provide ongoing support services
- **Reentry service partners** coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals and connect them to employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support
- **Veterans service organizations** refer military veterans experiencing housing insecurity and coordinate VA benefits enrollment
- **Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers** provide discounted or donated materials, reducing the per-unit cost of repair and rehabilitation work
- **Land owners in rural South Texas communities** donate or sell land at reduced cost, reducing capital requirements for site-based programs

### Financial Management and Compliance Systems

FAITH Foundation maintains its financial records using QuickBooks, configured to provide accurate, current, and complete disclosure of financial results and to separately identify the source and application of federal award funds. The organization is committed to full compliance with 2 CFR Part 200 Uniform Guidance requirements, including:

- Maintenance of internal controls adequate to ensure that federal award funds are used only for allowable, allocable, and reasonable purposes in accordance with 2 CFR Subpart E
- Compliance with procurement standards under 2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327, including competitive bidding requirements for construction contracts
- Property management of all equipment and real property acquired with federal funds in accordance with 2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316, including physical inventories at minimum every two years
- Records retention for a minimum of three years following award closeout
- Quarterly performance reporting and annual financial reporting to the board of directors and to RHS as required

As a newly established organization, FAITH Foundation has not previously been subject to the single audit requirement under 2 CFR § 200.501. The organization will monitor federal expenditure levels throughout the award period and will arrange for a single audit if cumulative federal expenditures in any fiscal year equal or exceed $750,000. For indirect costs, FAITH Foundation will apply the de minimis rate of 10% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC) as permitted under 2 CFR § 200.414(f), as the organization has not previously established a Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement.

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirm FAITH Foundation's SAM.gov registration status and provide the active UEI number for inclusion in the application. The UEI is required on all federal grant applications per 2 CFR § 200.1 and GSA policy effective April 4, 2022.]

---

## SECTION IV: EVALUATION PLAN AND DATA INTEGRITY

### Outcome Metrics

FAITH Foundation will track and report program outcomes across five domains aligned with HPG program purposes:

**1. Housing Preservation Volume**
- Number of very low- and low-income homeowner households assisted
- Number of rental units rehabilitated and made available to low- and very low-income persons
- Total dollar value of repair and rehabilitation assistance delivered
- Average cost per household assisted

**2. Housing Quality and Safety**
- Pre- and post-rehabilitation property condition assessments documenting resolution of identified health, safety, and habitability deficiencies
- Percentage of assisted units brought to full habitability standards upon project completion
- Documentation of specific repair categories addressed per unit

**3. Housing Retention and Stability**
- Percentage of assisted homeowners remaining stably housed at 6-month and 12-month intervals following rehabilitation completion
- Percentage of rehabilitated rental units occupied by low- or very low-income tenants at 12-month intervals
- Affordability agreement compliance rate for rental property owners

**4. Population-Specific Outcomes**
- Number of veteran households assisted
- Number of households headed by formerly incarcerated individuals assisted
- Number of households in active recovery assisted
- Number of single-parent households assisted

**5. Program Efficiency**
- Ratio of direct repair assistance to administrative costs
- Time from intake to project completion per household
- Percentage of approved repair scopes completed within budget

### Data Collection and Management

All program data will be collected through FAITH Foundation's case management system and maintained in compliance with federal data integrity requirements. Intake documentation, income verification records, property assessment reports, contractor procurement records, scope of work approvals, project completion certifications, and affordability agreements will be maintained in organized project files for each assisted household, retained for a minimum of three years following award closeout in compliance with 2 CFR Subpart D.

FAITH Foundation will submit performance reports to RHS on the schedule required by the award terms. Annual impact reports will be published and made available to all funders, donors, and community stakeholders. Beginning in Year 2, FAITH Foundation will pursue third-party outcome verification to strengthen the evidence base for program effectiveness.

### Coordination with Federal Program Requirements

FAITH Foundation will maintain open communication with the USDA Rural Development State Office throughout the award period, including timely submission of required performance and financial reports, prompt notification of any significant program changes or challenges, and compliance with any RHS monitoring or site visit requirements. All program modifications requiring prior RHS approval will be submitted through the appropriate approval process before implementation.

---

## SECTION V: BUDGET NARRATIVE AND FUND UTILIZATION

### Budget Framework

FAITH Foundation's proposed budget for the HPG-funded Housing Preservation Program prioritizes direct repair and rehabilitation assistance to very low- and low-income homeowners and qualifying rental property owners, consistent with the HPG program's purpose of direct housing preservation assistance. Administrative costs are maintained within HPG program allowances.

[NEEDS INPUT: Insert the specific dollar amount requested under this HPG application. The Notice indicates a maximum award of $50,000 for Calendar Year 2022 disaster assistance funds. Confirm whether FAITH Foundation is applying under the disaster assistance allocation, the Puerto Rico allocation, or the general HPG program, and confirm the amount requested.]

**Direct Repair and Rehabilitation Assistance**

The majority of HPG funds will be deployed as direct repair and rehabilitation assistance to eligible homeowners and qualifying rental property owners. Eligible expenditures include:

- Structural repair costs paid directly to licensed contractors procured through competitive bidding
- Roofing materials and installation
- Plumbing, electrical, and HVAC repair and replacement
- Accessibility modification materials and installation
- Weatherization materials and installation
- Health hazard remediation (mold, lead, pest infestation)
- Repair or replacement of deteriorated interior and exterior building components

All contractor procurements will follow the federal procurement standards of 2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327. Unallowable costs — including lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties — will not be charged to the federal award.

**Personnel Costs**

Personnel costs will support:
- Program coordination and administration (case manager time allocated to eligibility determination, property assessment coordination, contractor oversight, and reporting)
- Housing navigator time allocated to participant intake, referral coordination, and wraparound service connection

Personnel costs will be supported by timesheets documenting time spent on HPG program activities, allocated in proportion to actual time devoted to the award.

**Administrative and Indirect Costs**

Administrative and indirect costs will not exceed HPG program allowances. FAITH Foundation will apply the de minimis indirect cost rate of 10% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC) as permitted under 2 CFR § 200.414(f).

**In-Kind Contributions**

FAITH Foundation actively receives in-kind contributions of building materials, volunteer construction labor, and professional services including architectural, surveying, and construction management services. These in-kind contributions will be documented at fair market value and reported as matching contributions where applicable, reducing the cash cost of each repair and rehabilitation project and extending the reach of HPG funds to serve additional households.

### Post-Enrollment Fund Utilization

Following the close of the initial enrollment and intake period, HPG funds will continue to be deployed for:
- Completion of repair and rehabilitation projects initiated during the enrollment period
- Ongoing property assessments for households on the waitlist
- Affordability agreement monitoring for assisted rental properties
- Required performance reporting and program closeout documentation
- Retention of program records in compliance with 2 CFR Subpart D

No HPG funds will be expended on activities not authorized under 7 CFR Part 1944, Subpart N, or on costs prohibited under 2 CFR Subpart E.

---

## SECTION VI: INTENDED IMPACT AND SUSTAINABILITY

### Immediate Impact

Through the HPG-funded Housing Preservation Program, FAITH Foundation will:

- Assist very low- and low-income homeowners in rural South and Central Texas in repairing and rehabilitating their homes, preserving housing stability and preventing displacement into homelessness
- Assist qualifying rural rental property owners in rehabilitating units made available to low- and very low-income persons, expanding the supply of safe, affordable rental housing in rural communities
- Connect assisted homeowners and residents to FAITH Foundation's integrated program ecosystem, including financial literacy education, down payment assistance vouchers, case management, and pathway-to-homeownership programming

[NEEDS INPUT: Insert projected number of households to be served based on the specific dollar amount requested and average cost-per-unit of repair assistance. This will require the applicant to estimate average repair project cost based on assessed community need and local contractor market rates.]

### Long-Term Impact and Sustainability

FAITH Foundation's long-term sustainability is built on a rotating housing asset model that does not depend on any single funding source. As residents of Cornerstone Communities transition to permanent housing, units become available for new participants. Revenue streams include program fees assessed on a sliding scale based on participant income, rental income from stabilized housing units, recurring grant funding from federal, state, and private sources, corporate sponsorships and in-kind donations, church partnerships and congregational giving, and individual donor cultivation.

Physical assets — including land and modular housing units acquired through the Cornerstone Communities initiative — appreciate over time and reduce ongoing capital expenditure requirements. The Foundation actively pursues diversified funding across government grants, private foundations, corporate giving programs, faith-based funders, and community development financial institutions to avoid dependency on any single source.

The HPG program is consistent with this diversification strategy. Federal investment through the Rural Housing Service provides a foundational funding layer that, paired with FAITH Foundation's private and faith-based revenue streams and in-kind contributions, creates a sustainable, multi-source funding model for ongoing rural housing preservation and rehabilitation work in South and Central Texas.

Beyond the award period, FAITH Foundation intends to pursue renewal HPG funding, leveraging documented outcomes from this award period to demonstrate program effectiveness and community impact. The organization's construction expertise — embodied in Treasurer Scott Ellis's 15 years of roofing and construction business leadership and Founder Reid Whitesides's 20 years of construction and housing industry experience — positions FAITH Foundation to continue delivering cost-effective, high-quality housing preservation assistance to very low- and low-income rural Texans for years beyond this initial award.

### Vision

FAITH Foundation envisions a rural South Texas where no very low- or low-income homeowner loses their home to preventable deterioration, and where every veteran, individual in recovery, formerly incarcerated citizen, and single-parent family has access to a safe, preserved home as the foundation for building a stable, self-sufficient future. The Rural Housing Service's Housing Preservation Grant program is the essential tool through which that vision becomes reality — one repaired roof, one restored foundation, one rehabilitated home at a time.

---

- [ ] IRS 501(c)(3) determination letter
- [ ] Proof of active SAM.gov registration and UEI number **[NEEDS INPUT: Obtain and attach]**

- [ ] Signed certifications required under 7 CFR Part 1944, Subpart N
- [ ] Documentation of rural area eligibility for proposed service communities **[NEEDS INPUT: Confirm specific target communities and rural eligibility]**
- [ ] Letters of support from partner organizations **[NEEDS INPUT: Obtain signed letters from church partners, county social services agencies, housing authorities, recovery programs, reentry service providers, and veterans service organizations]**
- [ ] Résumés of key personnel **[NEEDS INPUT: Attach résumés for Reid Whitesides, Scott Ellis, and any additional program staff]**
- [ ] Sample property assessment form and intake documentation
- [ ] Draft affordability agreement template for rental property owners **[NEEDS INPUT: Develop in consultation with RHS State Office]**

---

All organizational facts contained herein are sourced from verified FAITH Foundation organizational records. Sections marked [NEEDS INPUT] require additional information from organizational leadership before submission.*

> - **Unique Entity Identifier (UEI)** — Confirm that a UEI has been assigned through SAM.gov. The UEI replaced the DUNS number in April 2022 and is required on all federal grant applications. [NEEDS INPUT: Insert UEI number]
> - **NICRA / Indirect Cost Rate** — FAITH Foundation should elect to use the de minimis indirect cost rate of 10% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC) if no Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA) has been established. Document this election in the budget narrative. (2 CFR § 200.414)
> - **Single Audit Threshold** — FAITH Foundation's current annual budget of $75,000 is well below the $750,000 federal expenditure threshold that triggers a Single Audit requirement (2 CFR § 200.501). No single audit is required at this funding level; however, all expenditures must be documented in compliance with 2 CFR Part 200 Subpart E.
> - **Financial Management System** — FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks for accounting. Confirm that the system is configured to separately track federal award receipts and expenditures, compare outlays against budget amounts, and maintain written procedures for cost allowability determinations. (2 CFR § 200.302)

---

## SECTION I: ORGANIZATIONAL ELIGIBILITY AND CAPACITY

### Organizational Overview

FAITH Foundation — the Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope — is a 501(c)(3) public charity incorporated in Wyoming and operating in the state of Texas (EIN: 33-2640449). The Foundation's mission is to break the cycle of housing insecurity by providing financial education, homeownership instruction, and direct housing assistance to veterans, individuals experiencing homelessness, single parents, those in recovery, those reentering society, and other economically disadvantaged populations. Faith-based organizations are expressly encouraged to apply under this announcement, and FAITH Foundation proudly submits this application as a faith-rooted, community-centered organization that serves all individuals regardless of religious affiliation.

FAITH Foundation's primary populations of focus align directly with the VETS Stand Down program's purpose: we serve military veterans experiencing or at risk of homelessness as a core constituency, alongside individuals in recovery and reentry who frequently share the same service gaps. This Stand Down event represents a natural and mission-aligned extension of our existing programming — bringing the full array of employment, housing, social, and health services to veterans in one coordinated, accessible location.

### Organizational Capacity to Execute a Stand Down Event

FAITH Foundation's leadership team brings demonstrated expertise in construction, housing, community development, financial management, and faith-based community mobilization — precisely the combination of skills required to coordinate a multi-agency Stand Down event in South and Central Texas.

**Reid Whitesides — Founder, President & Executive Director** brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries. His background in coordinating complex projects across multiple contractors and stakeholders provides direct operational capacity for Stand Down logistics, vendor coordination, and site management. His lived experience — nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas, followed by more than fifteen years of sustained sobriety — gives him unparalleled credibility with the veteran and reentry populations this event will serve. Reid personally understands what it means to need a Stand Down moment, and he leads this effort from that place of conviction.

**Scott Ellis — Treasurer & Board Chair** is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based company he has led for more than 15 years. Scott's expertise in budgeting, contractor management, site coordination, and project oversight provides the financial and operational infrastructure to ensure this event is executed responsibly and within budget. His 24-year residency in the Central Texas community provides established local networks that support event partnerships and logistics.

**Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary & Protector** brings nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience and more than 40 years of faith-based community leadership. His ministry has extended across the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. Pastor Valdez brings deep trust networks within faith communities across South Texas — networks that translate directly into volunteer recruitment, donated services, and community partner engagement for the Stand Down event. He and his wife, Martha, operated a successful business in San Antonio for 34 years, demonstrating the sustained community presence and reliability that event partnerships require.

**Volunteers and Community Mobilization:** FAITH Foundation actively recruits and trains volunteers for mentorship, community outreach, and program delivery. The organization maintains active partnerships with local churches, recovery programs, reentry service providers, county social services agencies, and housing authorities across South Texas — all of whom are positioned to contribute volunteers, staff, and in-kind services to the Stand Down event.

**Technology and Administration:** FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks for financial management and the Benavora platform for grant administration and compliance tracking. Financial records are maintained in compliance with federal cost principles (2 CFR Part 200 Subpart E), with all expenditures documented for allowability, allocability, and reasonableness. Federal award funds will be tracked separately from all other organizational revenues.

[NEEDS INPUT: Specify any prior events coordinated — community resource fairs, housing fairs, veteran outreach events — that demonstrate direct event management experience. If none, note this is the organization's first Stand Down event and describe compensating capacity such as partnering lead organizations.]

---

## SECTION II: VETERAN NEED AND TARGET POPULATION

### The Scale of Veteran Homelessness in Texas

Texas ranks among the states with the highest concentrations of veterans experiencing homelessness in the nation. The need for coordinated, accessible, one-day service delivery events — precisely what the VETS Stand Down program funds — is acute and well-documented.

- **1,837 veterans** were experiencing homelessness in Texas during the 2024 Point-in-Time count — a decrease of 9.7% from 2,036 in 2023, but still representing nearly two thousand individuals who served their country and are now sleeping without safe, stable housing. (VA/HUD 2024 PIT Count)
- **4,085 veterans** were served by Texas Continuums of Care as of December 2023, up from 3,962 in 2022, indicating that the pipeline of veterans in need of services continues to grow even as overall counts modestly decline. (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network)
- **44% of all Texans experiencing homelessness** were unsheltered in 2024 — meaning they had no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing. (HUD 2024 AHAR) This unsheltered rate is particularly significant for veterans in rural South and Central Texas, where shelter infrastructure is thin and distances to urban service centers are prohibitive.
- Nationally, **13,851 veterans were unsheltered** on a single night in January 2024 — individuals sleeping in cars, under bridges, in fields, and in abandoned structures with no connection to the service systems that could change their trajectory. (VA 2024 PIT Count)
- **Black veterans are disproportionately represented** among homeless veterans, comprising 14% of the overall veteran population but 31% of homeless veterans nationwide. (Mission Roll Call, 2024) FAITH Foundation's service area in South and Central Texas includes communities where this disparity is compounded by limited access to VA facilities and culturally responsive services.

### The Specific Barriers Veterans Face in Our Service Area

Veterans experiencing homelessness in South and Central Texas face compounding barriers that a coordinated Stand Down event is uniquely positioned to address:

**Employment Disconnection:** Many veterans in our service area have been out of the formal workforce for extended periods. Service-connected disabilities, gaps in employment history, and lack of civilian credential translation create barriers to re-employment that require hands-on, individualized support — the kind of support that Stand Down employment services directly provide.

**VA Benefits Navigation Gaps:** Rural veterans frequently lack access to VA benefits counselors, claims assistance, and enrollment support. The Stand Down event will bring these services directly to veterans who cannot travel to urban VA facilities.

**Housing Instability as a Workforce Barrier:** FAITH Foundation's mission and programming begin from a foundational truth: stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained workforce participation. Veterans who are unsheltered or precariously housed cannot hold jobs, maintain transportation, or access healthcare. The Stand Down event addresses this nexus directly by co-locating housing navigation services with employment services, health screenings, and social support in a single, trusted environment.

**Recovery and Reentry Co-Occurrence:** In Texas, veterans experiencing homelessness frequently present with co-occurring substance use disorders and, in some cases, histories of incarceration — both of which FAITH Foundation is specifically equipped to address through our Veterans Path Home, Recovery Housing, and Second Chance Reentry programs. # Texas Community Development Block Grant — Housing
## Program Narrative
### FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope)
**EIN: 33-2640449 | 501(c)(3) Public Charity | Texas Service Area**

---

## SECTION I: STATEMENT OF NEED

### The Housing Crisis in Rural Texas: A Data-Driven Case for Immediate Investment

Rural South and Central Texas communities are experiencing a housing crisis that is simultaneously invisible and acute. Unlike urban homelessness, rural housing insecurity rarely generates shelter bed counts or visible encampments — it manifests instead as couch-surfing, overcrowded households, deteriorating structures, and individuals cycling between incarceration, addiction treatment, and the streets because no affordable transitional housing exists to receive them when they exit these systems. FAITH Foundation was established precisely to address this gap in rural Texas housing infrastructure where traditional nonprofit capacity is thin, affordable inventory is critically low, and the populations most in need — veterans, formerly incarcerated individuals, people in addiction recovery, and single-parent families — are concentrated without a structured pathway to stability.

**Texas-Specific Housing Need**

The scale of housing insecurity in Texas is documented and severe. According to the HUD 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, nearly 28,000 Texans were experiencing homelessness during the 2024 Point-in-Time count, including 1,837 veterans. Of that total, 44% — more than 12,000 individuals — were entirely unsheltered, meaning they lacked access to emergency shelter or transitional housing of any kind. Texas is among the seven states that collectively account for 64% of all homelessness in the United States (HUD 2024 AHAR), and chronic homelessness in Texas rose sharply from 1,949 individuals in 2022 to 2,594 in 2023, a 33% increase in a single year (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network).

These numbers do not occur in a vacuum. Texas released tens of thousands of individuals from state correctional facilities in recent years, and nationally, formerly incarcerated people are approximately 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population (National Low Income Housing Coalition / Prison Policy Initiative). Between 23.1% and 47.8% of annual homeless shelter admissions nationally are formerly incarcerated individuals (Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019). Research across 24 states found that 82% of individuals released from prison were re-arrested within 10 years of release (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024), and the research is clear that housing instability is a primary driver of recidivism — people experiencing homelessness after release face increased law enforcement contact and supervision violations directly tied to their housing status (CSG Justice Center, 2025).

**Veteran Housing Insecurity**

Texas has one of the highest concentrations of homeless veterans in the nation. While veteran homelessness in Texas declined 9.7% between 2023 and 2024 — from 2,036 to 1,837 individuals — the state's Continuums of Care served 4,085 veterans as of December 2023, reflecting the volume of veterans cycling through the crisis response system (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network). Nationally, 13,851 veterans remained unsheltered on a single night in January 2024 (VA 2024 PIT Count). In rural communities, these veterans frequently fall outside the geographic reach of VA-affiliated transitional housing programs concentrated in urban centers. FAITH Foundation's model brings housing solutions directly to rural communities where these veterans live, rather than requiring them to relocate to access services.

**Recovery Population Housing Gap**

The intersection of addiction recovery and housing instability is well-documented. Individuals completing addiction treatment programs are discharged into communities where affordable transitional housing is scarce or nonexistent, and without stable housing, the risk of relapse and subsequent system involvement increases dramatically. In rural South Texas, the scarcity of recovery-supportive transitional housing means that individuals who complete treatment frequently have nowhere to go — no sober-living environment, no case management, and no structured pathway to independence. FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities model was designed specifically to fill this gap: purpose-built transitional micro-communities that provide structured, supportive housing environments for individuals in active recovery.

**The Down Payment Barrier and Homeownership Gap**

Even for individuals who stabilize economically, the path to permanent housing through homeownership remains blocked by the down payment barrier. First-time homebuyers now represent just 21% of the market — the lowest share since NAR began tracking in 1981, compared to approximately 40% before 2008 (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers). The median age of first-time buyers has reached a record 40 years old, reflecting how long working families must save before achieving ownership (NAR 2025 Profile). For the populations FAITH Foundation serves, this barrier is compounded by criminal records that restrict private rental options, addiction histories that disrupt employment continuity, and single-income household budgets that cannot absorb both childcare and housing costs simultaneously. The homeownership rate among single mothers stands at approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples without children (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024). Nationally, the shortage of affordable rental units available to extremely low-income households exceeds 7.3 million units (National Low Income Housing Coalition), ensuring that even the rental market offers no adequate landing point for families trying to exit homelessness.

**Why Rural South Texas Requires a Targeted Response**

Rural communities in South and Central Texas face housing challenges that differ structurally from urban markets. Traditional affordable housing development — requiring large capital investments, zoning approvals, and proximity to construction labor markets — is cost-prohibitive in rural settings. Nonprofit housing infrastructure in rural Texas is sparse. Existing transitional housing programs are concentrated in San Antonio, Austin, and Houston, leaving communities in the rural corridor between these cities underserved. FAITH Foundation's modular housing deployment model was designed to address exactly this structural barrier: modular and manufactured housing units can be sited on donated or acquired rural land at a fraction of traditional construction costs, bringing housing solutions directly to the communities where need is greatest without requiring participants to uproot from their support networks to access services.

The combined evidence — rising chronic homelessness, a demonstrable reentry housing gap, veteran housing insecurity concentrated in Texas, a broken down payment pathway for low-income families, and the absence of purpose-built transitional housing infrastructure in rural South Texas — establishes a clear, data-supported case for the investment requested in this application.

---

## SECTION II: PROJECT DESIGN AND HOUSING STRATEGY

### An Integrated, Three-Program Housing Model Aligned with CDBG-Eligible Activities

FAITH Foundation requests funding under the Texas Community Development Block Grant — Housing program to advance three interconnected, CDBG-eligible housing activities: (1) direct down payment assistance for qualifying low-to-moderate income individuals and families, (2) transitional housing placement with wraparound case management, and (3) acquisition of modular housing units for deployment in Cornerstone Communities micro-developments in rural Texas. Each activity is designed to address a specific stage of the pathway from housing crisis to permanent stability, and each serves the priority populations identified in this solicitation — reentry individuals, those in active recovery, and veterans experiencing housing insecurity.

**Program Component 1: Down Payment Assistance**

FAITH Foundation's Down Payment Assistance Program provides direct financial awards to qualifying low-to-moderate income individuals and families who are employment-stable but lack savings for upfront housing costs — a gap that is particularly acute for reentry populations, veterans transitioning off military stipends, and single parents managing childcare costs on single incomes. Awards are structured as $2,500 vouchers applied toward down payments or rental security deposits, enabling recipients to access permanent housing they could not otherwise secure.

All recipients must meet income eligibility requirements consistent with HUD low-to-moderate income (LMI) benefit standards, and FAITH Foundation will document LMI status for each recipient using income verification consistent with 24 CFR Part 570 requirements. Recipients are enrolled concurrently in FAITH Foundation's financial literacy and homeownership counseling programming to ensure housing retention and long-term stability following award disbursement.

With CDBG funding, FAITH Foundation targets distribution of [NEEDS INPUT: specific number of vouchers to be funded by this grant request] down payment assistance awards during the grant period, with a projected cost per household assisted of $2,500 in direct assistance plus case management support.

**Program Component 2: Transitional Housing Placement with Case Management**

FAITH Foundation's Transitional Housing Program places individuals exiting homelessness, incarceration, or addiction treatment into stable transitional housing units with structured case management support, financial literacy training, and peer mentorship for up to 24 months. This program directly addresses the reentry and recovery housing gaps documented in the need statement above.

Program participants are referred through partnerships with recovery treatment programs, reentry service organizations, county social services agencies, local housing authorities, and veterans service organizations across South and Central Texas. Upon referral, a housing navigator coordinates placement into an available transitional unit and connects the participant with the following wraparound supports:

- **Case management:** Assigned case managers maintain a maximum 15-to-1 client ratio, providing individualized service planning, goal-setting, and progress monitoring on a regular basis throughout the participant's transitional housing tenure.
- **Financial literacy instruction:** Participants complete structured financial literacy programming covering budgeting, credit-building, debt management, and mortgage readiness — the financial competencies required to sustain permanent housing and progress toward homeownership.
- **Peer mentorship:** Participants are matched with mentors who have successfully navigated similar challenges, including FAITH Foundation Founder and President Reid Whitesides, who brings more than 15 years of sustained sobriety and personal experience with incarceration, addiction, and homelessness to the mentorship model.
- **Employment navigation:** For reentry and recovery participants, case managers coordinate with employer partners and employment services organizations to support job placement within 90 days of program enrollment.
- **Veterans benefits navigation:** Veteran participants receive dedicated support in accessing VA benefits, coordinated with veterans service organization partners.

The transitional housing model is designed with a defined progression: participants enter transitional housing upon referral, stabilize over a structured 12-to-24-month period with decreasing support intensity, and exit into permanent housing — ideally through the FAITH Foundation down payment assistance pipeline — as they demonstrate sustained stability.

**Program Component 3: Modular Housing Unit Acquisition — Cornerstone Communities**

The Cornerstone Communities Initiative is FAITH Foundation's supply-side response to the affordable housing crisis in rural Texas. Through this initiative, FAITH Foundation acquires donated or low-cost land parcels in rural South and Central Texas and deploys modular and manufactured housing units to create purpose-built transitional micro-communities. This approach directly addresses the structural barrier that makes traditional affordable housing development cost-prohibitive in rural settings: by using modular units sited on donated or acquired land, FAITH Foundation delivers durable, move-in-ready housing at a cost of $30,000 to $60,000 per unit, a fraction of traditional construction costs in comparable markets.

CDBG funds requested in this application are targeted specifically toward the acquisition of modular housing units for Cornerstone Communities deployment. Each unit acquired expands the permanent transitional housing capacity available to program participants in rural communities that currently have no comparable housing infrastructure.

Each Cornerstone Community is designed to include:
- Individual modular housing units providing private, dignified residential space for each household
- Shared community spaces for programming, peer support, and community building
- On-site access to case management and wraparound support services
- On-site recovery programming for participants in active recovery
- Remote work and learning facilities supporting employment and educational advancement
- Shuttle transportation supporting participant access to employment, medical, and social services in rural areas where personal transportation is not available

Through FAITH Foundation's strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes, modular and manufactured housing units are supplied by a builder with direct experience in this housing type, enabling charitable contributions and grant funds to be converted directly into durable, permanent housing assets.

As residents stabilize and transition to permanent housing through the down payment assistance pipeline, their units become available for new participants — creating a rotating, self-sustaining cycle of community impact where each grant dollar invested generates recurring housing capacity rather than a single-use expenditure.

**Housing Type and Accessibility**

All modular housing units acquired and deployed through this grant will comply with applicable accessibility standards consistent with Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and ADA requirements to the extent required. FAITH Foundation is committed to ensuring that units are accessible to individuals with mobility limitations and service-connected disabilities, consistent with the veteran and recovery populations served. [NEEDS INPUT: specific ADA accessibility specifications for modular units, or confirmation of compliance approach from Bright Box Homes or project architect]

**Site Control and Location**

[NEEDS INPUT: specific rural Texas county or community name where first Cornerstone Communities site is targeted; any existing site control documentation, letters of intent from landowners, or confirmed donated land parcels. If no site has been formally identified yet, note that site identification is an early grant period activity and describe the site selection criteria.]

**Timeline**

[NEEDS INPUT: project implementation timeline including key milestones — site identification/control, environmental review initiation, unit acquisition, site preparation, unit installation, first occupancy, and program enrollment targets by quarter during the grant period.]

**Note on HUD Environmental Review Compliance:** FAITH Foundation acknowledges that all HUD-assisted activities under this grant are subject to HUD Environmental Review requirements under 24 CFR Part 58 prior to the commitment or expenditure of funds on any project. No choice-limiting actions — including signing leases, purchasing property, or beginning construction — will be undertaken until the responsible entity completes and certifies the required environmental review and HUD approval is obtained. FAITH Foundation will coordinate fully with the administering jurisdiction on this requirement at the earliest stage of project development.

**Note on Davis-Bacon Prevailing Wage Requirements:** If construction or rehabilitation activities funded through this grant involve 8 or more units, FAITH Foundation acknowledges the applicability of Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirements under 40 U.S.C. §§ 3141–3148 and 29 CFR Part 5. FAITH Foundation will obtain certified payrolls from all contractors and conduct on-site interviews consistent with HUD Handbook 1344.1 requirements.

**Note on Section 3 Hiring Requirements:** For HUD-funded construction or professional services contracts above applicable thresholds, FAITH Foundation will make best-effort outreach to hire Section 3 workers — low-income persons and public housing residents — consistent with 24 CFR Part 135, with a target of 25% of new hires from Section 3 categories. FAITH Foundation will document all outreach efforts and submit required annual Section 3 Summary Reports (HUD-60002).

**Note on Lead-Based Paint:** All modular housing units acquired through this grant are new construction and are not subject to lead-based paint regulations applicable to pre-1978 housing. Any site preparation or ancillary structures involving pre-1978 construction will be assessed in compliance with 24 CFR Part 35 requirements.

---

## SECTION III: COMMUNITY NEED AND TARGET POPULATION

### Serving the Populations Texas CDBG Prioritizes

FAITH Foundation's program design is built around the priority populations explicitly identified in this solicitation: reentry individuals, those in addiction recovery, and veterans experiencing housing insecurity. These are not incidental beneficiaries of a broader housing program — they are the populations FAITH Foundation was founded to serve, and every element of the program model reflects the specific barriers these populations face.

**Reentry Population:** Formerly incarcerated individuals face an immediate and compounding housing crisis upon release. Criminal records disqualify them from most private rental housing; they lack the rental history, credit scores, and deposit savings required for market-rate housing; and without stable housing, they are statistically at severe risk of reincarceration. FAITH Foundation's Second Chance Reentry program addresses this gap directly — providing immediate transitional housing placement, employment navigation, and case management that gives formerly incarcerated individuals the stable foundation from which recovery and reintegration become possible. FAITH Foundation Founder Reid Whitesides brings personal credibility and lived experience to this work, having spent nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas before achieving more than 15 years of sustained sobriety and building a career in construction and housing.

**Recovery Population:** Individuals completing addiction treatment are discharged into communities where recovery-supportive housing is scarce, particularly in rural Texas. FAITH Foundation's Recovery Housing program provides a structured continuum from transitional sober-living through permanent independent housing, with on-site support groups, peer accountability, and case management at every stage. Cornerstone Communities are designed to serve recovery participants specifically, providing the structured, supportive community environment that evidence demonstrates is essential for sustained sobriety.

**Veterans:** FAITH Foundation's Veterans Path Home program provides rental assistance, VA benefits navigation, and dedicated case management for military veterans transitioning from housing instability to permanent homes. Referrals are coordinated through veteran service organization partnerships. With 1,837 Texas veterans identified as homeless in the 2024 Point-in-Time count and Texas maintaining one of the highest concentrations of homeless veterans nationally, the need for veteran-focused housing services in rural Texas communities — outside the urban service corridors — is both documented and urgent.

**Additional Priority Populations:** FAITH Foundation also serves single-parent families, with particular focus on single mothers who face a homeownership rate of approximately 34% compared to 84% for married couples without children (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024), and individuals experiencing or at risk of homelessness across South and Central Texas.

All FAITH Foundation programs are open to all eligible individuals regardless of race, color, national origin, sex, religion, disability, or familial status, consistent with Fair Housing Act requirements (42 U.S.C. §§ 3601–3619). FAITH Foundation maintains an affirmative marketing commitment to reaching the underserved populations most in need of affordable housing, including outreach through recovery treatment programs, reentry service organizations, veterans service organizations, and county social services agencies serving low-to-moderate income communities. All program materials will be made available in both English and Spanish consistent with the demographic profile of rural South Texas communities served.

---

## SECTION IV: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY AND EXPERIENCE

### Leadership, Expertise, and Demonstrated Capacity to Manage Federal Funds

FAITH Foundation's leadership team brings together direct lived experience with the populations served, professional expertise in construction and housing development, financial management credentials, and decades of organizational governance experience — a combination that positions the organization to execute this project responsibly and effectively.

**Reid Whitesides — Founder, President & Executive Director**

Reid Whitesides brings more than 20 years of professional experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries to his role as FAITH Foundation's executive leader. His background in real estate and construction is the direct foundation of the Cornerstone Communities model — he understands modular housing deployment, site development, construction cost management, and contractor coordination from professional experience. Equally important, Reid's personal history — nearly twenty years incarcerated in Texas, followed by more than 15 years of sustained sobriety — gives him firsthand credibility and insight into the challenges facing every population FAITH Foundation serves. He leads the organization with the conviction that lives are transformed when people are given access to stable housing and genuine opportunity.

**Scott Ellis — Treasurer and Board Chair**

Scott Ellis is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based construction company he has led successfully for more than 15 years. His hands-on experience in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems provides the Foundation with direct construction expertise for modular housing acquisition and community development projects. As Treasurer and Board Chair, Scott provides financial oversight and fiduciary accountability, ensuring that all grant funds are managed with integrity and reported accurately. FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks for financial management, with board-level review of financial reports on a regular basis.

**Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary and Protector**

Pastor Juan Valdez brings nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience and more than 40 years of faith-based leadership to his role providing spiritual oversight, governance accountability, and mission stewardship. His business ownership experience — operating a successful community business at the same San Antonio location for 34 years — reflects the consistency, reliability, and long-term stewardship that characterize the Foundation's approach to housing development and community investment.

**Partnership Infrastructure Supporting Capacity**

FAITH Foundation's capacity extends beyond its leadership team through an active network of community partnerships. Church partners provide volunteer labor, mentorship volunteers, and meeting space for participant programming. Recovery program partners refer individuals completing treatment and provide ongoing support for residents in active recovery. Reentry service partners coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals and connect them with employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support. County social services agencies and local housing authorities coordinate benefits enrollment and case management collaboration. Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers — including strategic partner Bright Box Homes — provide discounted or donated units and materials. Veterans service organizations refer veterans and coordinate VA benefits enrollment. This partnership ecosystem significantly expands FAITH Foundation's effective service capacity beyond what its operating budget alone would reflect.

**Federal Funds Management**

FAITH Foundation maintains financial management systems capable of supporting federal grant compliance requirements, including QuickBooks accounting software, board-level financial oversight, and commitment to the reporting and documentation requirements of CDBG-funded activities. FAITH Foundation's annual operating budget is $75,000, and the organization is committed to maintaining indirect costs below 15% of total program budget, with the substantial majority of grant funds directed to direct program delivery. ## SECTION V: BUDGET JUSTIFICATION AND COST EFFECTIVENESS

### Maximizing Direct Housing Impact with Every Grant Dollar

FAITH Foundation's budget allocation for this grant prioritizes direct program delivery and housing asset acquisition, with administrative overhead maintained below 15% of total program budget. The following narrative describes the cost rationale for each major budget category.

**Direct Housing Assistance — Down Payment Vouchers**

Down payment assistance awards are disbursed at $2,500 per household, a targeted amount designed to bridge the specific gap between a recipient's available savings and the upfront cost required to secure permanent housing. At this award level, FAITH Foundation achieves a cost-per-household-assisted that is among the most efficient available in the affordable housing assistance landscape, while providing meaningful impact — a $2,500 award can represent the difference between securing permanent housing and returning to homelessness for a family with steady income but no savings reserve.

Each unit acquired is a durable, permanent housing asset that generates recurring program capacity — as residents transition to permanent housing, the unit is made available for the next participant, multiplying the effective impact of the initial acquisition investment over the life of the asset.

## SECTION VI: SUSTAINABILITY AND LONG-TERM IMPACT

### A Self-Sustaining Housing Model Built to Outlast Any Single Grant

FAITH Foundation's sustainability model is not contingent on continued grant funding — it is structurally designed to generate ongoing housing capacity through the rotating housing asset model at the core of the Cornerstone Communities initiative.

**Rotating Housing Asset Model**

Each modular housing unit acquired through grant funding is a permanent, appreciating asset. As residents complete their transitional housing tenures and transition to permanent housing through FAITH Foundation's down payment assistance pipeline, their units become available for new participants at no additional acquisition cost. A single unit investment generates recurring capacity for the life of the asset — potentially decades of housing provision for successive generations of program participants. This structure means that CDBG investment in unit acquisition creates permanent, self-renewing housing capacity in rural Texas communities that currently have none.

**Diversified Revenue Streams**

FAITH Foundation's operational sustainability rests on diversified revenue that avoids dependency on any single funding source:

- **Program fees:** Assessed on a sliding scale based on participant income, ensuring affordability while generating operational revenue
- **Rental income:** From stabilized housing units as the Cornerstone Communities portfolio grows
- **Recurring grant funding:** Federal, state, and private foundation grants across housing, reentry, recovery, and veterans programming categories
- **Bright Box Homes partnership:** $2,500 per home sold donated to FAITH Foundation for down payment vouchers — a renewable, self-sustaining funding mechanism tied to new home construction
- **Corporate sponsorships and in-kind donations:** Building materials, professional services, and equipment from corporate partners
- **Church partnerships and congregational giving:** Volunteer labor, meeting space, and financial contributions from faith community partners
- **Individual donor cultivation:** Growing individual donor base supporting the Foundation's mission

**Community Partnerships Ensuring Long-Term Resident Support**

Participants transitioning out of FAITH Foundation transitional housing into permanent housing maintain connections to the broader support network — recovery program partners, veterans service organizations, reentry service providers, and employer partners — ensuring that the Foundation's investment in each participant's stability is reinforced by community infrastructure that extends beyond the program tenure.

**Long-Term Vision**

Within five years, FAITH Foundation intends to operate a network of Cornerstone Communities across rural South Texas, serving as a replicable model for how modular housing, faith-based mentorship, and wraparound support services can permanently break the cycle of homelessness for veterans, reentry individuals, those in recovery, and single-parent families. By demonstrating measurable outcomes in housing retention, employment placement, recidivism reduction, and homeownership conversion, FAITH Foundation will build the evidence base for scaling this model through sustained federal, state, and private funding partnerships.

## SECTION VII: EQUITY, FAIR HOUSING, AND COMPLIANCE COMMITMENTS

### Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing

FAITH Foundation is committed to full compliance with the Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 3601–3619) and all applicable civil rights requirements of HUD-funded programs, including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act.

Outreach channels include recovery treatment programs, reentry service organizations, veterans service organizations, county social services agencies, and faith communities serving low-income populations across rural South and Central Texas. Program materials are prepared in both English and Spanish, and staff and volunteers with lived experience in reentry, recovery, and veteran transition serve as trusted messengers within target communities.

**Non-Discrimination:** FAITH Foundation maintains a written non-discrimination policy prohibiting discrimination based on race, color, national origin, sex, religion, disability, familial status, or any other protected class in the administration of all housing programs. This policy applies to participant intake, housing placement, program services, and all aspects of housing assistance administration.

**LMI Benefit Documentation:** All program participants will be documented as meeting HUD low-to-moderate income (LMI) benefit requirements consistent with 24 CFR Part 570. Income verification will be completed at intake using documentation acceptable under HUD guidelines, and LMI compliance will be tracked and reported as required by the administering jurisdiction.

**Accessibility:** FAITH Foundation is committed to ensuring that all housing units and facilities developed or operated with CDBG funds meet applicable accessibility requirements for individuals with disabilities consistent with Section 504 and ADA standards.
