# IMPORTANT NOTICE TO APPLICANT — READ BEFORE SUBMITTING

**This grant narrative has been prepared using FAITH Foundation's verified organizational data. However, the opportunity for which this narrative was requested — the Personnel Demonstration Project at the United States Army Communications-Electronics Command (CECOM) Software Engineering Center (SEC) Science and Technology Reinvention Laboratory (STRL) — is a Federal Register Notice (FRN) announcing a proposed internal federal personnel management demonstration project applicable only to CECOM SEC STRL civilian employees. It is not a grant competition open to external nonprofit organizations.**

**FAITH Foundation, as a 501(c)(3) housing nonprofit, is not an eligible entity for this personnel demonstration project. The FRN does not solicit grant applications from community organizations; it proposes changes to federal civilian workforce personnel systems under 5 U.S.C. § 4703.**

**Submitting a grant narrative in response to this FRN will not result in funding and may not receive a response. FAITH Foundation should redirect its federal funding strategy toward eligible opportunities such as HUD's Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), HOME Investment Partnerships Program, HUD Continuum of Care (CoC), VA Supportive Services for Veteran Families (SSVF), or USDA Rural Housing programs.**

**The narrative below has been drafted as requested and is structured to demonstrate organizational capacity to the maximum extent possible using verified organizational data. All compliance gaps required by federal standards have been flagged. This document should be reviewed by qualified grant counsel before any submission.**

---

# Grant Narrative

## FAITH Foundation — Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope
**EIN:** 33-2640449
**Organization Type:** 501(c)(3) Public Charity
**Primary Service Area:** South and Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast Region
**Founder & President:** Reid Whitesides

---

## SECTION I: STATEMENT OF NEED

### The Housing Crisis Confronting the Populations FAITH Foundation Serves

The United States is experiencing a housing crisis of historic proportions, and the populations FAITH Foundation serves — military veterans, individuals in addiction recovery, formerly incarcerated citizens reentering society, single-parent families, and individuals experiencing or at risk of homelessness — sit at the most acute intersection of that crisis. The evidence is documented across every federal data source and research institution tracking housing stability in America.

**National Homelessness Data**

On a single night in January 2025, 745,652 people were experiencing homelessness across the United States, including 266,320 living entirely unsheltered (HUD 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report). While homelessness declined 3.3% between 2024 and 2025 — representing the first overall decrease since 2016 — chronic homelessness increased 2.1% in the same period, and homelessness among adults aged 65 and older increased 6.8% (HUD 2025 AHAR). Critically, the national homelessness response system maintains permanent housing units for only 9.5% of people in need and has only enough shelter capacity to house 16% of households currently in shelter (National Alliance to End Homelessness, 2025). The system is not closing the gap; it is managing the overflow.

Texas is among the states bearing the greatest burden: 64% of all people experiencing homelessness live in just seven states, of which Texas is one (HUD 2024 AHAR).

**Texas-Specific Data**

Nearly 28,000 Texans were experiencing homelessness in the 2024 Point-in-Time count, including 1,837 veterans (HUD 2024 AHAR, cited in Texas HB 158). Of those Texans without housing, 44% were entirely unsheltered — without access to emergency shelter or transitional housing of any kind (HUD 2024 AHAR). Chronic homelessness in Texas grew from 1,949 individuals in 2022 to 2,594 in 2023, a 33% increase in a single year (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network). Texas is not solving its homelessness problem; it is watching it deepen.

**Veteran Housing Instability**

32,882 veterans were experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2024 — a record low since measurement began in 2009, but still representing tens of thousands of men and women who served this country (VA 2024 PIT Count). Of those, 13,851 were unsheltered. In Texas specifically, veteran homelessness decreased 9.7% between 2023 and 2024, from 2,036 to 1,837 (VA/HUD 2024 PIT Count), a positive trend that nonetheless leaves nearly two thousand Texas veterans without stable housing on any given night. Black veterans make up 14% of the overall veteran population but represent 31% of homeless veterans (Mission Roll Call, 2024) — a disparity that reflects systemic inequities FAITH Foundation's programs are specifically designed to address.

**Reentry and Formerly Incarcerated Populations**

Formerly incarcerated people are approximately ten times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population (National Low Income Housing Coalition, 2018; Prison Policy Initiative). They make up between 23.1% and 47.8% of annual homeless shelter admissions nationally (Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019). Nearly 450,000 individuals were released from state and federal prisons in 2021 alone, and the average formerly incarcerated individual spends more than six months unemployed post-release (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024). 82% of individuals released from prison across 24 states were re-arrested within ten years of release — a recidivism rate that correlates directly with housing instability at the time of release (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024).

Compounding this crisis is the national shortage of 7.3 million rental units affordable and available to extremely low-income households — units from which people with criminal records are additionally excluded by private landlord screening policies (National Low Income Housing Coalition).

**The Down Payment Barrier**

First-time homebuyers now make up just 21% of the housing market, the lowest share since the National Association of Realtors began tracking in 1981 (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers). The median age of first-time homebuyers has climbed to a record 40 years old (NAR 2025 Profile). 67% of millennials have no savings for a home down payment (REsimpli 2025 Market Survey). 74.2% of homeowner households with incomes below $30,000 are cost-burdened, paying more than 30% of income on housing — the highest rate in over 20 years (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University, 2023). The homeownership rate among single mothers is approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples without children (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024).

**The Gap FAITH Foundation Fills**

The data reveals two interconnected failures. First, there is insufficient housing inventory affordable to the populations FAITH Foundation serves. Second, there is insufficient direct financial assistance to bridge the gap between rental instability and permanent homeownership. Most existing programs address one or the other — they provide rental assistance, emergency shelter, or counseling, but stop short of homeownership. FAITH Foundation addresses both: the demand side through direct down payment assistance vouchers and housing counseling, and the supply side through our Cornerstone Communities land acquisition and development initiative. In rural South Texas, where nonprofit housing infrastructure is critically thin, this integrated approach represents the only pathway from crisis to permanent ownership for the populations we serve.

---

## SECTION II: PROGRAM DESIGN

### Theory of Change

Stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery from addiction, successful community reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. FAITH Foundation's model addresses the root cause of cyclical homelessness: the absence of affordable transitional housing in rural communities. By deploying modular housing units in purpose-built Cornerstone Communities, paired with case management, peer mentorship, financial literacy education, and direct down payment assistance, individuals progress through a structured pathway from crisis to stability to permanent homeownership. Each successful transition frees capacity for the next participant, creating a self-sustaining cycle of community impact.

### Integrated Program Ecosystem

FAITH Foundation operates eight interconnected programs, each addressing a different stage of the journey from housing instability to permanent ownership. Participants may enter through any program door; all pathways converge on the same destination.

**1. Homeownership Counseling**
Our flagship program provides pre-purchase counseling, mortgage readiness assessment, and buyer education to prepare families for sustainable homeownership. Counseling is delivered through individual sessions and group workshops tailored to participants' financial situations and housing goals.

**2. Down Payment and Housing Vouchers**
FAITH Foundation provides direct financial assistance in the form of $2,500 vouchers toward down payments and rental deposits for qualifying families. This program is sustained in part through our strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes, a modular and container home builder that donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold — creating a self-reinforcing funding cycle in which each new home built generates assistance for the next family.

**3. Emergency Bridge Housing**
Rapid rental and deposit assistance for families facing sudden housing crises prevents evictions before they cascade into homelessness. Emergency bridge housing serves as the first point of contact for families in acute crisis and links them immediately to longer-term program supports.

**4. Veterans Path Home**
Dedicated rental assistance, VA benefits navigation, and individualized case management for military veterans transitioning from housing instability to permanent homes. This program addresses both the financial and bureaucratic barriers that prevent veterans from accessing the benefits they have earned.

**5. Recovery Housing**
A structured continuum from sober living through transitional housing to permanent independent housing, with on-site support groups and accountability at every stage. Recovery housing participants progress through clearly defined milestones that parallel their sobriety milestones, ensuring that housing stability and recovery reinforce each other.

**6. Second Chance Reentry**
Transitional housing, employment support, and case management for formerly incarcerated individuals rebuilding stability after release. The program coordinates with reentry service partners to place individuals into housing upon release and connects them with employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support.

**7. Single Parent Stability**
Affordable housing assistance paired with childcare navigation and financial coaching for single-parent families working toward homeownership. Given that the homeownership rate among single mothers is approximately 34% — less than half the rate for married couples — this program addresses a specific and severe gap in the housing market.

**8. Financial Literacy**
Hands-on budgeting, credit-building, and debt management education that prepares families to qualify for and sustain homeownership. Financial literacy is integrated into all other programs and delivered as a standalone offering for community members not yet enrolled in housing services.

### Cornerstone Communities Initiative

Beyond direct voucher assistance, FAITH Foundation addresses the supply side of the housing crisis through the Cornerstone Communities initiative — the organization's flagship development model and its most distinctive contribution to the housing landscape in rural South Texas.

FAITH Foundation acquires donated land from private owners, churches, municipalities, and developers, then develops purpose-built residential micro-communities using modular and manufactured housing units supplied through our strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes. Each Cornerstone Community includes individual housing units, shared community spaces, and on-site access to wraparound services including recovery programming, remote work and learning centers, community laundry facilities, shuttle transportation for rural case management outreach, and dedicated case management.

Residents enter Cornerstone Communities as transitional housing participants and graduate into permanent homeownership through FAITH Foundation's voucher pipeline. As residents transition to permanent housing, their units become available for new participants — creating a self-sustaining cycle of community impact without continuous capital reinvestment.

This model is specifically designed for rural South Texas, where traditional construction timelines and costs make conventional affordable housing development prohibitive and where nonprofit infrastructure is sparse. Modular units can be sited on donated or acquired rural land without the delays associated with traditional construction, bringing housing solutions directly to underserved communities rather than concentrating resources in urban centers.

**Capital Requirements for Cornerstone Communities Development**

The capital needs of the Cornerstone Communities initiative are specific and well-defined: land parcels suitable for micro-community development; modular housing units at $30,000 to $60,000 per unit; site preparation and utility infrastructure; community common spaces; and program vehicles for rural case management outreach.

### Participant Pathway and Enrollment

[NEEDS INPUT: A detailed participant enrollment timeline with specific recruitment, screening, and onboarding procedures consistent with any applicable program evaluation schedule. FAITH Foundation is in its inaugural operating year and has not yet established a formal enrollment tracking system. The following framework represents intended procedures, which should be refined with input from program staff before submission to a federal agency.]

FAITH Foundation's intended enrollment process proceeds through four stages:

**Stage 1 — Outreach and Referral.** Participants are identified through active referral partnerships with local churches, recovery programs, reentry service providers, county social services agencies, local housing authorities, and veterans service organizations. The Foundation also accepts direct applications through its website and community outreach events.

**Stage 2 — Screening and Eligibility Determination.** All applicants are screened for program eligibility based on income level, housing status, and alignment with one or more priority population categories (veteran status, recovery, reentry, single-parent household, or general housing instability). Screening is conducted by a housing navigator who coordinates placement across transitional and permanent housing options.

**Stage 3 — Enrollment and Case Plan Development.** Enrolled participants complete a comprehensive intake assessment that establishes baseline housing status, financial readiness, employment status, and support service needs. Each participant receives an individualized case plan with defined milestones and timelines.

**Stage 4 — Ongoing Case Management and Milestone Tracking.** Case managers maintain a maximum 15-to-1 client ratio and conduct regular check-ins to monitor progress, adjust case plans, and connect participants with wraparound services. All participant data is recorded in FAITH Foundation's case management system and reported quarterly to the board of directors.

**Year 1 Enrollment Targets:**
- 10 down payment assistance vouchers distributed
- 25 families enrolled in homeownership counseling and financial literacy programming
- 15 families served through emergency bridge housing assistance
- 20 volunteers recruited and trained for mentorship, financial literacy instruction, and outreach

---

## SECTION III: EVALUATION AND DATA INTEGRITY

### How FAITH Foundation Measures Success

FAITH Foundation tracks and reports on five impact domains across all programs:

**1. Housing Placement:** Number of individuals and families transitioned from homelessness or unstable housing into transitional units and permanent housing, tracked by 30-, 60-, and 90-day retention rates.

**2. Financial Stability:** Number of down payment assistance awards disbursed, average award amount, and percentage of recipients maintaining stable housing at 12 months.

**3. Reentry Success:** Number of formerly incarcerated individuals housed, employment placement rates within 90 days of program enrollment, and recidivism reduction compared to regional averages.

**4. Recovery Outcomes:** Number of individuals in active recovery housed through the program, sobriety milestones maintained, and connection rates to ongoing treatment and support services.

**5. Community Development:** Number of Cornerstone Communities sites developed, total modular housing units acquired and placed, occupancy rates, and successful transitions from transitional to permanent housing.

### Key Performance Indicators

The following KPIs are tracked quarterly across all programs:

- **Vouchers Distributed:** Total number and dollar value of down payment and housing vouchers issued per quarter
- **Housing Retention Rate:** Percentage of voucher recipients who remain stably housed at 6-month and 12-month intervals
- **Homeownership Conversion Rate:** Percentage of program participants who transition from rental housing to homeownership within 24 months of enrollment
- **Financial Readiness Score:** Measured improvement in credit score, debt-to-income ratio, and savings rate among financial literacy program completers
- **Employment Placement Rate:** Percentage of reentry and recovery participants placed in employment within 90 days of program enrollment
- **Recidivism Prevention Rate:** Percentage of reentry participants who avoid reincarceration within 24 months of program completion
- **Recovery Stability Rate:** Percentage of recovery housing participants who maintain sobriety and stable housing at 12-month intervals
- **Volunteer Engagement:** Total volunteer hours and number of active mentor-mentee relationships
- **Cornerstone Communities Occupancy:** Units built, units occupied, and percentage of residents progressing toward homeownership

### Data Collection and Reporting

All program data is collected through FAITH Foundation's case management system. FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks for financial management and accounting. Program data is reported quarterly to the board of directors. Annual impact reports are published and made available to all funders, donors, and stakeholders. The Foundation is committed to transparency in both financial stewardship and program outcomes and intends to pursue third-party outcome verification beginning in Year 2 of operations.

[NEEDS INPUT: Specific data management software or case management platform name used for participant tracking. If no platform has been selected, this should be identified before federal submission, as federal evaluators will expect a named system with defined data integrity protocols.]

## SECTION IV: BUDGET JUSTIFICATION AND FUND UTILIZATION

### How Funds Will Be Used

FAITH Foundation's budget allocation prioritizes direct program delivery over administrative overhead. All expenditures are structured to ensure that funds are used for allowable, allocable, and reasonable costs consistent with 2 CFR Part 200 Subpart E.

**Personnel Costs**
Personnel expenditures support case managers maintaining a maximum 15-to-1 client ratio, a housing navigator who coordinates placement across transitional and permanent housing options, and program administration. Personnel costs are budgeted to remain within appropriate proportions of total program expenditure to ensure sufficient direct program investment.

**Capital Expenditures**
- Modular housing unit acquisition: $30,000 to $60,000 per unit
- Site preparation and utility infrastructure installation
- Community common space construction
- Program vehicles for rural case management outreach

**Operating Costs**
- Property maintenance and insurance
- Participant support services
- Transportation for rural case management outreach
- Program supplies and materials

**Direct Assistance**
- Down payment assistance vouchers: $2,500 per voucher
- Emergency bridge housing deposits and rental assistance

**Indirect Costs**
Indirect costs are maintained below 15% of total program budget and cover organizational administration, accounting, reporting, and compliance. In-kind donations of building materials, volunteer labor, and professional services significantly reduce cash outlays and are documented at fair market value for matching fund requirements.

[NEEDS INPUT: Total funding amount requested, specific budget line items with dollar amounts, and a detailed budget narrative broken down by program area. FAITH Foundation's annual operating budget is $75,000; for any federal award exceeding this amount, a revised budget will need to be prepared.]

## SECTION V: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY AND ADMINISTRATIVE INFRASTRUCTURE

### Leadership Team

FAITH Foundation is led by a governance team whose combined expertise spans construction, financial management, faith-based ministry, nonprofit administration, and firsthand lived experience of the barriers the Foundation exists to address.

**Reid Whitesides — Founder, President, and Executive Director**
Reid Whitesides brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries. His commitment to FAITH Foundation's mission is deeply personal: during a long struggle with addiction, Reid spent nearly 20 years incarcerated in the State of Texas. Those experiences gave him firsthand insight into the challenges many face when rebuilding their lives after addiction, incarceration, and homelessness. Today, he has been sober for more than 15 years. Reid also has expertise in technology development, including websites, software applications, and automation tools that support nonprofit and housing-focused initiatives — capabilities directly applicable to FAITH Foundation's data management and program tracking infrastructure.

**Scott Ellis — Treasurer and Board Chair**
Scott Ellis is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based company he has led for more than 15 years. His experience in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems provides the Foundation with construction expertise directly applicable to Cornerstone Communities development. As Treasurer and Board Chair, Scott oversees financial stewardship, strategic guidance, and governance accountability. He has been a Georgetown, Texas resident for more than 24 years and brings demonstrated community rootedness to the Foundation's leadership.

**Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary and Protector**
Pastor Juan Valdez brings more than 40 years of Christian faith and nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience to his role providing spiritual oversight, governance accountability, and mission stewardship. His ministry has extended across the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. Beyond ministry, Pastor Valdez and his wife Martha operated a successful business in San Antonio for 34 years — a record of sustained community presence and operational consistency that directly reflects the qualities of reliability and stewardship he brings to the Foundation's governance. He currently serves as an Associate Pastor at Temple of Praise in Texas.

### Financial Management Systems

FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks for financial management and accounting. The organization is committed to maintaining a financial management system that provides accurate, current, and complete disclosure of financial results; records that adequately identify the source and application of funds; and written procedures for determining the allowability of costs, consistent with the requirements of 2 CFR § 200.302.

### Partnership Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation maintains active partnerships across multiple sectors to maximize program reach and reduce operational costs:

- **Church partners:** Provide volunteer labor, congregational fundraising, mentorship volunteers, and meeting space for participant programming
- **Recovery program partners:** Refer individuals completing treatment who need stable transitional housing and provide ongoing support services for residents in active recovery
- **Reentry service partners:** Coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals into transitional housing upon release and connect them with employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support
- **County social services agencies and local housing authorities:** Refer eligible families and individuals, coordinate benefits enrollment, and provide case management collaboration
- **Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers:** Provide discounted or donated materials and units for Cornerstone Communities development
- **Land owners in rural South Texas:** Donate or sell land at reduced cost for community development sites
- **Veterans service organizations:** Refer military veterans experiencing housing insecurity and coordinate VA benefits enrollment
- **Bright Box Homes:** Strategic partner supplying modular and manufactured housing units for Cornerstone Communities and generating recurring voucher funding through a $2,500-per-sale donation mechanism

### In-Kind Resource Mobilization

FAITH Foundation actively accepts and coordinates in-kind donations including land, building materials, modular and manufactured housing units, construction equipment and labor, furnishings, appliances, household goods, and professional services including legal, architectural, surveying, and construction management. In-kind contributions are documented at fair market value for matching fund and reporting purposes.

### Organizational Stage and Funding History

FAITH Foundation is in its inaugural year of operations. The organization was established to address critical gaps in rural South Texas housing infrastructure, with initial operations funded through founder investment and church community support. As a pre-revenue organization, FAITH Foundation has not yet produced measurable program outcomes; the targets described in this narrative represent intended Year 1, Year 2, and Year 3 goals based on evidence-based models documented by HUD, the VA, and peer organizations operating similar housing voucher and community development programs.

---

## SECTION VI: SUSTAINABILITY PLAN

FAITH Foundation's long-term sustainability is built on a rotating housing asset model that reduces ongoing capital requirements as the organization matures.

**Cornerstone Communities as a Sustainable Asset**
As residents transition from Cornerstone Communities to permanent homeownership, their units become available for new participants. This rotation model generates ongoing program capacity without proportional capital reinvestment. Physical assets — land parcels and modular housing units — appreciate over time and reduce the organization's dependence on recurring grant funding for capital needs.

**Diversified Revenue Streams**
- Program fees assessed on a sliding scale based on participant income
- Rental income from stabilized housing units
- Recurring grant funding from federal, state, and private sources
- Corporate sponsorships and in-kind donations
- Church partnerships and congregational giving
- Individual donor cultivation
- Bright Box Homes partnership donations ($2,500 per home sold)

**Cost Control Mechanisms**
Operational costs are controlled through volunteer labor, donated materials, and shared administrative infrastructure across program sites. The Foundation actively pursues diversification across government grants, private foundations, corporate giving programs, faith-based funders, and community development financial institutions to avoid dependency on any single revenue source.

**Five-Year Vision**
Within five years, FAITH Foundation intends to be the leading housing voucher and community development organization serving veterans, reentry, recovery, and single-parent populations in Texas. The Cornerstone Communities model is designed to be replicable in any state where donated land and housing inventory shortages intersect. By demonstrating measurable outcomes in homeownership conversion, housing retention, and community stability, FAITH Foundation intends to establish the evidence base for scaling this model through federal, state, and private funding partnerships.

---

## SECTION VII: INTENDED IMPACT

### Year 1 Targets (Founding Year)
- Distribute 10 down payment assistance vouchers ($2,500 each), totaling $25,000 in direct housing assistance
- Enroll 25 families in homeownership counseling and financial literacy programming
- Provide emergency bridge housing assistance to 15 families facing immediate housing crises
- Establish partnerships with a minimum of 3 local employers for reentry and recovery program participants
- Secure the first donated land parcel for Cornerstone Communities development
- Recruit and train 20 volunteers for mentorship, financial literacy instruction, and community outreach

### Year 2 Targets
- Distribute 40 housing vouchers, totaling $100,000 in direct assistance
- Graduate 20 families from homeownership counseling into active homebuyer status
- Begin construction on the first Cornerstone Community with on-site programming
- Expand recovery housing partnerships to serve 30 individuals annually
- Place 15 reentry participants into stable employment within 90 days of program enrollment
- Achieve a 90% housing retention rate among voucher recipients at the 12-month mark

### Year 3 Targets
- Distribute 100 housing vouchers, totaling $250,000 in direct assistance
- Complete and occupy the first Cornerstone Community with a minimum of 20 residential units
- Achieve a homeownership conversion rate of 30% among program participants who entered in Year 1
- Expand geographic service area beyond initial Texas communities
- Establish a second corporate partnership generating recurring voucher funding
- Publish the first annual impact report with independently verified outcome data

### Long-Term Impact Thesis

The ultimate measure of FAITH Foundation's success is not how many families we serve temporarily, but how many families we move permanently into homes they own. Homeownership is the single most effective vehicle for long-term stability, intergenerational wealth building, and community investment. Our model is designed to move families not just out of crisis, but into ownership — and by doing so, to break the cycle of housing insecurity for the populations most systematically excluded from that opportunity.

---

## COMPLIANCE FLAGS — ACTION REQUIRED BEFORE FEDERAL SUBMISSION

The following compliance items require immediate attention before FAITH Foundation submits any application for federal financial assistance. These flags are generated by applicable federal regulations and are not optional.

> **[REQUIRED] Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) — MISSING OR NON-COMPLIANT**
> All applicants for federal financial assistance must have a Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) assigned through SAM.gov. The UEI replaced the DUNS number in April 2022 and is required on all federal grant applications and award documents. *(2 CFR § 200.1; GSA UEI transition policy, April 4, 2022)*
> **Action Required:** Register for or confirm your active UEI at SAM.gov before submitting any federal application.

> **[REQUIRED] SAM.gov Active Registration — REQUIRES ATTENTION**
> All organizations applying for or receiving federal financial assistance must be registered and maintain an active registration in SAM.gov. Registration must be renewed annually. A lapsed registration can delay or disqualify an award. *(2 CFR § 200.206; FAR 52.204-7)*
> **Action Required:** Confirm that FAITH Foundation's SAM.gov registration is active and current.

> **[REQUIRED] Financial Management System Standards — REQUIRES ATTENTION**
> Recipients must maintain a financial management system providing accurate, current, and complete disclosures of financial results; records identifying the source and application of funds; effective internal controls; comparison of outlays with budget amounts; and written procedures for determining allowability of costs. *(2 CFR § 200.302)*
> **Action Required:** Document FAITH Foundation's financial management procedures in writing, including QuickBooks configuration for federal fund tracking and internal controls.

> **[REQUIRED] Federal Cost Principles Compliance — REQUIRES ATTENTION**
> All costs charged to federal awards must be allowable, allocable, and reasonable, consistently applied and conforming to any limitations in the federal award. Unallowable costs include lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties. Documentation must support all expenditures. *(2 CFR Part 200 Subpart E, §§ 200.400–200.476)*
> **Action Required:** Establish written cost allocation policies before receiving federal funds.

> **[REQUIRED] Administrative Requirements — REQUIRES ATTENTION**
> Recipients must maintain internal controls, comply with federal statutes and regulations, and follow the terms and conditions of the federal award, including performance reporting, financial reporting, records retention (3 years minimum), subrecipient monitoring, and prior approval for certain budget modifications. *(2 CFR Part 200 Subpart D, §§ 200.300–200.345)*
> **Action Required:** Develop written policies for records retention, performance reporting, and budget modification approval before receiving federal funds.

> **[REQUIRED] Property Management Standards — REQUIRES ATTENTION**
> Equipment and real property acquired with federal funds must be managed per federal standards, including maintaining a property inventory, conducting physical inventories at least every two years, calculating depreciation, securing federal approval for disposal, and returning residual inventory upon award closeout. *(2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316)*
> **Action Required:** Given that FAITH Foundation's programs involve modular housing units and land parcels, a formal property management policy compliant with federal standards must be developed before acquiring any federally funded real property.

> **[REQUIRED] Federal Procurement Standards — REQUIRES ATTENTION**
> Procurements under federal awards must follow documented procedures providing full and open competition. Methods include micro-purchases (under $10,000), small purchases ($10,000–$250,000), sealed bids, competitive proposals, and noncompetitive proposals. Conflicts of interest must be avoided and documented. *(2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327)*
> **Action Required:** Develop written procurement policies, including conflict of interest procedures, before making any purchases with federal funds. Note that Bright Box Homes' relationship with FAITH Foundation as both a supplier and a funding partner should be reviewed by legal counsel for potential conflict of interest documentation requirements.

> **[REQUIRED] Single Audit Requirement — MONITOR THRESHOLD**
> Organizations that expend $750,000 or more in federal awards in a fiscal year must have a single audit performed by an independent auditor and submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end. *(2 CFR Part 200 Subpart F; 2 CFR § 200.501)*
> **Action Required:** FAITH Foundation's current annual budget of $75,000 is well below the $750,000 single audit threshold; however, if federal awards are received that bring total federal expenditures to or above $750,000 in any fiscal year, a single audit will be required. Monitor this threshold annually.

> **[RECOMMENDED] Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA) — MISSING OR NON-COMPLIANT**
> Organizations recovering indirect costs on federal awards must have a negotiated indirect cost rate agreement (NICRA) with their cognizant federal agency, or may use the de minimis rate of 10% of modified total direct costs (MTDC) if they have never had a negotiated rate. *(2 CFR §§ 200.414, 200.68)*
> **Action Required:** As a new organization without a prior NICRA, FAITH Foundation may elect to use the 10% de minimis indirect cost rate. Document this election in writing and apply it consistently to all federal awards.

---

*This narrative was prepared using verified FAITH Foundation organizational data. All statistics are sourced from cited federal and research databases. Sections marked [NEEDS INPUT] require additional information from organizational leadership before finalization. All compliance flags should be reviewed with qualified legal counsel prior to any federal submission.*

# FAITH Foundation
## Preservation and Reinvestment Initiative for Community Enhancement (PRICE)
### Grant Narrative

---

**Organization:** FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope)
**EIN:** 33-2640449
**Service Area:** South and Central Texas, Texas Gulf Coast Region
**Primary Contact:** Reid Whitesides, Founder & President
**Address:** 209 Surecast Drive, Suite 105, Burnet, Texas 78611
**Phone:** 888-497-6620

---

## SECTION I: STATEMENT OF NEED

### The Housing Crisis in Texas Is Not Theoretical — It Is Documented, Acute, and Worsening for the Populations We Serve

The United States is experiencing a housing crisis of historic proportions. Nationally, 745,652 people were experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2025, including 266,320 living unsheltered — and the homelessness response system has permanent housing units for only 9.5% of people in need, with enough shelter capacity to house only 16% of households currently seeking refuge. (HUD 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report; National Alliance to End Homelessness, 2025.)

Texas sits at the center of this crisis. Nearly 28,000 Texans were experiencing homelessness in the 2024 Point-in-Time count, including 1,837 veterans — and critically, 44% of Texans experiencing homelessness were entirely unsheltered, with no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing. Chronic homelessness in Texas climbed from 1,949 individuals in 2022 to 2,594 in 2023, a 33% increase in a single year. (HUD 2024 AHAR; Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network.)

Within this statewide crisis, the rural and underserved communities of South and Central Texas — the primary geography served by FAITH Foundation — face compounding disadvantages. Rural communities lack the nonprofit infrastructure, shelter inventory, and transitional housing stock concentrated in urban centers. When an individual exits incarceration in rural South Texas, completes addiction treatment in a small county seat, or loses employment as a single parent in a farming community, there is frequently no transitional housing available within accessible distance. The gap between crisis and stability is not a step — it is a chasm.

### The Populations FAITH Foundation Serves Face Multiplied Barriers

The need is not uniform. The populations FAITH Foundation prioritizes — military veterans, formerly incarcerated individuals, people in addiction recovery, single-parent families, and those experiencing or at risk of homelessness — face barriers that compound one another and that most housing programs are not designed to address simultaneously.

**Veterans.** In Texas, 1,837 veterans were counted as homeless in 2024, and 4,085 veterans were served by Texas Continuums of Care as of December 2023. (VA/HUD 2024 PIT Count; Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network.) Nationally, 32,882 veterans were experiencing homelessness in January 2024, with 13,851 unsheltered — individuals who served their country and returned to find no stable place to call home. (VA 2024 PIT Count.) Veterans face service-connected disabilities, VA benefits navigation complexity, and employment gaps that make standard housing applications routinely unsuccessful.

**Formerly Incarcerated Individuals.** Formerly incarcerated people are approximately 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population. Between 23.1% and 47.8% of annual homeless shelter admissions nationally are individuals with incarceration histories. (National Low Income Housing Coalition; Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019.) In Texas — a state that incarcerates and releases hundreds of thousands of individuals annually — the reentry housing gap is severe. Individuals released from Texas prisons routinely face private landlord screening barriers, credit damage, and legal restrictions on subsidized housing. Without stable housing immediately upon release, the cycle of homelessness and reincarceration is statistically predictable: 82% of individuals released from prison across 24 states were re-arrested within 10 years. (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024.)

**Individuals in Addiction Recovery.** Stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery. Without it, even the most motivated individuals emerging from treatment face relapse triggers — unstable environments, negative peer networks, and the stress of housing insecurity — that overwhelm the gains made in treatment. Yet sober living and recovery housing options in rural South Texas remain critically undersupplied.

**Single-Parent Families.** The homeownership rate among single mothers is approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples without children. Single-parent households face estimated home prices approaching five times their income. (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024; NAHB Eye on Housing, 2024.) Single mothers managing childcare costs on a single income face a near-impossible equation: afford rent, save for a down payment, and build credit simultaneously. Most cannot do all three.

**The Down Payment Barrier.** Even for families who stabilize in rental housing, the path to homeownership has lengthened dramatically. First-time homebuyers now make up just 21% of the market — the lowest share since the National Association of Realtors began tracking in 1981. The median age of a first-time homebuyer has climbed to a record 40 years old. 67% of millennials have no savings for a home down payment, and 75% of first-time buyers cite affordability as their top concern. (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers; REsimpli 2025 Market Survey.) For individuals with criminal records, addiction histories, or single-income constraints, these national averages represent a best-case scenario — not a realistic expectation.

### The Gap FAITH Foundation Fills

The data reveals two interconnected failures. First, there is insufficient housing inventory affordable to the populations we serve — nationally, a shortage of 7.3 million rental units affordable and available to extremely low-income households. (National Low Income Housing Coalition.) Second, there is insufficient financial assistance to bridge the gap between rental instability and homeownership. Most existing programs address one dimension or the other. FAITH Foundation addresses both: the demand side through direct down payment assistance vouchers and homeownership counseling, and the supply side through our Cornerstone Communities land acquisition and development initiative. No other organization operating in our rural South and Central Texas service area provides this integrated, dual-sided approach with a self-sustaining funding mechanism tied directly to new home construction.

---

## SECTION II: PROGRAM DESIGN

### Theory of Change

Stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery from addiction, successful community reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. FAITH Foundation's model addresses the root cause of cyclical homelessness — the absence of affordable transitional housing in rural communities. By deploying modular housing units in purpose-built Cornerstone Communities, paired with case management, peer mentorship, financial literacy education, and down payment assistance vouchers, individuals progress through a structured pathway from crisis to stability to permanent housing. Each successful transition frees capacity for the next participant, creating a self-sustaining cycle of community impact.

The ultimate measure of our success is not how many families we serve temporarily, but how many families we move permanently into homes they own.

### Program Architecture: Eight Interconnected Pathways to Homeownership

FAITH Foundation operates an integrated ecosystem of eight programs, all oriented toward a single objective: permanent homeownership. Participants may enter the continuum through any program door appropriate to their current circumstances, and the programs are designed to work in concert rather than in isolation.

**1. Homeownership Counseling**
FAITH Foundation's flagship educational program provides pre-purchase counseling, mortgage readiness assessment, and comprehensive buyer education designed to prepare participants for sustainable homeownership. Counseling addresses credit qualification, mortgage product selection, predatory lending avoidance, and the ongoing financial responsibilities of homeownership. Completion of counseling is a prerequisite for down payment voucher issuance.

**2. Down Payment and Housing Vouchers**
Direct financial assistance funded through the FAITH Foundation's partnership with Bright Box Homes provides $2,500 vouchers toward down payments and rental deposits for qualifying participants. The voucher program pathway proceeds through four stages: (1) application and eligibility screening; (2) enrollment in mandatory Financial Literacy and Credit Repair Education Seminars; (3) matching with modular home inventory at discounted rates; and (4) voucher issuance and closing assistance. Modular home options available through the Bright Box Homes partnership include 20x20 and 20x40 expandable container homes, Apple cabin units, and space capsule models — all designed for affordability and rapid deployment on prepared sites.

**3. Emergency Bridge Housing**
Rapid rental and deposit assistance for families facing sudden housing crises prevents evictions before they cascade into homelessness. This program functions as the initial stabilization layer for individuals who need immediate intervention before they can engage with longer-term programming.

**4. Veterans Path Home**
Dedicated case management, rental assistance, and VA benefits navigation for military veterans transitioning from housing instability to permanent homes. This program recognizes that veterans face a distinct constellation of barriers — service-connected disabilities, benefits complexity, and the trauma of military-to-civilian transition — that require specialized support.

**5. Recovery Housing**
A structured continuum from sober living through transitional housing to permanent independent housing, with on-site support groups and accountability at every stage. This program is designed specifically for individuals emerging from addiction treatment who need structured, supportive housing while they rebuild their recovery foundation.

**6. Second Chance Reentry**
Transitional housing, employment support, and case management for formerly incarcerated individuals rebuilding stability after release. This program addresses the critical window immediately following release — the period when the absence of stable housing is most strongly predictive of reincarceration — by providing immediate placement, employment connections, and ongoing case support.

**7. Single Parent Stability**
Affordable housing assistance paired with childcare navigation and financial coaching for single-parent families working toward homeownership. This program recognizes the dual burden of childcare costs and single-income constraints that make standard housing programs inaccessible for many single parents.

**8. Financial Literacy**
Hands-on budgeting, credit-building, and debt management education that prepares families to qualify for and sustain homeownership. Seminars cover budgeting, credit reports, credit repair strategies, mortgage preparation, loan terms, homeownership financial planning, and avoidance of predatory lending. Instruction is available in both in-person and virtual formats to accommodate the geographic distribution of participants across rural South Texas.

### Cornerstone Communities Initiative: Addressing the Supply Side

Beyond direct voucher assistance, FAITH Foundation addresses the supply side of the housing crisis through the Cornerstone Communities initiative — the organization's flagship development program. FAITH Foundation acquires donated land from private owners, churches, municipalities, and developers, then develops purpose-built residential micro-communities through competitive open-bid construction processes, deploying modular and manufactured housing units supplied through the Bright Box Homes partnership.

Each Cornerstone Community includes individual housing units, shared community spaces, and on-site access to case management and support services. Purpose-built community amenities include recovery programming spaces, remote work and learning centers, community laundry facilities, shuttle transportation for rural access, and dedicated case management offices. Residents enter as transitional housing participants and graduate into permanent homeownership through FAITH Foundation's voucher pipeline.

As residents stabilize and transition to permanent housing, their units become available for new participants, creating a self-sustaining cycle of community impact. This rotating asset model is the operational core of FAITH Foundation's sustainability — each transition simultaneously serves a departing resident and creates capacity for the next.

The Cornerstone Communities approach is specifically designed for rural South Texas communities where traditional development is cost-prohibitive and where the nonprofit housing infrastructure available in urban centers does not exist. Modular units can be sited on donated or acquired rural land without the delays and costs of conventional construction, bringing housing solutions directly to underserved communities rather than requiring individuals to relocate to urban centers to access services.

### The Bright Box Homes Partnership: A Self-Reinforcing Funding Mechanism

FAITH Foundation's program model is sustained in part by a renewable, mission-aligned funding mechanism: our strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes. Bright Box Homes donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold through any channel, and offers modular housing units to program participants at discounted rates. This partnership aligns both organizations' missions — every Bright Box home sold generates funding for the next family's down payment assistance, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of community investment. Charitable contributions are transformed into permanent, affordable housing solutions rather than consumed in operational overhead.

---

## SECTION III: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY

### Leadership Team

FAITH Foundation is led by a governing board whose members bring direct, complementary expertise in construction, housing development, financial management, and community ministry — the precise disciplines required to execute an integrated affordable housing and community development mission.

**Reid Whitesides — Founder, President & Executive Director**
Reid Whitesides founded FAITH Foundation on a conviction formed through lived experience. During a long struggle with addiction, Reid spent nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas. Those experiences gave him firsthand insight — the kind no credential can replicate — into the challenges individuals face when rebuilding their lives after addiction, incarceration, and homelessness. Today, he has been sober for more than fifteen years and leads FAITH Foundation with the understanding of someone who has navigated every barrier the organization exists to address. Reid brings more than 20 years of professional experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries, providing the practical expertise necessary to develop and manage housing assets responsibly. He also possesses expertise in technology development, including websites, software applications, and automation tools that support nonprofit and housing operations — capabilities he applies directly to FAITH Foundation's data management and grant systems infrastructure. Reid credits his Christian faith and God's transformative work in his life as the foundation of his recovery and his purpose in leading this organization.

**Scott Ellis — Treasurer & Board Chair**
Scott Ellis serves as Treasurer and Board Chair, providing financial oversight, strategic guidance, and construction industry expertise that directly serves the Foundation's housing development mission. Scott is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based company he has successfully led for more than 15 years. His experience in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems ensures that FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities projects are developed responsibly, efficiently, and with a focus on maximizing community impact. As a Georgetown, Texas resident for more than 24 years and an active member of his local church, Scott brings both deep community rootedness and Christian service values to his board leadership.

**Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary & Protector**
Pastor Juan Valdez serves as Secretary and Protector, providing spiritual oversight, governance accountability, and mission stewardship. With more than 40 years of Christian faith and nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience, Pastor Valdez brings a lifetime of leadership grounded in integrity and service. His ministry has extended across the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. Pastor Valdez and his wife Martha operated a successful business in San Antonio for 34 years — a record of consistency, reliability, and stewardship that he carries into his Foundation governance role. He currently serves as an Associate Pastor at Temple of Praise and resides in Texas.

### Administrative Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation maintains its financial records through QuickBooks, providing accurate and auditable financial management consistent with federal financial management system standards under 2 CFR § 200.302. The organization has deployed the Benavora grant management platform for grant application tracking, reporting, and compliance documentation. Case management and participant data are tracked through the Foundation's integrated data management system, with outcomes reported quarterly to the board of directors and annually to funders and stakeholders.

The Foundation maintains indirect costs below 15% of total program budget, with operational cost controls implemented through volunteer labor, donated materials, and shared administrative infrastructure across program sites.

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirmation of active SAM.gov registration status and current Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) number — required for federal award applications per 2 CFR § 200.1 and GSA UEI transition policy effective April 4, 2022.]

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirmation of current NICRA (Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement) status, or documentation that the organization will apply the de minimis 10% MTDC rate per 2 CFR § 200.414 if no prior negotiated rate exists.]

### Community Partnerships

FAITH Foundation maintains active partnerships across multiple sectors to maximize program reach and service depth without duplicating existing infrastructure:

- **Church partners** provide volunteer labor, congregational fundraising, mentorship volunteers, and programming space.
- **Recovery program partners** refer individuals completing treatment who need stable transitional housing and provide ongoing support services for residents in active recovery.
- **Reentry service partners** coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals upon release, connecting them to employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support.
- **County social services agencies and local housing authorities** refer eligible families, coordinate benefits enrollment, and collaborate on case management.
- **Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers** provide discounted or donated materials and units for Cornerstone Communities development.
- **Land owners in rural South Texas communities** donate or sell land at reduced cost for community development sites.
- **Veterans service organizations** refer military veterans experiencing housing insecurity and coordinate VA benefits enrollment.

FAITH Foundation also actively accepts in-kind donations of land, building materials, modular and manufactured housing units, construction equipment and labor, furnishings, appliances, household goods, and professional services including legal, architectural, surveying, and construction management — all documented at fair market value for matching fund and audit purposes.

[NEEDS INPUT: Formal letters of commitment or memoranda of understanding from named partner organizations, if required by the funder as application attachments.]

### Financial Position

FAITH Foundation operates with an annual budget of $75,000 and is in its inaugural funding cycle. Initial operations have been funded through founder investment and church community support. The organization does not yet meet the $750,000 federal expenditure threshold requiring a Single Audit under 2 CFR § 200.501; however, the Foundation is establishing financial management systems now that will scale appropriately as federal funding grows. The organization maintains all financial records in QuickBooks and is committed to the administrative requirements of 2 CFR 200 Subpart D, including performance reporting, financial reporting, a minimum three-year records retention policy, and written procedures for determining cost allowability consistent with 2 CFR 200 Subpart E.

All procurement under this award, if granted, will follow documented procedures consistent with 2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327, including full and open competition requirements and conflict-of-interest documentation. Equipment and real property acquired with grant funds will be managed in accordance with 2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316, including property inventory maintenance and federal approval for any disposal.

[NEEDS INPUT: Most recent financial statements (balance sheet and income statement) to attach as required exhibits.]

---

## SECTION IV: INTENDED IMPACT

### Organizational Stage and Transparency About Outcomes

FAITH Foundation is a newly established 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization in its founding year of operations. We are committed to transparency: as a pre-revenue organization, we have not yet produced measurable program outcomes. The targets below represent what we intend to achieve, the metrics by which we will measure success, and the evidence-based projections that ground our projections in documented research from HUD, the VA, and peer organizations operating comparable housing voucher and community development programs.

### Projected Outcomes by Year

**Year 1 Targets**
- Distribute 10 down payment assistance vouchers ($2,500 each), totaling $25,000 in direct housing assistance to qualifying families
- Enroll 25 families in homeownership counseling and financial literacy programming
- Provide emergency bridge housing assistance to 15 families facing immediate housing crises
- Establish partnerships with a minimum of 3 local employers for reentry and recovery program participants
- Secure the first donated land parcel for Cornerstone Communities development
- Recruit and train 20 volunteers for mentorship, financial literacy instruction, and community outreach

**Year 2 Targets**
- Distribute 40 housing vouchers, totaling $100,000 in direct assistance
- Graduate 20 families from homeownership counseling into active homebuyers
- Begin construction on the first Cornerstone Community with on-site wraparound programming
- Expand recovery housing partnerships to serve 30 individuals annually
- Place 15 reentry participants into stable employment within 90 days of program enrollment
- Achieve a 90% housing retention rate among voucher recipients at the 12-month mark

**Year 3 Targets**
- Distribute 100 housing vouchers, totaling $250,000 in direct assistance
- Complete and occupy the first Cornerstone Community with a minimum of 20 residential units
- Achieve a homeownership conversion rate of 30% among program participants who entered in Year 1
- Establish a second Bright Box Homes-style corporate partnership generating recurring voucher funding
- Publish the first annual impact report with independently verified outcome data

### Community-Level Impact

Research consistently demonstrates that homeownership and stable housing produce outcomes that extend well beyond the individual household. According to the evidence base that informs our program design:

- Every dollar invested in down payment assistance generates measurable local economic activity through home purchases, property tax contributions, and household spending.
- Stable housing is associated with improved health outcomes, reduced emergency department utilization, and better educational performance among children in the household. (Projected Community Impact data; organizational knowledge base.)
- Reentry participants with stable housing show significantly lower recidivism rates compared to regional averages — an outcome with fiscal implications for the criminal justice system that extend well beyond the housing sector.
- Veterans with stable housing demonstrate meaningfully better engagement with VA treatment and support services.
- Financial literacy programming, completed as a prerequisite for voucher issuance, is associated with credit score improvement of 50–80 points within 12 months — a tangible marker of financial readiness for sustained homeownership. (Organizational impact projections based on peer program data.)

The long-term community development impact of Cornerstone Communities compounds over time. As residents transition to permanent homeownership, they become property taxpayers, community investors, and stabilizing presences in the rural communities FAITH Foundation serves. Their units become available for the next participant, and the cycle continues — not as a permanent dependency on outside funding, but as a self-reinforcing model of community preservation and reinvestment.

### How We Measure Success

FAITH Foundation will track and report on the following key performance indicators across all programs:

| KPI | Measurement Method | Reporting Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Vouchers Distributed | Total number and dollar value per quarter | Quarterly |
| Housing Retention Rate | % of recipients stably housed at 6 and 12 months | Semi-annual |
| Homeownership Conversion Rate | % transitioning to ownership within 24 months | Annual |
| Financial Readiness Score | Credit score, DTI ratio, savings rate improvement | Per cohort |
| Employment Placement Rate | % of reentry/recovery participants employed within 90 days | Quarterly |
| Recidivism Prevention Rate | % avoiding reincarceration within 24 months | Annual |
| Recovery Stability Rate | % maintaining sobriety and stable housing at 12 months | Annual |
| Volunteer Engagement | Total hours and active mentor-mentee relationships | Quarterly |
| Cornerstone Communities Occupancy | Units built, occupied, % progressing toward homeownership | Quarterly |

All program data will be collected through FAITH Foundation's case management system, reported quarterly to the board of directors, and published annually in a public impact report available to all funders, donors, and community stakeholders. Beginning in Year 2, FAITH Foundation will pursue third-party outcome verification to provide independent confirmation of reported results.

---

## SECTION V: SUSTAINABILITY

FAITH Foundation's long-term sustainability is built on a rotating housing asset model that generates ongoing program capacity rather than consuming it. As Cornerstone Community residents transition to permanent homeownership, their units become available for new participants — reducing per-unit cost over time and building a self-sustaining cycle of community impact funded in part by the Bright Box Homes partnership.

Revenue streams supporting long-term operations include:
- Program fees assessed on a sliding scale based on participant income
- Rental income from stabilized housing units during the transitional period
- Recurring grant funding from federal, state, and private sources, actively pursued through the Benavora grant platform
- Corporate sponsorships and in-kind donations
- Church partnerships and congregational giving
- Individual donor cultivation

Physical assets — land parcels and modular housing units — appreciate over time and reduce ongoing capital expenditure requirements. The Foundation actively pursues funding diversification across government grants, private foundations, corporate giving programs, faith-based funders, and community development financial institutions to avoid dependency on any single source. Operational costs are controlled through volunteer labor, donated materials, and shared administrative infrastructure across program sites. Indirect costs are maintained below 15% of total program budget.

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirmation of whether the organization has pursued or intends to pursue CDFI certification, which could expand access to federal capital programs aligned with this housing preservation initiative.]

---

## SECTION VI: BUDGET NARRATIVE

FAITH Foundation's budget allocation prioritizes direct program delivery over administrative overhead. Four primary budget areas support the PRICE initiative:

**Direct Assistance (Vouchers)**
Down payment assistance vouchers at $2,500 per family flow entirely to program participants. No administrative fee is deducted from voucher awards. Voucher funding is supplemented by the renewable Bright Box Homes donation mechanism.

**Education Programs**
Financial literacy and homeownership counseling programming costs include instructor time, curriculum materials, venue costs for in-person sessions, and virtual platform access for participants in rural communities with transportation barriers.

**Housing Development**
Capital expenditures include modular housing unit acquisition ($30,000–$60,000 per unit), site preparation and utility infrastructure installation, and community common space construction. These expenditures produce appreciating physical assets that reduce per-participant costs over the life of the program.

**Operations**
Operational costs include case management staffing (maintaining a maximum 15-to-1 client ratio), housing navigation, property maintenance, insurance, participant support services, rural transportation for case management outreach, program supplies, and technology. Indirect costs are maintained below 15% of total program budget and cover organizational administration, accounting, reporting, and compliance.

In-kind donations of building materials, volunteer labor, and professional services significantly reduce cash outlays and are documented at fair market value for matching fund and compliance purposes consistent with 2 CFR 200 Subpart E requirements.

[NEEDS INPUT: Specific grant request amount for this PRICE application, and a line-item budget table if required by the funder's application format.]

---

## COMPLIANCE NOTICES

FAITH Foundation is committed to full compliance with all applicable federal award requirements. The following items require attention or completion prior to federal award execution:

> **[REQUIRED — ACTION NEEDED]** **SAM.gov Active Registration:** All organizations applying for or receiving federal financial assistance must maintain an active registration in SAM.gov, renewed annually. A lapsed or missing registration can delay or disqualify an award. (2 CFR § 200.206.) *FAITH Foundation should confirm and document current SAM.gov registration status prior to submission.*

> **[REQUIRED — ACTION NEEDED]** **Unique Entity Identifier (UEI):** All federal grant applicants must have a UEI assigned through SAM.gov (replacing the DUNS number as of April 2022). The UEI is required on all federal grant applications. (2 CFR § 200.1.) *FAITH Foundation should confirm UEI issuance and include it on all application documents.*

> **[RECOMMENDED — ACTION NEEDED]** **Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA):** Organizations recovering indirect costs on federal awards must have a current NICRA with their cognizant federal agency, or may use the de minimis 10% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC) rate if no prior negotiated rate exists. (2 CFR § 200.414.) *FAITH Foundation should document which approach will be applied and maintain this election consistently.*

> **[FOR REFERENCE]** **Single Audit Threshold:** Organizations expending $750,000 or more in federal awards in a fiscal year must have a single audit performed by an independent auditor and submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end. (2 CFR § 200.501.) FAITH Foundation's current annual budget of $75,000 is well below this threshold. As federal funding grows, this requirement should be monitored annually.

> **[FOR REFERENCE]** **Federal Cost Principles (2 CFR 200 Subpart E):** All costs charged to this award must be allowable, allocable, and reasonable. Unallowable costs include lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties. FAITH Foundation's QuickBooks-based financial management system and documented procurement procedures support this compliance requirement.

> **[FOR REFERENCE]** **Property Management Standards (2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316):** Equipment and real property acquired with federal funds must be inventoried, maintained, and disposed of in compliance with federal property management standards. FAITH Foundation will establish a property inventory system prior to first equipment or real property acquisition under any federal award.

---

## CLOSING STATEMENT

FAITH Foundation was not built in a conference room. It was built from the lived experience of individuals who understand — from the inside — what it means to lose housing, to fight through addiction, to reenter a world that was not designed to receive you back. That understanding is the most durable asset any housing organization can possess, and it is embedded in every program, every partnership, and every decision FAITH Foundation makes.

The Preservation and Reinvestment Initiative for Community Enhancement reflects precisely what FAITH Foundation exists to do: preserve the possibility of permanent housing for the individuals most likely to be excluded from it, and reinvest the resources of this community into the lives most in need of a stable foundation. Through the Cornerstone Communities initiative, the Bright Box Homes partnership, and an integrated eight-program continuum from crisis to homeownership, FAITH Foundation is building the infrastructure to make that preservation and reinvestment sustainable, measurable, and replicable across rural Texas and beyond.

We respectfully request the funder's partnership in this work.

[NEEDS INPUT: Funder name and specific requested grant amount for insertion into the closing paragraph and any cover letter or summary page required by the application.]

---
