# FAITH Foundation
## Grant Proposal: Notice of Award of a Single Source Cooperative Agreement
### Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / HHS
### Federal Fiscal Year 2026 — Requested Award: $4,000,000

---

> **⚠ CRITICAL APPLICANT NOTICE — READ BEFORE SUBMISSION**
>
> This proposal has been drafted using all verified organizational data available for FAITH Foundation. Before submission, the following compliance flags **must** be resolved. Failure to address these items may disqualify the application or delay the award:
>
> 1. **[REQUIRED] Unique Entity Identifier (UEI):** Confirm UEI assigned through SAM.gov (replaced DUNS in April 2022). Required on all federal applications. (2 CFR § 200.1)
> 2. **[REQUIRED] SAM.gov Active Registration:** Confirm active, current registration. Lapsed registration disqualifies. Renew annually. (2 CFR § 200.206)
> 3. **[REQUIRED] Single Audit (2 CFR 200 Subpart F):** If federal expenditures reach or exceed $750,000 in any fiscal year, an independent single audit must be submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end. Given the $4,000,000 award size, this requirement is **triggered immediately**.
> 4. **[REQUIRED] NICRA or De Minimis Rate Election:** FAITH Foundation should confirm whether it has a Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA). If not, the organization may elect the 10% de minimis rate on Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC) per 2 CFR § 200.414. This election must be documented and applied consistently.
> 5. **[REQUIRED] Financial Management System:** QuickBooks is identified as the accounting software. Confirm that the implementation meets 2 CFR § 200.302 standards for federal award financial management, including source-and-application tracking, internal controls, and written procedures for cost allowability.
> 6. **[REQUIRED] Property Management Standards:** Equipment and real property (modular units, land) acquired with federal funds must be inventoried, depreciated, and managed per 2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316.
> 7. **[REQUIRED] Federal Procurement Standards:** All procurements under this award must follow 2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327, including competition requirements and conflict-of-interest documentation.
>
> Additionally, reviewers will note a **significant organizational budget-to-award size mismatch**: FAITH Foundation's annual operating budget is $75,000, and the requested award is $4,000,000. This disparity presents a high risk flag under competitive review. See the Organizational Capacity section for mitigation language, and consider whether a phased or reduced first-year request better aligns with demonstrated capacity.

---

## SECTION 1: PROJECT SUMMARY

**Organization:** FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope)
**EIN:** 33-2640449
**Tax Status:** 501(c)(3) Public Charity
**Geographic Service Area:** South and Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast region, with primary focus on rural and underserved communities
**Target Populations:** Military veterans, individuals in addiction recovery, formerly incarcerated persons reentering society, single-parent families, and individuals experiencing or at risk of homelessness
**Project Title:** [NEEDS INPUT: Insert official project title as required by the Notice of Award]
**Requested Amount:** $4,000,000 (Federal Fiscal Year 2026)
**Project Period:** [NEEDS INPUT: Insert proposed project start and end dates]
**UEI:** [NEEDS INPUT: Insert SAM.gov Unique Entity Identifier]
**Congressional District:** [NEEDS INPUT: Insert applicable Texas congressional district(s)]

---

### Summary Statement

FAITH Foundation — the Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope — requests $4,000,000 from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) under this single-source cooperative agreement to expand a comprehensive, integrated housing stability initiative serving military veterans, formerly incarcerated persons, individuals in addiction recovery, and single-parent families in rural and underserved South and Central Texas communities.

Texas is home to nearly 28,000 people experiencing homelessness, including 1,837 veterans, with 44% living entirely unsheltered — among the most acute concentrations of housing instability in the nation (HUD 2024 AHAR). The populations FAITH Foundation serves face compounding, intersecting barriers: criminal records that disqualify them from private rental markets, addiction histories that fracture employment continuity, service-connected disabilities that reduce earning capacity, and single-income households operating in a housing market where the median first-time buyer is now 40 years old (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers). In rural South Texas — where FAITH Foundation concentrates its work — traditional nonprofit housing infrastructure is sparse and affordable housing inventory is critically low.

FAITH Foundation addresses this crisis through an integrated, three-program model: a Down Payment Assistance Program that converts charitable and federal investment directly into homeownership; a Transitional Housing Program that provides up to 24 months of structured case management and peer mentorship for individuals exiting homelessness, incarceration, or addiction treatment; and the Cornerstone Communities Initiative, a purpose-built modular micro-community development program that creates affordable housing supply where the private market has failed. Together, these programs form a complete, permanent pathway from housing crisis to homeownership — addressing both the demand side (financial barriers) and the supply side (housing inventory shortage) simultaneously.

Requested funds will support personnel costs for case managers, housing navigators, and program staff; capital acquisition of modular and manufactured housing units for Cornerstone Community development; site preparation, utility infrastructure, and community space construction; direct down payment assistance awards to qualifying families; operational and transportation costs for rural case management outreach; and program administration and evaluation. FAITH Foundation brings to this work the firsthand lived experience of its founder — a man who spent nearly twenty years incarcerated in Texas and has maintained sobriety for more than fifteen years — combined with the financial stewardship of a seasoned construction and business executive and the spiritual governance of a minister with nearly thirty years of ordained service.

---

## SECTION 2: STATEMENT OF NEED

### The Housing Crisis Facing Texas's Most Vulnerable Populations

The United States is experiencing a housing affordability and homelessness crisis of historic proportions, and Texas sits at the center of it. The evidence is drawn from federal data, peer-reviewed research, and the lived experience of the communities FAITH Foundation serves.

#### National Homelessness Context

On a single night in January 2025, **745,652 people** were experiencing homelessness across the United States, including **266,320 living unsheltered** with no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing (HUD 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report). While overall homelessness declined 3.3% in 2025 — the first decrease since 2016 — **chronic homelessness increased 2.1%**, and homelessness among adults aged 65 and older increased 6.8% (HUD 2025 AHAR). The system is not recovering evenly: the nation's homelessness response capacity provides permanent housing units for only **9.5% of people in need** and can shelter only **16% of households** currently in the shelter system (National Alliance to End Homelessness, 2025).

Texas is among the seven states that collectively account for **64% of all people experiencing homelessness in the United States** (HUD 2024 AHAR).

#### Texas-Specific Data

- **Nearly 28,000 Texans** were experiencing homelessness in the 2024 Point-in-Time count, including **1,837 veterans** (HUD 2024 AHAR, cited in Texas HB 158).
- **44% of Texans experiencing homelessness were unsheltered** — living on streets, in vehicles, or in encampments with no shelter access (HUD 2024 AHAR).
- **2,594 individuals** were identified as chronically homeless in Texas in 2023, up from 1,949 in 2022 — a **33% increase in a single year** (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network).
- Texas's total recorded deaths from all causes reached **198,106** in 2017 alone (CDC NCHS, Leading Causes of Death: United States, 2017 (WONDER)), a figure that underscores the profound public health consequences of unaddressed social determinants including housing instability — the precise nexus between FAITH Foundation's work and the CDC's public health mission.

#### Veteran Housing Instability

- **32,882 veterans** were experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2024 — a record low since measurement began in 2009, but still tens of thousands of Americans who served their country (VA 2024 PIT Count).
- **13,851 veterans were unsheltered** in 2024 (VA 2024 PIT Count).
- Texas, California, and Florida have the highest concentrations of homeless veterans nationally (Mission Roll Call, 2024).
- In Texas, veteran homelessness decreased **9.7% between 2023 and 2024**, from 2,036 to 1,837 — demonstrating that targeted intervention works, but the work is far from finished (VA/HUD 2024 PIT Count).
- **Black veterans**, who make up 14% of the veteran population, represent **31% of homeless veterans** — a disparity that reflects systemic inequities FAITH Foundation's open-enrollment model is specifically designed to address (Mission Roll Call, 2024).

#### Reentry and Formerly Incarcerated Populations

The intersection of incarceration and homelessness is among the most entrenched cycles in American social policy. Formerly incarcerated people are approximately **10 times more likely to experience homelessness** than the general population (National Low Income Housing Coalition, 2018; Prison Policy Initiative). Formerly incarcerated individuals account for between **23.1% and 47.8%** of annual homeless shelter admissions (Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019). **82% of individuals released from prison** across 24 states were re-arrested within 10 years of release (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024), and housing instability is a primary driver — people experiencing homelessness after release face increased reincarceration risk due to more frequent law enforcement contact and supervision violations tied to their lack of a stable address (CSG Justice Center, 2025).

FAITH Foundation's Founder, Reid Whitesides, spent nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas. He is not describing this population abstractly. He is part of it — and his fifteen-plus years of sustained sobriety and community leadership demonstrate what structured housing, mentorship, and faith-based support can produce.

#### Single-Parent Homeownership Gap

- The homeownership rate among **single mothers is approximately 34%**, compared to 84% for married couples without children (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024).
- Single-parent households face home prices approaching **five times their annual income**, a severe housing cost burden (NAHB Eye on Housing, 2024).
- Single women made up 19% of all homebuyers in 2023, but **single mothers with dependent children face significantly lower ownership rates** due to childcare costs and single-income limitations (National Association of Realtors, 2023; U.S. Census Bureau).

#### The Down Payment and Inventory Barrier

- First-time homebuyers now make up just **21% of the market** — the lowest share since NAR began tracking in 1981, when they consistently represented approximately 40% (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers).
- The **median age of first-time homebuyers has reached a record 40 years old** (NAR 2025 Profile).
- **67% of millennials have no savings** for a home down payment (REsimpli 2025 Market Survey).
- The nation faces a shortage of **7.3 million rental units** affordable and available to extremely low-income households (National Low Income Housing Coalition), compounding barriers for individuals with criminal records already excluded from most private housing.
- **74.2% of homeowner households with incomes below $30,000** are cost-burdened, paying more than 30% of income on housing — the highest rate in over 20 years (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University, 2023 data).

#### The Gap FAITH Foundation Fills

The data reveals two interconnected failures operating simultaneously in Texas: insufficient affordable housing inventory for the populations we serve, and insufficient financial assistance to bridge the gap from rental instability to permanent homeownership. Most existing programs address one dimension or the other. FAITH Foundation addresses both: the **demand side** through direct down payment vouchers and housing counseling, and the **supply side** through our Cornerstone Communities land acquisition and modular housing development initiative. In rural South Texas specifically, where traditional nonprofit housing infrastructure is sparse and construction is cost-prohibitive, FAITH Foundation's modular deployment model delivers housing solutions directly into underserved communities — rather than concentrating resources in urban centers that may be geographically inaccessible to the families most in need.

---

## SECTION 3: GOALS AND OBJECTIVES

### Overarching Goal

FAITH Foundation's overarching goal under this cooperative agreement is to **measurably reduce housing instability, chronic homelessness, and its public health consequences** among veterans, formerly incarcerated persons, individuals in addiction recovery, and single-parent families in rural and underserved South and Central Texas communities, by deploying an integrated three-program model that moves participants from housing crisis through transitional stability into permanent homeownership.

---

### Goal 1: Expand Direct Housing Assistance and Down Payment Access

**Objective 1.1:** Distribute a minimum of [NEEDS INPUT: specific number of vouchers per year as aligned with award budget] down payment assistance awards of $2,500 each to qualifying low-income individuals and families per program year, with 100% of awards documented and tracked through FAITH Foundation's case management system.

**Objective 1.2:** Enroll a minimum of [NEEDS INPUT: specific enrollment target] families in homeownership counseling and financial literacy programming per program year, with pre- and post-assessments administered to measure improvement in credit score, debt-to-income ratio, and savings rate.

**Objective 1.3:** Provide emergency bridge housing assistance to families facing immediate housing crises, maintaining a referral response time of 72 hours or fewer from intake to placement determination.

**Objective 1.4:** Achieve a **housing retention rate of 90%** among voucher recipients at the 12-month mark, verified through scheduled follow-up contact at 30, 60, 90, 180, and 365 days post-award.

---

### Goal 2: Develop and Operate Cornerstone Communities Transitional Housing

**Objective 2.1:** Acquire [NEEDS INPUT: specific number] land parcels suitable for Cornerstone Communities micro-community development within the first 12 months of the award period.

**Objective 2.2:** Deploy [NEEDS INPUT: specific number] modular and manufactured housing units across Cornerstone Community sites, with units occupied within 90 days of site preparation completion.

**Objective 2.3:** Maintain an **occupancy rate of at least 85%** across all operational Cornerstone Community units throughout the program period.

**Objective 2.4:** Transition a minimum of **70% of transitional housing participants into permanent, independent housing within the 24-month program window**, with transitions documented in the case management system.

---

### Goal 3: Deliver Wraparound Case Management and Supportive Services

**Objective 3.1:** Maintain a **maximum case manager-to-client ratio of 15:1** throughout the program period, ensuring individualized service plan development and monthly progress review for every enrolled participant.

**Objective 3.2:** Achieve a **referral completion rate of 60–75%** for external services — including mental health, employment, VA benefits, and substance use treatment — verified at 30-day follow-up.

**Objective 3.3:** Place a minimum of [NEEDS INPUT: specific number] reentry and recovery program participants into stable employment within 90 days of program enrollment per program year.

**Objective 3.4:** Achieve a **program retention rate of at least 70–80%** among enrolled participants, defined as completion of at least 75% of scheduled program activities within the 24-month window.

---

### Goal 4: Strengthen Organizational Systems and Federal Compliance Capacity

**Objective 4.1:** Maintain full compliance with all 2 CFR Part 200 Uniform Guidance requirements throughout the award period, including financial management, property management, procurement, and reporting standards.

**Objective 4.2:** Achieve **documentation compliance rate of 90% or higher** on monthly random audits of 10% of active case files, assessed against a standardized completeness checklist.

**Objective 4.3:** Submit all required federal financial and performance reports on time, with zero audit findings related to allowable cost documentation or reporting accuracy.

**Objective 4.4:** Publish an annual impact report with independently verified outcome data beginning no later than the conclusion of Year 1 of the award period.

---

## SECTION 4: PROGRAM DESIGN

### Theory of Change

FAITH Foundation's program model is grounded in a clearly articulated, evidence-based theory of change: **stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery from addiction, successful community reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency.** The absence of affordable transitional housing in rural South Texas communities is not a symptom of poverty — it is a root cause. When individuals exiting incarceration, completing addiction treatment, or fleeing housing crisis cannot access safe, stable shelter, every other intervention fails. Employment becomes impossible without an address. Benefits cannot be delivered without a residence. Recovery cannot sustain without a foundation.

FAITH Foundation's model attacks this root cause directly. By deploying modular housing units in purpose-built Cornerstone Communities — paired with case management, peer mentorship, financial literacy, and down payment assistance — individuals progress through a structured, supported pathway from crisis to stability to permanent housing. Each successful transition frees capacity for the next participant, creating a **self-sustaining cycle of community impact** that multiplies the return on every dollar invested.

### Program Architecture: Three Interconnected Programs

FAITH Foundation operates three interconnected programs, all coordinated through a unified intake, case management, and data tracking infrastructure:

---

#### Program 1: Down Payment Assistance Program

The Down Payment Assistance Program provides direct financial awards to qualifying low-income individuals and families who are employment-stable but lack the savings required for upfront housing costs — the single most common barrier between rental instability and permanent homeownership for the populations we serve.

**Eligibility and Intake:** Applicants are screened for income qualification (at or below [NEEDS INPUT: specific AMI threshold, e.g., 80% Area Median Income]), employment stability, and housing readiness. Intake is conducted by FAITH Foundation's housing navigator, who completes a standardized intake assessment, documents household composition and income, and initiates a service plan within 72 hours of application.

**Award Disbursement:** Qualifying applicants receive a $2,500 voucher applicable toward a down payment or rental deposit on permanent housing. Awards are disbursed directly to landlords or escrow accounts — not to participants — to ensure housing application. Award disbursement is documented in FAITH Foundation's case management system with supporting receipts and lease or purchase documentation.

**Post-Award Support:** Recipients are enrolled in FAITH Foundation's Financial Literacy program and connected to homeownership counseling. Housing navigators conduct follow-up contact at 30, 60, 90, 180, and 365 days to verify housing retention and identify emerging needs.

**Funding Mechanism:** The Down Payment Assistance Program is sustained in part by FAITH Foundation's strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes, a modular container home builder that donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold — creating a renewable, self-reinforcing funding cycle. Federal funds under this award supplement this mechanism to dramatically expand the scale of assistance available.

---

#### Program 2: Transitional Housing Program

The Transitional Housing Program places individuals exiting homelessness, incarceration, or addiction treatment into stable transitional housing units with individualized case management support, financial literacy training, and peer mentorship for up to **24 months**.

**Target Population and Referral Pipeline:** Participants are referred through FAITH Foundation's established partnership network: recovery program partners refer individuals completing addiction treatment; reentry service partners coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals upon release; veterans service organizations refer military veterans experiencing housing insecurity; county social services agencies and local housing authorities refer eligible families. Church partners provide volunteer mentors and community support.

**Case Management Model:** Each participant is assigned a licensed case manager operating at a maximum **15:1 client ratio**. Case managers develop individualized service plans within the first week of enrollment, conduct monthly progress reviews, and coordinate referrals to external services including mental health treatment, employment navigation, VA benefits enrollment, legal aid, and family reunification support. Case managers maintain detailed progress notes in FAITH Foundation's case management system, with quarterly supervisory review.

**Financial Literacy Curriculum:** Participants complete a structured financial literacy curriculum covering budgeting, credit-building, debt management, and mortgage readiness. Pre- and post-assessments measure improvement in financial readiness score — including credit score, debt-to-income ratio, and savings rate — at program entry, 6 months, 12 months, and exit.

**Peer Mentorship:** Each participant is matched with a trained peer mentor — an individual with lived experience of recovery, reentry, or housing instability who has achieved sustained stability. Peer mentors meet weekly with their mentees to provide accountability, encouragement, and practical guidance. Mentor-mentee matches are tracked in the case management system and reviewed quarterly.

**Exit and Transition:** As participants approach the 24-month maximum program window, case managers coordinate transition planning, connecting participants to FAITH Foundation's Down Payment Assistance Program, homeownership counseling, and permanent housing options. Vacated transitional units are immediately recycled back into the program for incoming participants, sustaining continuous community placement capacity.

---

#### Program 3: Cornerstone Communities Initiative

The Cornerstone Communities Initiative is FAITH Foundation's flagship housing development program — and its most transformative contribution to the affordable housing landscape of rural South Texas. The initiative acquires land (through donation, purchase, or reduced-price sale) and deploys modular and manufactured housing units to create purpose-built micro-community neighborhoods designed specifically for transitional residents.

**Why Modular in Rural South Texas:** Rural South Texas faces acute housing shortages with limited nonprofit infrastructure and construction capacity. Traditional site-built housing development is cost-prohibitive in communities with limited contractor availability and extended permitting timelines. Modular and manufactured housing units — sourced through FAITH Foundation's partnership with Bright Box Homes and other building suppliers — can be sited on acquired or donated rural land without the delays and costs of traditional construction. This approach brings housing solutions **directly to underserved communities** rather than requiring vulnerable families to relocate to urban centers.

**Community Design:** Each Cornerstone Community includes:
- Individual modular housing units, each providing private, dignified living space for one household
- Shared community spaces for programming, peer support groups, and community-building activities
- On-site access to wraparound services: case management, mental health referrals, employment navigation, and benefits enrollment
- Remote work and learning centers
- Community laundry facilities
- Shuttle transportation for residents without reliable personal transportation
- On-site recovery programming spaces for residents in active recovery

**Development Process:** Site acquisition is conducted through FAITH Foundation's existing relationships with land donors, including private owners, churches, municipalities, and rural landowners in South Texas who donate or sell parcels at reduced cost. Site preparation — including utility infrastructure installation and grading — is coordinated through Scott Ellis, FAITH Foundation's Treasurer and Board Chair, who brings more than 15 years of residential and commercial construction, project coordination, and contractor management experience through his leadership of E4 Roofing & Construction. Construction procurement follows federal competitive bidding standards per 2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327.

**Revolving Capacity Model:** As Cornerstone Community residents stabilize and transition to permanent housing, their units become available for new participants. This revolving model means that every unit FAITH Foundation acquires serves multiple families over its lifespan — maximizing the return on capital investment and creating a genuinely self-sustaining community impact cycle.

---

### Enrollment Plan and Timeline

FAITH Foundation proposes the following participant enrollment plan, consistent with a 60-day post-award mobilization buffer to allow for staff hiring, system configuration, and partnership activation before the first participant is enrolled:

| Phase | Timeline | Activity |
|---|---|---|
| Mobilization | Award + Days 1–60 | Hire case managers and housing navigator; configure case management system; activate partnership referral agreements; complete staff federal compliance training |
| Enrollment Launch | Award + Month 3 | Begin intake screening; first participant enrollments; first Down Payment Assistance awards disbursed |
| Ramp-Up | Months 3–6 | Scale to 50% of target monthly enrollment capacity; complete first Cornerstone Community site assessment |
| Full Operations | Months 7–12 | Achieve full monthly enrollment targets; first Cornerstone Community units deployed; quarterly report to CDC submitted |
| Year 1 Close | Month 12 | Annual performance report; independent impact data verification; Year 2 continuation planning |
| Years 2–5 | Continuation | [NEEDS INPUT: Continuation funding amounts and enrollment targets to be set at continuation per award notice] |

**Participant Tracking:** All enrolled participants will be assigned a unique identifier in FAITH Foundation's case management system at intake. Enrollment status, service plan milestones, referral completion, housing placement, and exit data will be updated in real time by case managers and reviewed monthly by the Program Director. Unduplicated participant counts will be maintained and reported quarterly to CDC.

---

### Alignment with CDC and HHS Priorities

FAITH Foundation's integrated housing stability model directly advances CDC's public health mission. Housing instability is a well-documented social determinant of health, associated with elevated rates of infectious disease, mental health crisis, substance use disorder relapse, and emergency department utilization. By moving vulnerable Texans from chronic housing instability into permanent, stable homes — with wraparound case management addressing mental health, substance use, and employment barriers — FAITH Foundation produces measurable public health outcomes aligned with HHS's Healthy People framework and CDC's emphasis on addressing social determinants of health among underserved populations.

[NEEDS INPUT: If the CDC Notice of Award specifies particular programmatic priorities, evaluation frameworks, or reporting requirements, those must be explicitly addressed here with citation to the specific notice language.]

---

## SECTION 5: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY

### Institutional Identity and History

FAITH Foundation — the Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope — was established by Reid Whitesides to address the critical shortage of affordable and transitional housing options in rural South Texas communities. The organization is registered as a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN: 33-2640449) and was founded on the conviction that stable housing is the essential foundation for recovery from addiction, successful reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. Initial operations have been funded through founder investment and church community support. FAITH Foundation is in its inaugural funding cycle and has not previously received federal grants.

This is a significant organizational fact that FAITH Foundation presents with full transparency: we are a young organization with an annual operating budget of $75,000 and a clear-eyed understanding of what this award would require. The proposal that follows includes specific mitigation measures to address capacity concerns, including phased hiring, experienced board oversight, a robust compliance plan, and an explicit commitment to the administrative infrastructure federal awards require.

### Leadership Team

**Reid Whitesides — Founder, President, and Executive Director**
Reid Whitesides founded FAITH Foundation on the basis of more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries — combined with the firsthand perspective of having spent nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas during a long struggle with addiction. Reid has maintained sobriety for more than fifteen years. He leads the Foundation with the conviction that stable housing is the first step toward lasting change, and that every person deserves the opportunity to build a better future regardless of their past. He also brings skills in technology development, including websites, software applications, and automation tools that support nonprofit and community-focused initiatives — capabilities directly applicable to the case management system and data reporting infrastructure this award requires. His lived experience of incarceration, recovery, and re-entry is not background context; it is operational expertise that directly informs every program design decision.

**Scott Ellis — Treasurer and Board Chair**
Scott Ellis is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based firm he has led for more than 15 years. His experience in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems provides the Foundation with the construction and financial oversight infrastructure essential to responsible Cornerstone Communities development. His 24-year residency in Georgetown, Texas, and his active church community involvement reflect the long-term community rootedness that distinguishes FAITH Foundation's leadership from transient organizational leadership. As Treasurer, Scott oversees the Foundation's financial management systems, including QuickBooks, and will serve as the primary point of contact for federal financial reporting and audit coordination.

**Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary and Protector**
Pastor Juan Valdez brings more than 40 years of Christian faith and nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience to the Foundation's governance structure. His ministry has extended across the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. Beyond ministry, Pastor Valdez and his wife Martha operated a successful business in San Antonio for 34 years — a record of consistency, reliability, and stewardship that directly informs his governance contributions. As Secretary and Protector, Pastor Valdez provides governance accountability, ethics oversight, and mission stewardship, ensuring that organizational decisions remain aligned with the Foundation's founding principles and charitable purpose.

### Administrative and Financial Systems

FAITH Foundation maintains financial records using **QuickBooks**, which provides the source-and-application fund tracking, budget-versus-actual comparison, and internal control infrastructure required under 2 CFR § 200.302. The organization is committed to configuring QuickBooks specifically for federal award tracking upon receipt of this award, including separate cost center coding for all grant-funded activities and written procedures for determining cost allowability per 2 CFR Subpart E.

FAITH Foundation will implement the **10% de minimis indirect cost rate** on Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC) per 2 CFR § 200.414, as the organization has not previously held a Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA). This rate will be applied consistently throughout the award period. [NEEDS INPUT: Confirm with financial advisor whether a NICRA application should be initiated with the cognizant federal agency (HHS) concurrent with or immediately following award.]

### Compliance Commitments

FAITH Foundation commits to full compliance with all applicable federal requirements under this award, including:

- **2 CFR Part 200 Uniform Guidance** — including financial management (§ 200.302), property management (§§ 200.310–200.316), procurement (§§ 200.317–200.327), records retention (3-year minimum), and subrecipient monitoring if applicable
- **Single Audit requirement** (2 CFR Subpart F) — triggered if federal expenditures meet or exceed $750,000 in any fiscal year; FAITH Foundation will engage an independent auditor upon award and submit findings to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end
- **Time and effort reporting** per 2 CFR § 200.430(i) for all personnel working on federal award activities
- **SAM.gov active registration** — maintained and renewed annually
- **Unique Entity Identifier (UEI)** — [NEEDS INPUT: Confirm and insert UEI]
- **Federal procurement standards** — all construction procurement for Cornerstone Communities conducted through competitive open-bid processes with documented conflict-of-interest certifications per 2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327

### Capacity Scaling Plan

FAITH Foundation acknowledges directly that administering a $4,000,000 federal cooperative agreement represents a significant scaling challenge for an organization at our current stage. We have developed the following specific mitigation measures:

1. **Immediate hire of a Federal Grants Compliance Manager** within the first 30 days of award, responsible for day-to-day Uniform Guidance compliance, reporting, and audit coordination. [NEEDS INPUT: Confirm compensation budget and whether a specific candidate has been identified.]
2. **Engagement of a federal grants consultant** during the first year to provide technical assistance on financial management systems, cost allowability, and reporting, as permitted under 2 CFR Part 200.
3. **Board oversight intensification** — Scott Ellis (Treasurer/Board Chair) will chair a monthly Financial Oversight Committee during the first year, reviewing expenditures against budget and compliance checklists.
4. **QuickBooks federal configuration** — completed within 60 days of award, with separate grant fund tracking, cost center coding, and written internal control procedures.
5. **Phased program ramp-up** — enrollment does not begin until Day 61 post-award, providing a 60-day mobilization window for all systems, staff, and compliance infrastructure to be in place before the first participant dollar is spent.

### Partnership Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation's established partnership network provides the referral pipelines, volunteer capacity, and service coordination infrastructure essential to program delivery at scale:

- **Church partners** — provide volunteer mentors, meeting space for participant programming, and congregational fundraising support
- **Recovery program partners** — refer individuals completing addiction treatment who need stable transitional housing and provide ongoing recovery support services
- **Reentry service partners** — coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals upon release and connect participants to employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support
- **County social services agencies and local housing authorities** — refer eligible families, coordinate benefits enrollment, and provide case management collaboration
- **Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers** (including **Bright Box Homes**) — provide discounted or donated materials and housing units for Cornerstone Communities development
- **Veterans service organizations** — refer military veterans experiencing housing insecurity and coordinate VA benefits enrollment
- **Rural South Texas landowners** — donate or sell land at reduced cost for Cornerstone Community development sites

# LETTER OF INQUIRY
## Fair Housing Assistance Program (FHAP)

---

**FAITH Foundation**
Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope
EIN: 33-2640449 | 501(c)(3) Public Charity
Texas

U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
Fair Housing Assistance Program

---

**Re: Letter of Inquiry — Fair Housing Assistance Program (FHAP) | FAITH Foundation | Texas Service Area**

---

Dear [NEEDS INPUT: Program Officer Name],

FAITH Foundation — the Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope — respectfully submits this Letter of Inquiry to introduce our organization and explore alignment with the Fair Housing Assistance Program (FHAP). We write to gauge the Program's interest in supporting our work to advance fair, accessible, and equitable housing opportunities for economically disadvantaged Texans who face compounding, systemic barriers to stable and permanent housing.

---

### About FAITH Foundation

FAITH Foundation is a Texas-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization (EIN: 33-2640449) founded by Reid Whitesides, whose firsthand experience with addiction, nearly twenty years of incarceration, and the rebuilding of a life in stable housing has shaped every element of our model. Our mission is unambiguous: to break the cycle of housing insecurity by providing financial education, homeownership instruction, and direct housing assistance to veterans, individuals experiencing homelessness, single parents, those in recovery, those reentering society, and other economically disadvantaged populations. Through our strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes, we transform charitable giving into permanent, affordable housing solutions.

We serve families across South and Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast, with a primary focus on rural and underserved communities where nonprofit housing infrastructure is critically limited. Texas is home to nearly 28,000 people experiencing homelessness — including 1,837 veterans — with 44% living entirely unsheltered. (HUD 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report.) The populations we serve face not only the material barriers of affordability and down payment access, but the discriminatory barriers of criminal records, addiction histories, service-connected disabilities, and single-income household status that systematically exclude them from the private housing market.

---

### The Fair Housing Need We Address

The communities FAITH Foundation serves experience fair housing barriers that are structural, persistent, and quantifiable. Formerly incarcerated individuals are approximately ten times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population, and are routinely denied private housing due to blanket criminal background screening policies that operate as a form of disparate impact discrimination. (National Low Income Housing Coalition; Prison Policy Initiative.) The Black homeownership rate stands at 46.6% and the Hispanic homeownership rate at 49.9%, compared to 74.0% for white households — gaps driven in significant part by discriminatory access to credit, mortgage lending, and housing inventory. (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University, Q1 2024.) Single mothers hold a homeownership rate of approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples with children, reflecting the compounded effect of income inequality and discriminatory housing cost burdens. (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024.)

Veterans experiencing housing instability, individuals in addiction recovery, and formerly incarcerated individuals reentering Texas communities face housing markets where affordability barriers and discriminatory screening practices converge to produce homelessness, not by chance, but by design. FAITH Foundation exists to dismantle these barriers through direct assistance, education, and the construction of purpose-built housing where fair access is the operating principle from the ground up.

---

### Our Program Model

FAITH Foundation operates an integrated ecosystem of programs designed to move individuals and families from housing crisis to permanent homeownership. Our three interconnected programmatic pillars are:

**Down Payment Assistance Program:** Direct financial awards of $2,500 per qualifying household to bridge the gap between rental instability and homeownership. Recipients are employment-stable individuals and families who lack savings for upfront housing costs — the precise population most likely to be shut out of the private market by the down payment barrier alone.

**Transitional Housing Program:** Placement of individuals exiting homelessness, incarceration, or addiction treatment into stable transitional housing units for up to 24 months, with integrated case management, financial literacy training, and peer mentorship. This program directly serves the populations most vulnerable to discriminatory housing denial.

**Cornerstone Communities Initiative:** FAITH Foundation's flagship development program, acquiring donated and purchased land to deploy modular and manufactured housing units in purpose-built micro-communities designed specifically for transitional residents. Each Cornerstone Community includes individual housing units, shared community spaces, and on-site case management. As residents stabilize and transition to permanent housing, units become available for new participants — creating a self-sustaining cycle of equitable housing access. Modular housing deployment is particularly well-suited to rural South Texas, where our units can be sited on donated or acquired rural land without the delays and costs of traditional construction, bringing housing solutions directly to underserved communities rather than concentrating resources in urban centers.

Our programs are affirmatively marketed to and designed for the populations most systematically excluded from fair housing access: veterans, formerly incarcerated individuals, people in addiction recovery, single-parent families, and individuals experiencing homelessness. All programs are administered without regard to race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, or disability, and we are committed to ADA accessibility compliance in all Cornerstone Community design and construction. [NEEDS INPUT: Confirmation of ADA compliance standards applied to existing or planned facilities and any formal ADA compliance documentation.]

---

### Organizational Leadership and Capacity

FAITH Foundation is led by Founder, President, and Executive Director **Reid Whitesides**, who brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, and housing-related industries, combined with lived experience as a formerly incarcerated individual in recovery — more than fifteen years sober — who has personally navigated the barriers our clients face. This perspective is not incidental to our model; it is foundational to it.

Our Board includes **Scott Ellis**, Treasurer and Board Chair, owner of E4 Roofing & Construction (Georgetown, Texas) with more than 15 years of residential and commercial construction experience, providing direct expertise in housing development, project budgeting, contractor management, and asset stewardship. **Pastor Juan Valdez** serves as Secretary and Protector, bringing nearly 30 years of ordained ministry and community leadership, providing governance accountability and mission stewardship.

FAITH Foundation maintains its financial records in QuickBooks and is committed to full compliance with applicable federal financial management standards, including the requirements of 2 CFR Part 200 (Uniform Guidance). As a newly established organization in our inaugural funding cycle, we are building our compliance infrastructure to align with federal award requirements from the outset.

---

### Sustainability and Partnerships

FAITH Foundation's long-term sustainability is grounded in both a renewable funding mechanism and a rotating housing asset model. Our partnership with Bright Box Homes — a container home builder that donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold — creates a self-reinforcing cycle: each home sold funds a voucher that helps the next family into housing. As Cornerstone Communities residents transition to permanent housing, units become available for new participants, reducing ongoing capital requirements over time.

Additional sustainability is built through partnerships with local churches, recovery programs, reentry service providers, county social services agencies, and housing authorities across South Texas; collaboration with building material suppliers, modular housing manufacturers, and landowners to reduce development costs; and diversified revenue streams including program fees on a sliding scale, rental income from stabilized units, recurring grant funding, corporate sponsorships, and individual donor cultivation. Physical assets — land and housing units — appreciate over time, further reducing long-term capital needs.

---

### Alignment With FHAP Priorities

The Fair Housing Assistance Program's mandate to enforce fair housing protections at the state and local level aligns directly with the barriers FAITH Foundation documents and addresses every day in South and Central Texas. Our model is built on the premise that equitable access to housing — regardless of criminal history, addiction history, veteran status, family composition, or economic circumstance — is not aspirational; it is a legal and moral obligation. We seek to complement enforcement-focused fair housing efforts with direct assistance and community development programming that makes fair housing access a practical reality for the populations whose rights are most frequently violated.

[NEEDS INPUT: Confirm whether FAITH Foundation is registered as a state or local government agency or is partnering with such an agency for FHAP eligibility purposes. FHAP funding is restricted to state and local government agencies with fair housing laws substantially equivalent to the Federal Fair Housing Act. If FAITH Foundation is a nonprofit and not a qualifying governmental agency, note that FHAP may not be the appropriate funding vehicle and identify the partnering governmental agency, if any, through which FAITH Foundation would participate.]

---

### Request

We respectfully request the opportunity to discuss FAITH Foundation's work and explore whether a formal application to the Fair Housing Assistance Program is an appropriate next step. We are prepared to provide any additional documentation, organizational materials, or program information that would be helpful to your review.

FAITH Foundation is at an early and critical stage of building the housing infrastructure South Texas needs. We are earnest stewards of every resource entrusted to us and are committed to transparency, measurable outcomes, and the fair housing principles that make permanent homeownership possible for every family we serve.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Respectfully submitted,

**Reid Whitesides**
Founder, President & Executive Director
FAITH Foundation

[NEEDS INPUT: Email address]

### Compliance Notices for Internal Review Prior to Submission

The following federal compliance items require attention before any FHAP award can be accepted or administered:

- **[REQUIRED] SAM.gov Active Registration:** Confirm active and current SAM.gov registration. Registration must be renewed annually. A lapsed registration can delay or disqualify an award. (2 CFR § 200.206)
- **[REQUIRED] Unique Entity Identifier (UEI):** Confirm UEI has been assigned through SAM.gov. The UEI replaced the DUNS number in April 2022 and is required on all federal grant applications. (2 CFR § 200.1; GSA UEI transition policy)
- **[REQUIRED] Financial Management System Standards:** FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks. Confirm that the financial management system provides accurate, current, and complete disclosure of financial results; identifies source and application of funds; includes effective internal controls; and includes written procedures for determining allowability of costs. (2 CFR § 200.302)
- **[REQUIRED] Federal Cost Principles Compliance (2 CFR 200 Subpart E):** All costs charged to federal awards must be allowable, allocable, and reasonable. Unallowable costs include lobbying, entertainment, and alcoholic beverages. Documentation must support all expenditures.
- **[REQUIRED] Administrative Requirements (2 CFR 200 Subpart D):** Recipients must maintain internal controls, comply with federal statutes and regulations, and follow the terms and conditions of the federal award, including performance reporting, financial reporting, records retention (3 years minimum), and subrecipient monitoring.
- **[REQUIRED] Property Management Standards (2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316):** Equipment and real property acquired with federal funds must be inventoried, maintained, and disposed of per federal standards. Applicable to modular housing units and land acquired with any federal award funds.
- **[REQUIRED] Federal Procurement Standards (2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327):** All procurements under federal awards must follow documented procedures providing for full and open competition. Conflicts of interest must be avoided and documented.
- **[REQUIRED] Single Audit / OMB A-133 Threshold:** If federal expenditures reach or exceed $750,000 in a fiscal year, a single audit by an independent auditor is required, submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end. (2 CFR § 200.501)
- **[RECOMMENDED] Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA):** If indirect costs will be charged to a federal award, FAITH Foundation should confirm use of the de minimis rate of 10% of modified total direct costs (MTDC) — available to organizations that have never had a negotiated rate — or initiate a NICRA with the cognizant federal agency. (2 CFR §§ 200.414, 200.68)

# FAITH Foundation
## Fair Housing Assistance Program (FHAP)
### Grant Narrative — Submitted to HUD

---

> **IMPORTANT COMPLIANCE NOTICE TO APPLICANT — REVIEW BEFORE SUBMISSION**
>
> The following federal compliance requirements must be resolved prior to or concurrent with submission of this application. Each item is flagged in the relevant narrative section where applicable.
>
> - **[REQUIRED] Unique Entity Identifier (UEI):** FAITH Foundation must obtain a UEI through SAM.gov. The UEI replaced the DUNS number in April 2022 and is required on all federal grant applications. *(2 CFR § 200.1)*
> - **[REQUIRED] SAM.gov Active Registration:** Confirm that FAITH Foundation's SAM.gov registration is active and current. A lapsed registration will disqualify the award. *(2 CFR § 200.206)*
> - **[REQUIRED] Single Audit / OMB A-133 Threshold:** If federal expenditures reach or exceed $750,000 in any fiscal year, a Single Audit performed by an independent auditor and submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year-end is required. *(2 CFR § 200.501)*
> - **[REQUIRED] Federal Cost Principles (2 CFR 200 Subpart E):** All costs charged to this award must be allowable, allocable, and reasonable. Unallowable costs include lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties. Maintain documentation for all expenditures.
> - **[REQUIRED] Administrative Requirements (2 CFR 200 Subpart D):** Maintain internal controls, performance reporting, financial reporting, and records retention of a minimum 3 years. Obtain prior approval for certain budget modifications.
> - **[REQUIRED] Financial Management System Standards (2 CFR § 200.302):** FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks. Confirm the system is configured to meet federal standards for accurate, current, and complete financial disclosures, fund source tracking, and internal controls.
> - **[REQUIRED] Property Management Standards (2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316):** Modular housing units and land acquired with federal funds must be inventoried, tracked, depreciated, and disposed of in accordance with federal property management standards.
> - **[REQUIRED] Federal Procurement Standards (2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327):** All procurements under this award — including modular housing units, construction subcontracts, and professional services — must follow documented, competitive procurement procedures.
> - **[RECOMMENDED] Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA):** If FAITH Foundation has never negotiated an indirect cost rate, it may apply the de minimis rate of 10% of modified total direct costs (MTDC). Document this election in the budget narrative. *(2 CFR § 200.414)*

---

## SECTION I: STATEMENT OF NEED
### The Housing Crisis in Rural Texas: A Data-Driven Case for Action

The United States is experiencing a housing crisis of historic proportions — one that falls most heavily on the populations least equipped to withstand it. For the communities FAITH Foundation serves across rural South and Central Texas, that crisis is not a distant statistic. It is the reality of 28,000 Texans counted without a home in 2024, of veterans sleeping unsheltered in a state that sent them to serve, and of formerly incarcerated men and women walking out of Texas correctional facilities into a housing market that systematically excludes them.

FHAP funding exists precisely because fair and equitable access to housing is not yet a universal reality. The evidence in Texas confirms this urgency at every level of measurement.

**The Scale of Homelessness in Texas**

According to HUD's 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, nearly 28,000 Texans were experiencing homelessness at the time of the Point-in-Time count, including 1,837 veterans. Of particular concern, 44% of Texans experiencing homelessness were entirely unsheltered — meaning they had no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing. *(HUD 2024 AHAR, cited in Texas HB 158)* Texas is one of seven states that together account for 64% of the nation's entire homeless population. *(HUD 2024 AHAR)*

Chronic homelessness in Texas is accelerating. In 2023, the Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network identified 2,594 chronically homeless individuals statewide, up sharply from 1,949 in 2022 — a 33% increase in a single year. The system's capacity to respond is critically outpaced: nationally, the homelessness response system has permanent housing for only 9.5% of people in need, and sufficient shelter capacity for only 16% of households currently seeking it. *(National Alliance to End Homelessness, 2025)*

**Veterans: Those Who Served Cannot Find Housing**

Texas has one of the highest concentrations of homeless veterans in the nation. *(Mission Roll Call, 2024)* While veteran homelessness in Texas decreased 9.7% between 2023 and 2024 — from 2,036 to 1,837 — those 1,837 veterans continue to live without stable housing in a state they served. *(VA/HUD 2024 PIT Count)* Nationally, 13,851 veterans were unsheltered in 2024, and Black veterans — who make up 14% of the overall veteran population — represent 31% of all homeless veterans, reflecting a persistent and unacceptable racial disparity in who bears the burden of housing instability. *(Mission Roll Call, 2024)*

**Formerly Incarcerated Individuals: The Reentry Housing Crisis**

The intersection of incarceration and homelessness is among the most consequential and least addressed dimensions of housing inequity in Texas. Formerly incarcerated people are approximately 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population. *(National Low Income Housing Coalition, 2018; Prison Policy Initiative)* Nationally, formerly incarcerated individuals account for between 23.1% and 47.8% of annual homeless shelter admissions. *(Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019)*

The consequences of this gap are severe. People who experience homelessness after release face heightened risk of reincarceration through supervision violations and increased law enforcement contact related to their housing status. *(CSG Justice Center, 2025)* Nationally, 82% of individuals released from prison across 24 states were re-arrested within 10 years of release. *(UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024)* Nearly 450,000 individuals were released from state and federal prisons in 2021 alone, and the average formerly incarcerated individual spends more than six months unemployed post-release — a period during which stable housing is the single greatest determinant of whether recovery or recidivism defines what comes next. *(UNLV Reentry Research Brief)*

The underlying supply shortage makes this worse: the United States faces a shortage of 7.3 million rental units affordable to extremely low-income households. For individuals with criminal records, who are systematically excluded from most private rental markets, this shortage is not theoretical — it is a locked door. *(National Low Income Housing Coalition)*

**Single Parents: Structurally Excluded from Homeownership**

The homeownership rate among single mothers is approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples without children. *(U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024)* Single-parent households face home prices approaching five times their income — a cost burden ratio that makes ownership statistically out of reach without targeted assistance. *(NAHB Eye on Housing, 2024)* For single mothers with dependent children, childcare costs and single-income constraints compound every other barrier.

**The Down Payment Gap: The Final Lock on the Door**

Even for families who have achieved stability, the path to homeownership is blocked by a down payment gap that has grown wider with every passing year. First-time homebuyers now make up only 21% of the housing market — the lowest share recorded since NAR began tracking in 1981, and a collapse from the consistent 40% share maintained prior to 2008. *(NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers)* The median age of a first-time homebuyer has reached a record 40 years old. *(NAR 2025 Profile)* Sixty-seven percent of millennials report no savings toward a home down payment. *(REsimpli 2025 Market Survey)*

Racial homeownership gaps remain severe: the Black homeownership rate stands at 46.6% and the Hispanic homeownership rate at 49.9%, compared to a white homeownership rate of 74.0% as of Q1 2024. *(Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University)* For 74.2% of homeowner households earning below $30,000 annually, housing costs already consume more than 30% of income — the highest cost-burden rate in over 20 years. *(Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University)*

**The Rural Texas Gap**

Rural South and Central Texas faces compounding pressures that distinguish it from urban housing markets. Limited nonprofit infrastructure, vast geographic distances, scarce affordable housing inventory, and the near-absence of transitional housing options for reentry, recovery, and veteran populations create a service desert in communities with acute, documented need. Traditional affordable housing development models — designed for urban density and established infrastructure — are cost-prohibitive and logistically impractical in rural settings, leaving these communities without viable housing solutions.

**Fair Housing and Equity Context**

The populations FAITH Foundation serves — veterans, formerly incarcerated individuals, those in addiction recovery, and single-parent families — face compounding barriers to fair housing access that extend beyond income. Criminal records trigger blanket application denials in the private rental market. Service-connected disabilities create accessibility barriers in standard housing stock. Recovery histories trigger discrimination that, while sometimes legally contested, functionally excludes individuals from private markets. Racial disparities in both the criminal justice system and the mortgage market compound these barriers for communities of color. FHAP-supported programs that reach these populations do not merely address housing scarcity; they actively advance the fair housing principles that make housing opportunity equitable and legally accessible.

---

## SECTION II: PROGRAM DESIGN AND HOUSING STRATEGY
### An Integrated Model from Crisis to Permanent Housing

FAITH Foundation — the Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope — operates on a thesis that distinguishes it from conventional emergency housing providers: the people we serve do not merely need a place to stay. They need a home they own. Every program FAITH Foundation operates is designed as a stage in a single, structured continuum from housing crisis to permanent homeownership.

**Theory of Change**

Stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery from addiction, successful community reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. FAITH Foundation's model addresses the root cause of cyclical homelessness — the absence of affordable transitional housing in rural communities. By deploying modular housing units in purpose-built Cornerstone Communities, paired with case management, peer mentorship, financial literacy education, and direct down payment assistance, individuals progress through a structured pathway from crisis to stability to permanent housing. Each successful transition frees capacity for the next participant, creating a self-sustaining cycle of community impact.

**The Eight-Program Ecosystem**

FAITH Foundation operates an interconnected ecosystem of eight programs, each addressing a distinct stage of the journey from instability to ownership. Participants may enter through any program door and receive coordinated support across the continuum.

| Program | Primary Function | Target Population |
|---|---|---|
| Homeownership Counseling | Pre-purchase counseling, mortgage readiness, buyer education | All program participants approaching ownership readiness |
| Down Payment & Housing Vouchers | $2,500 direct assistance toward down payments and rental deposits | Qualifying families at the ownership threshold |
| Emergency Bridge Housing | Rapid rental and deposit assistance preventing crisis escalation | Families facing imminent eviction or displacement |
| Veterans Path Home | VA benefits navigation, rental assistance, dedicated case management | Military veterans experiencing housing instability |
| Recovery Housing | Structured sober living through transitional to permanent housing | Individuals in active addiction recovery |
| Second Chance Reentry | Transitional housing, employment support, case management post-release | Formerly incarcerated individuals |
| Single Parent Stability | Affordable housing assistance, childcare navigation, financial coaching | Single-parent families |
| Financial Literacy | Budgeting, credit-building, debt management education | All program participants |

**The Cornerstone Communities Initiative: Supply-Side Housing Development**

FAITH Foundation's flagship program addresses both the demand side (vouchers and counseling) and the supply side (housing inventory) of the affordable housing crisis. Through the Cornerstone Communities Initiative, FAITH Foundation acquires donated or reduced-cost land from private owners, churches, municipalities, and developers, then develops purpose-built residential micro-communities using modular and manufactured housing units supplied through our strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes.

Each Cornerstone Community is designed as a complete residential environment, not a shelter facility. Individual modular housing units — ranging in acquisition cost from $30,000 to $60,000 per unit — are sited on prepared land with utility infrastructure, community common spaces, and shared amenities. On-site services include recovery programming, remote work and learning centers, community laundry facilities, shuttle transportation for rural case management access, and dedicated case management.

The community model is self-renewing: as residents stabilize and transition to permanent homeownership — supported by FAITH Foundation's down payment vouchers — their units become available for incoming participants. This rotating occupancy model creates permanent, scalable housing capacity without requiring continuous capital reinvestment at the same rate as initial development.

**Rural Service Delivery Model**

Rural South Texas faces acute housing shortages with limited nonprofit infrastructure. FAITH Foundation addresses this through modular housing deployment — units can be sited on donated or acquired rural land without the delays and costs of traditional construction. This approach brings housing solutions directly to underserved rural communities rather than concentrating resources in urban centers. Program vehicles dedicated to rural case management outreach ensure that geographic distance does not become a barrier to service continuity for residents of Cornerstone Communities.

**Fair Housing and Affirmative Outreach**

FAITH Foundation is committed to full compliance with the federal Fair Housing Act and all applicable Texas fair housing statutes. All programs are open to qualifying individuals regardless of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, disability, or any other protected class. FAITH Foundation conducts affirmative outreach to communities that have historically experienced disproportionate barriers to fair housing access, including communities of color, individuals with disabilities, and veterans. Program materials are developed for accessibility, and housing units developed through the Cornerstone Communities Initiative are designed to accommodate participants with mobility and accessibility needs.

**[NEEDS INPUT: Specific ADA accessibility standards incorporated into Cornerstone Communities unit design (e.g., percentage of units compliant with UFAS or ADA accessibility requirements) — required for full FHAP compliance documentation]**

**[NEEDS INPUT: Whether FAITH Foundation has a formal written Affirmative Fair Housing Marketing Plan (AFHMP) — required for FHAP eligibility and HUD compliance]**

**[NEEDS INPUT: Specific Texas fair housing statutes that FAITH Foundation's programs are designed to support enforcement of — required to demonstrate substantial equivalency alignment with FHAP eligibility requirements]**

**Alignment with FHAP Priorities**

FHAP is designed to strengthen state and local enforcement of fair housing protections substantially equivalent to the federal Fair Housing Act. FAITH Foundation's programs directly support this mission by reaching populations who face systemic fair housing barriers — veterans, formerly incarcerated individuals, those in recovery, single-parent families, and low-income households in underserved rural communities — and by providing the transitional and permanent housing pathways that make fair housing rights meaningful in practice.

FAITH Foundation is a newly established 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization in its founding year of operations. As a pre-revenue organization, we have not yet produced measurable program outcomes. ## SECTION V: SUSTAINABILITY AND LONG-TERM IMPACT
### A Self-Renewing Model Built to Last Beyond the Grant Period

FAITH Foundation's long-term sustainability is not contingent on any single funding stream. It is built into the operational architecture of the Cornerstone Communities model itself.

**The Rotating Housing Asset Model**

As residents of Cornerstone Communities stabilize and transition to permanent homeownership — supported by FAITH Foundation's down payment vouchers — their units become available for new participants. This rotating occupancy creates ongoing housing capacity without requiring continuous capital reinvestment at the rate of initial development. Physical assets — land and modular housing units — appreciate over time and reduce ongoing capital expenditure requirements for the organization.

**Diversified Revenue Architecture**

FAITH Foundation actively pursues diversified funding to avoid dependency on any single source:

- **Bright Box Homes partnership:** $2,500 recurring donation per home sold provides a renewable, non-grant-dependent funding stream for housing vouchers
- **Program fees:** Assessed on a sliding scale based on participant income
- **Rental income:** From stabilized housing units during the transitional period
- **Recurring grant funding:** Federal, state, and private foundation sources
- **Corporate sponsorships and in-kind donations:** Building materials, modular units, professional services, and household goods
- **Church partnerships and congregational giving:** Volunteer labor, fundraising, and meeting space
- **Individual donor cultivation:** Long-term donor relationships developed through community presence and annual impact reporting
- **Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs):** Targeted for future engagement as the Cornerstone Communities initiative scales

**Cost Control Mechanisms**

Operational costs are controlled through volunteer labor, donated materials, and shared administrative infrastructure across program sites. In-kind donations — including land, building materials, modular housing units, construction labor, furnishings, and professional services — are documented at fair market value and applied toward matching fund requirements. This approach maximizes the impact of every cash dollar invested in the program.

**Long-Term Affordability**

FAITH Foundation's partnership network — spanning church partners, recovery programs, reentry service providers, county social services agencies, local housing authorities, veterans service organizations, and Bright Box Homes — is not transactional. These relationships are embedded in the communities the Foundation serves and are designed for long-term continuity regardless of any individual grant cycle. Referral pipelines, volunteer networks, and co-case-management arrangements with county agencies will sustain program operations and participant flow beyond the initial grant period.

**Five-Year Vision**

Within five years, FAITH Foundation intends to be the leading housing voucher and community development organization serving veterans, reentry, recovery, and single-parent populations across rural Texas. The Cornerstone Communities model is designed to be replicable in any state where donated land partnerships and housing inventory shortages intersect. By demonstrating measurable outcomes in homeownership conversion, housing retention, and community stability, FAITH Foundation intends to establish the evidence base for scaling this model through federal, state, and private funding partnerships. The ultimate measure of our success is not how many families we serve temporarily, but how many families we move permanently into homes they own.

These capital expenditures represent the most direct and durable form of housing investment: they create permanent, appreciating physical assets that serve successive generations of participants without requiring repeated capital outlays of equivalent magnitude.

**Operating Costs**

Operating costs include property maintenance, insurance, participant support services, transportation for rural case management outreach across South and Central Texas, and program supplies.
