FAITH Foundation
Centers of Excellence for Veteran Student Success (CEVSS) Program
Grant Narrative - U.S. Department of Labor / U.S. Department of Education

CRITICAL ELIGIBILITY NOTICE - READ BEFORE SUBMISSION

The CEVSS Program is authorized under Section 101 of the Higher Education Act of 1965, as amended (20 U.S.C. 1001), and is restricted to Institutions of Higher Education (IHEs) as defined therein. FAITH Foundation is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit housing and social services organization, not an institution of higher education. As currently structured, FAITH Foundation does not meet the statutory eligibility threshold for this solicitation.

Before investing further in this application, FAITH Foundation must either: (a) identify an eligible IHE partner willing to serve as the lead applicant with FAITH Foundation as a named subrecipient or community partner; or (b) confirm that the organization's programs include a postsecondary education component qualifying it under the HEA definition.

All sections below have been drafted to demonstrate maximum alignment between FAITH Foundation's verified mission and the CEVSS Program's stated priorities, so that this narrative can be rapidly adapted once a compliant application structure is confirmed. Every section where the organization's current profile cannot satisfy a program requirement has been marked with a [NEEDS INPUT] placeholder.

Compliance flags related to federal award administration are noted throughout and must be resolved prior to submission.

SECTION I: ABSTRACT / EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization based in Texas (EIN: 33, 2640449), and we're submitting this application in response to the U.S. Department of Labor's solicitation on behalf of the U.S. Department of Education for the Centers of Excellence for Veteran Student Success (CEVSS) Program.

[NEEDS INPUT: Name of IHE partner institution, if applicable, and its role as lead applicant or co, applicant]

FAITH Foundation exists to break the cycle of housing insecurity for veterans and other economically disadvantaged populations through financial education, homeownership instruction, and direct housing assistance. Texas is home to 1,837 veterans experiencing homelessness, according to the HUD 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, and it's among the three states in the nation with the highest concentrations of homeless veterans (Mission Roll Call, 2024). Veteran students navigating postsecondary education face barriers that stack on top of one another: housing instability, financial hardship, service, connected disabilities, and a persistent disconnect between campus services and the community resources that could actually help. The CEVSS Program's mandate to develop model programs that coordinate academic, financial, physical, and social support for veteran students aligns precisely with the wraparound service architecture FAITH Foundation has designed and is deploying across South and Central Texas.

[NEEDS INPUT: Specific IHE campus(es) where the CEVSS model program would be implemented, enrollment figures for veteran students, and campus veteran services office contact information]

This proposal requests up to $3,000,000 over [NEEDS INPUT: grant period length, typically 3, 5 years per CEVSS program design] to establish a Center of Excellence for Veteran Student Success. The Center would integrate FAITH Foundation's housing stabilization, financial literacy, and wraparound case management model with [NEEDS INPUT: IHE partner name]'s existing veteran student support infrastructure, creating a replicable, evidence, based approach to veteran student success in postsecondary education.

SECTION II: STATEMENT OF NEED

A. The National and Texas, Specific Context for Veteran Student Challenges

The United States made a generational commitment to veteran postsecondary education through the Post, 9/11 GI Bill and its predecessors. Access to education benefits doesn't automatically translate into academic success. Veteran students face a distinctive set of barriers, including housing instability, financial insecurity, physical and mental health challenges, and the social isolation of transitioning from military to civilian campus life. These are barriers that existing postsecondary support structures were never designed to address in a coordinated, integrated way. The CEVSS Program exists precisely because coordination failures, not resource scarcity alone, prevent veteran students from finishing their degrees and achieving economic independence.

Veteran Housing Instability in Texas

Texas is one of the most urgent places for this work. Nearly 28,000 Texans experienced homelessness in the 2024 Point, in, Time count, including 1,837 veterans (HUD 2024 AHAR, cited in Texas HB 158). Veteran homelessness in Texas decreased 9.7% between 2023 and 2024, dropping from 2,036 to 1,837, but the state still ranks alongside California and Florida as one of the three states with the highest concentrations of homeless veterans in the country (Mission Roll Call, 2024). Nationally, 32,882 veterans were experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2024, with 13,851 living unsheltered (VA 2024 PIT Count). In Texas alone, 44% of people experiencing homelessness had no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing of any kind (HUD 2024 AHAR).

Housing instability among veteran students isn't a peripheral concern. It's an enrollment and completion barrier. A veteran student who can't secure stable, affordable housing near campus can't attend class consistently, can't complete coursework reliably, and can't benefit from campus, based services that assume residential stability. That's the root cause FAITH Foundation targets directly.

The Racial Equity Dimension

Black veterans make up 14% of the overall veteran population but represent 31% of homeless veterans (Mission Roll Call, 2024). The Black homeownership rate stands at 46.6% and the Hispanic homeownership rate at 49.9%, both well below the white homeownership rate of 74.0% as of Q1 2024 (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University). In a state as demographically diverse as Texas, a Center of Excellence that doesn't address racial equity in housing and financial access will fail to serve the full range of veteran students on any Texas campus.

Financial Barriers to Veteran Student Success

First, time homebuyers now represent just 21% of the market, the lowest share since NAR began tracking in 1981, with a median buyer age that has climbed to a record 40 years old (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers). Sixty, seven percent of millennials have no savings for a home down payment (REsimpli 2025 Market Survey), and 74.2% of homeowner households with incomes below $30,000 are cost, burdened, the highest rate in over 20 years (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University, 2023). For veteran students managing GI Bill stipends, part, time work, and service, connected disability income, those pressures are acute. Without financial literacy programming built into their academic support ecosystem, a veteran student can earn a degree and still lack the financial foundation to turn that credential into long, term housing stability.

The Coordination Gap

The need the CEVSS Program addresses isn't simply the absence of individual services. Most campuses with significant veteran enrollment have some combination of veterans' resource centers, counseling services, disability services, financial aid offices, and housing offices. What they don't have is a coordinating infrastructure that identifies veteran students in crisis early, routes them to the right combination of services at the same time, tracks outcomes over time, and adjusts the service mix based on each student's actual needs. FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities model and its integrated eight, program ecosystem were built on exactly that coordination logic. Families can enter through any door, and the model moves them through a structured pathway rather than leaving them to navigate disconnected systems on their own.

The Gap FAITH Foundation and Its IHE Partner Fill

The data points to two connected failures for veteran students in Texas: not enough affordable housing near campuses, and not enough financial capability programming integrated with academic support. FAITH Foundation addresses both. We work the housing supply side through the Cornerstone Communities development model, and the financial side through direct down payment assistance, housing counseling, and financial literacy education. No existing program in our service area puts both of those interventions together with campus, based academic and social support services in a single coordinated model.

[NEEDS INPUT: Campus, specific data on veteran student enrollment, retention rates, degree completion rates, and identified unmet needs from the IHE partner's student needs assessment or veterans' resource center records]

SECTION III: PROJECT DESIGN - MODEL PROGRAM DESCRIPTION

A. Program Philosophy and Theory of Change

FAITH Foundation's model rests on an insight documented across HUD, VA, and peer organization research: stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery, successful reentry, and, critically for this application, academic persistence and completion. A veteran student who is housing, stable is far more likely to attend class consistently, engage with tutoring and counseling, finish course requirements on time, and persist to graduation.

The CEVSS model proposed here puts that insight to work through a four, domain coordination framework aligned with the program's statutory mandate covering the academic, financial, physical, and social needs of veteran students.

Inputs, Activities, Outputs, Outcomes, and Impact by Domain

In the academic domain, inputs include case managers, IHE faculty and staff, and existing tutoring resources. Activities include academic needs assessments, early alert coordination, tutoring referrals, and course planning support. Those activities produce students receiving documented academic support, which leads to improved GPA and fewer course withdrawals, and ultimately to degree completion.

In the financial domain, FAITH Foundation housing vouchers, our financial literacy curriculum, and Bright Box Homes partnership funding serve as inputs. Activities include down payment assistance, financial literacy workshops, VA benefits navigation, and emergency bridge assistance. Outputs include vouchers issued and financial literacy completers, with short, term outcomes of improved credit scores, reduced housing cost burden, and enrolled VA benefits, all building toward housing stability and homeownership.

In the physical domain, Cornerstone Communities units, VA and community health referrals, and case management feed into housing stabilization, health service navigation, and disability accommodation coordination. The result is measurable reductions in housing instability and addressed health barriers, which sustain enrollment and reduce medical crisis withdrawals over time.

In the social domain, mentorship volunteers, peer support networks, and church and community partners support mentor matching, veteran peer group facilitation, and community integration events. Participants gain a sense of belonging and reduced isolation that carries them through to graduation and into community life afterward.

B. The Four Coordination Pillars

Pillar 1 - Academic Support Coordination

[NEEDS INPUT: Description of the IHE partner's existing academic support services for veteran students, including early alert systems, tutoring infrastructure, veteran, specific academic advising, and any existing veterans' resource center programming]

FAITH Foundation contributes case management capacity that bridges community, side housing and financial crises with campus, side academic support. A dedicated FAITH Foundation Veterans Student Success Navigator, [NEEDS INPUT: position title, FTE, and qualifications as defined by the IHE partner], will be embedded within [NEEDS INPUT: IHE partner name]'s veterans' resource center or student services office. That navigator will conduct intake assessments of incoming veteran students, catch housing instability and financial hardship early, and coordinate referrals to both campus academic services and FAITH Foundation's community, side programs at the same time. The navigator will carry a maximum caseload of 15 students to one staff member, consistent with FAITH Foundation's documented case management staffing standards, so every veteran student receives genuine individual attention.

Pillar 2 - Financial Support Integration

FAITH Foundation's financial support model for veteran students has three integrated parts.

Down Payment and Housing Vouchers: Direct financial assistance is funded through our partnership with Bright Box Homes, which donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home the company sells. Those funds become $2,500 vouchers toward down payments and rental deposits for qualifying veteran students. The vouchers address the immediate financial barrier to securing stable housing near campus, giving students a real shot at academic persistence through those critical first semesters.

VA Benefits Navigation: FAITH Foundation's Veterans Path Home program already provides dedicated VA benefits navigation and case management for veterans moving out of housing instability. Under the CEVSS model, that navigation extends explicitly to veteran students, making sure GI Bill benefits, housing allowances, disability ratings, and supplemental support are fully enrolled and working for each participating student. Many veterans leave significant benefits on the table simply because the system is hard to navigate. This component fixes that.

Financial Literacy Education: FAITH Foundation's Financial Literacy program provides hands, on budgeting, credit, building, and debt management education. Under the CEVSS model, the curriculum will be adapted for delivery in formats that fit enrolled veteran students' schedules, including workshops that work around class times, one, on, one financial coaching, and online modules where appropriate. [NEEDS INPUT: Any existing IHE financial literacy infrastructure with which this curriculum will be integrated or coordinated]

Pillar 3 - Physical and Housing Needs

FAITH Foundation's housing stabilization model is the core of what makes this CEVSS proposal different from a campus, only approach. Three programs bear directly on veteran student housing needs.

The Transitional Housing Program places individuals, including veterans, coming out of housing instability into transitional units with case management, financial literacy training, and peer mentorship for up to 24 months. For veteran students, that creates the stable residential foundation from which academic engagement becomes possible.

The Cornerstone Communities Initiative is FAITH Foundation's flagship development program. We acquire land and deploy modular and manufactured housing units, at $30,000 to $60,000 per unit, to create purpose, built micro, communities. Each Cornerstone Community includes on, site case management, recovery programming support, remote work and learning infrastructure, and shared community spaces. [NEEDS INPUT: Identification of a specific Cornerstone Communities site proximate to the IHE partner campus, or a plan to develop such a site within the grant period]

The Emergency Bridge Housing program provides rapid rental and deposit assistance for veteran students facing sudden housing crises, stopping evictions before they interrupt enrollment. That program will remain available to CEVSS participants throughout the grant period.

For veteran students with physical health needs, service, connected disabilities, or mental health challenges, FAITH Foundation coordinates with VA healthcare resources and community health partners. [NEEDS INPUT: Specific VA healthcare facility or community health partner agreements relevant to the IHE campus service area]

Pillar 4 - Social Support and Community Integration

Social isolation is one of the most consistently documented challenges veteran students face on civilian campuses. The cultural gap between military and academic environments, combined with the reality that most veteran students are older than their classmates, creates disconnection that erodes persistence even when academic and financial supports are in place.

FAITH Foundation addresses social integration through peer mentorship. Volunteer mentors, including people with lived experience in military service, housing instability, recovery, and reentry, are recruited, trained, and matched with program participants. Under the CEVSS model, we'll specifically recruit veteran mentors with postsecondary education experience to serve veteran students navigating academic transitions. Church and community partners provide additional social infrastructure: congregational community, volunteer opportunities, and social networks that extend well beyond the campus.

[NEEDS INPUT: Description of existing veteran student peer networks, student veterans organizations such as a Student Veterans of America chapter, or peer support programming at the IHE partner campus that will be integrated with FAITH Foundation's mentorship model]

## SECTION II: STATEMENT OF NEED

### A. The National and Texas-Specific Context for Veteran Student Challenges

The United States made a generational commitment to veteran postsecondary education through the Post-9/11 GI Bill and its predecessors. Yet access to education benefits does not automatically translate into academic success. Veteran students face a distinctive constellation of barriers — housing instability, financial insecurity, physical and mental health challenges, and the social isolation of transitioning from military to civilian campus life — that existing postsecondary support structures were not designed to address in an integrated, coordinated way. The CEVSS Program was created precisely because coordination failures, not resource scarcity alone, prevent veteran students from completing their degrees and achieving economic independence.

**Veteran Housing Instability in Texas**

Texas represents one of the most urgent theaters for this work. Nearly 28,000 Texans experienced homelessness in the 2024 Point-in-Time count, including **1,837 veterans** (HUD 2024 AHAR, cited in Texas HB 158). While veteran homelessness in Texas decreased 9.7% between 2023 and 2024 — from 2,036 to 1,837 — the state remains among California, Florida, and Texas as the three states with the highest concentrations of homeless veterans nationally (Mission Roll Call, 2024). Nationally, **32,882 veterans were experiencing homelessness** on a single night in January 2024, with 13,851 living unsheltered (VA 2024 PIT Count). Forty-four percent of Texans experiencing homelessness were unsheltered, with no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing (HUD 2024 AHAR).

Housing instability among veteran students is not a peripheral concern — it is an enrollment and completion barrier. A veteran student who cannot secure stable, affordable housing near campus cannot attend class consistently, cannot complete coursework reliably, and cannot benefit from campus-based support services that assume residential stability. FAITH Foundation's primary intervention targets this root cause directly.

**The Racial Equity Dimension**

Black veterans make up 14% of the overall veteran population but represent 31% of homeless veterans (Mission Roll Call, 2024). The Black homeownership rate (46.6%) and Hispanic homeownership rate (49.9%) remain significantly below the white homeownership rate (74.0%) as of Q1 2024 (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University). In a state as demographically diverse as Texas, a Center of Excellence that fails to address racial equity in housing and financial access will fail to serve the full spectrum of veteran students on any Texas campus.

**Financial Barriers to Veteran Student Success**

First-time homebuyers now represent just 21% of the market — the lowest share since NAR began tracking in 1981 — with a median age that has climbed to a record 40 years old (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers). Sixty-seven percent of millennials have no savings for a home down payment (REsimpli 2025 Market Survey), and 74.2% of homeowner households with incomes below $30,000 are cost-burdened (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University, 2023). For veteran students managing GI Bill stipends, part-time employment, and service-connected disability income, these financial pressures are acute. Without financial literacy programming integrated into their academic support ecosystem, veteran students may complete degrees but still lack the financial capability to convert educational attainment into long-term housing stability and wealth.

**The Coordination Gap**

The need the CEVSS Program addresses is not simply the absence of individual services. Most campuses with significant veteran enrollment have some combination of veterans' resource centers, counseling services, disability services, financial aid offices, and housing offices. What they lack — and what this proposal provides — is a **coordinating infrastructure** that identifies veteran students in crisis early, routes them to the appropriate combination of services simultaneously, tracks outcomes longitudinally, and adjusts the service mix based on individual student need. FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities model and its integrated eight-program ecosystem were designed on exactly this coordination logic: families may enter through any door, and the model moves them through a structured pathway rather than leaving them to navigate siloed systems independently.

**The Gap FAITH Foundation and Its IHE Partner Fill**

The data reveals two interconnected failures facing veteran students in Texas: insufficient affordable housing near campuses, and insufficient financial capability programming integrated with academic support. FAITH Foundation addresses both — the housing supply side through our Cornerstone Communities development model, and the financial demand side through direct down payment assistance, housing counseling, and financial literacy education. No existing program in our service area integrates these two interventions with campus-based academic and social support services in a single coordinated model.

The CEVSS model proposed here operationalizes this insight through a four-domain coordination framework aligned precisely with the program's statutory mandate: **academic, financial, physical, and social needs of veteran students.**

Assessment results will generate an individualized Student Success Plan specifying which combination of CEVSS components each student will access.

**Bi-Weekly Case Review:** The FAITH Foundation Veterans Student Success Navigator will convene bi-weekly case reviews with [NEEDS INPUT: IHE partner's designated student services staff] to review student progress, identify emerging risks, and adjust service plans proactively. This structured coordination meeting is the operational mechanism that prevents students from falling through the gaps between community-side and campus-side service systems.

**Early Alert Integration:** [NEEDS INPUT: Description of how the CEVSS early alert process will integrate with the IHE partner's existing early alert or academic early intervention system]

**Data Sharing Protocol:** FAITH Foundation and [NEEDS INPUT: IHE partner name] will execute a data sharing agreement consistent with FERPA requirements, enabling coordinated tracking of academic progress alongside housing, financial, and social outcome metrics. All data will be maintained in FAITH Foundation's case management system with QuickBooks-integrated financial tracking for grant reporting purposes.

### A. Evaluation Framework

FAITH Foundation is committed to rigorous, transparent outcome measurement. Consistent with best practices documented by HUD, the VA, and peer organizations, FAITH Foundation will track outcomes across five domains aligned with the CEVSS Program's four statutory support areas:

# FAITH Foundation
## Rural Housing Preservation Grant Program
### Application Narrative

**Applicant Organization:** FAITH Foundation (Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope)
**EIN:** 33-2640449
**Tax Status:** 501(c)(3) Public Charity
**Service Area:** South and Central Texas; Texas Gulf Coast Region
**Primary Contact:** Reid Whitesides, Founder & President

---

> **COMPLIANCE NOTICE — Required Actions Before Submission**
> The following federal compliance items require attention prior to submitting this application. Reviewers are advised to resolve each item and document resolution in the application file.
>
> - **[REQUIRED] Unique Entity Identifier (UEI):** Confirm UEI is assigned through SAM.gov. The UEI replaced the DUNS number in April 2022 and is required on all federal grant applications. *(2 CFR § 200.1)*
> - **[REQUIRED] SAM.gov Active Registration:** Confirm registration is active and current. Lapsed registration can delay or disqualify an award. *(2 CFR § 200.206)*
> - **[REQUIRED] Single Audit / OMB A-133 Threshold:** If federal expenditures reach or exceed $750,000 in any fiscal year, a single audit by an independent auditor is required and must be submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end. *(2 CFR § 200.501)*
> - **[REQUIRED] Federal Cost Principles (2 CFR 200 Subpart E):** All costs charged to this award must be allowable, allocable, and reasonable. Unallowable costs include lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties. Maintain documentation for all expenditures.
> - **[REQUIRED] Administrative Requirements (2 CFR 200 Subpart D):** Maintain internal controls, performance and financial reporting, 3-year minimum records retention, subrecipient monitoring, and prior approval for budget modifications.
> - **[REQUIRED] Financial Management System Standards (2 CFR § 200.302):** Financial systems must provide accurate, current, and complete disclosure of financial results, with written procedures for cost allowability and drawdown/disbursement timing. *(FAITH Foundation uses QuickBooks.)*
> - **[REQUIRED] Property Management Standards (2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316):** Equipment and real property acquired with federal funds must be inventoried, depreciated properly, and disposed of only with federal approval.
> - **[REQUIRED] Federal Procurement Standards (2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327):** All procurements must follow documented, competitive procedures. Micro-purchases under $10,000 require no bid; $10,000–$250,000 requires price/rate quotes. Conflicts of interest must be documented and avoided.
> - **[RECOMMENDED] Indirect Cost Rate Agreement (NICRA):** If indirect costs are recovered on this award, obtain a negotiated rate agreement with the cognizant federal agency, or apply the de minimis rate of 10% of modified total direct costs (MTDC) if no prior negotiated rate exists. *(2 CFR § 200.414)*

---

## SECTION I: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

FAITH Foundation — the Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope — is a 501(c)(3) faith-based and community organization headquartered in Texas, established to break the cycle of housing insecurity for veterans, individuals experiencing homelessness, those in addiction recovery, formerly incarcerated individuals reentering society, and single-parent families in rural and underserved South and Central Texas communities. The Foundation requests funding under the USDA Rural Housing Service Housing Preservation Grant (HPG) program to provide qualifying very low- and low-income homeowners in rural Texas with critical home repair and rehabilitation assistance that preserves their ability to remain safely and affordably housed.

FAITH Foundation's model is uniquely suited to this program. Our Founder and President, Reid Whitesides, brings more than 20 years of hands-on experience in construction, roofing, project management, and housing rehabilitation. Our Treasurer and Board Chair, Scott Ellis, owns and operates E4 Roofing & Construction and brings more than 15 years of residential and commercial construction expertise directly to bear on our housing programs. Together, this leadership team possesses the construction knowledge, project coordination capacity, and commitment to rural community service that the HPG program is designed to amplify.

Rural South Texas faces acute housing preservation deficits. Aging housing stock, limited nonprofit infrastructure, and concentrated very low-income populations create conditions where deferred maintenance rapidly becomes structural crisis — threatening the health, safety, and housing stability of homeowners who have nowhere else to turn. HPG funds deployed through FAITH Foundation will be paired with our existing network of church partners, building material suppliers, construction volunteers, and case management infrastructure to deliver maximum preservation impact per federal dollar invested.

[NEEDS INPUT: specific dollar amount requested from this HPG application]

---

## SECTION II: STATEMENT OF NEED

### The Rural Housing Preservation Crisis in Texas

The United States is experiencing a housing crisis of historic proportions, and rural Texas communities sit at its most acute intersection: aging housing stock, concentrated poverty, limited nonprofit service infrastructure, and populations — veterans, individuals in recovery, formerly incarcerated persons, and single-parent families — who face the highest barriers to accessing repair assistance through traditional channels.

**National Context**

On a single night in January 2025, 745,652 people were experiencing homelessness across the United States, including 266,320 living entirely unsheltered. (HUD 2025 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report.) The national system has permanent housing capacity for only 9.5% of people in need. (National Alliance to End Homelessness, 2025.) These figures represent the acute end of a continuum that begins with housing instability — deteriorating homes that cannot be safely occupied, deferred repairs that accelerate displacement, and homeowners too poor to maintain the assets they legally own.

The nation faces a shortage of 7.3 million rental units affordable and available to extremely low-income households. (National Low Income Housing Coalition.) For rural homeowners, the parallel crisis is one of preservation: homes that were once affordable to purchase have become costly or impossible to maintain, and the gap between what very low-income homeowners can afford to spend on repairs and what those repairs actually cost is growing wider every year.

**Texas-Specific Housing Data**

Texas is one of the six states accounting for 64% of all people experiencing homelessness nationally. (HUD 2024 AHAR.) Nearly 28,000 Texans were experiencing homelessness in the 2024 Point-in-Time count, including 1,837 veterans — and 44% of that population was entirely unsheltered, meaning no access to emergency shelter or transitional housing existed for them. (HUD 2024 AHAR, cited in Texas HB 158.) Chronic homelessness in Texas increased from 1,949 individuals in 2022 to 2,594 in 2023. (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network.) These figures do not capture the larger population of rural Texans who remain housed but are at imminent risk of housing loss due to unaddressed repair needs.

Among the specific populations FAITH Foundation serves, the housing instability picture is particularly severe:

- **Veterans:** 32,882 veterans were experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2024. (VA 2024 PIT Count.) Texas has one of the nation's highest concentrations of homeless veterans, and in-state veteran homelessness, while declining 9.7% between 2023 and 2024, remains a documented crisis for 1,837 individuals who served their country. Many more Texas veterans are housed but living in substandard conditions in rural areas where VA services and housing repair programs do not reach.

- **Formerly Incarcerated Individuals:** Formerly incarcerated people are approximately 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population. (National Low Income Housing Coalition, 2018; Prison Policy Initiative.) Those who do obtain housing — frequently in rural communities where affordable stock is available — often occupy the oldest, most deteriorated units in the local market, where deferred repairs become displacement risks within months of placement.

- **Single-Parent Families:** The homeownership rate among single mothers is approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples without children. (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024.) Single-parent homeowners face estimated home prices approaching five times their household income. (NAHB Eye on Housing, 2024.) When repair needs arise, single-income households have no financial cushion to address them, making HPG-funded rehabilitation assistance transformational rather than incremental.

- **Individuals in Recovery:** People in addiction recovery disproportionately occupy the least-maintained housing in rural communities. A deteriorating home accelerates recovery failure by increasing stress, reducing safety, and creating conditions incompatible with health and stability.

**The Rural South Texas Service Gap**

Rural South Texas — the primary geography of FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities initiative — presents a specific and documented service gap. The region combines the population characteristics described above with limited nonprofit infrastructure, absence of large housing authorities, and housing stock that is substantially older and less maintained than urban Texas markets. USDA Rural Development data consistently identifies Texas rural counties as high-need for housing preservation investment. Traditional development approaches — permitting, site costs, union labor, urban supply chains — are cost-prohibitive in these communities, which is precisely why modular and manufactured housing deployment and targeted preservation repair programs represent the most effective deployment strategies available.

**The Cost Burden on Very Low-Income Homeowners**

74.2% of homeowner households with incomes below $30,000 are cost-burdened, paying more than 30% of income on housing — the highest rate in over 20 years. (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University, 2023 data.) For homeowners in this income bracket, any unexpected repair expense — a failing roof, deteriorating foundation, non-functioning HVAC, plumbing failure — represents an unresolvable financial crisis. Without HPG-funded intervention, these homeowners face one of three outcomes: continued deterioration into unsafe conditions, displacement into homelessness, or high-interest debt that accelerates financial collapse. The HPG program is designed precisely for this population, and FAITH Foundation is designed precisely to deliver it.

[NEEDS INPUT: county-specific rural housing condition data or USDA-designated rural area confirmation for specific Texas counties in service area]

---

## SECTION III: PROGRAM DESIGN

### Housing Preservation Program Description

FAITH Foundation will administer HPG funds to provide home repair and rehabilitation assistance to very low- and low-income homeowners in eligible rural areas of South and Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast region. The program is structured to maximize the number of households served per federal dollar invested by leveraging volunteer construction labor, donated materials, in-kind professional services, and the construction expertise of our board leadership.

**Program Model and Theory of Change**

FAITH Foundation's theory of change is grounded in a documented, evidence-based premise: stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery from addiction, successful community reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. When a homeowner's residence becomes structurally compromised or unsafe, the cascading effects extend far beyond the building itself — employment is threatened, health deteriorates, children's educational stability is disrupted, and the pathway to permanent displacement accelerates.

By intervening at the point of housing preservation need — before deterioration becomes displacement — the HPG program inverts this cascade. Families who receive timely, competent repair assistance remain stably housed, maintain their homeownership equity, and preserve the foundation on which all other recovery and stability outcomes rest. Each successful preservation repair is a measurable prevention of a housing loss event that would otherwise cost the community far more in emergency services, shelter capacity, and social support.

**Eligible Activities**

FAITH Foundation will use HPG funds for the following eligible activities under 7 CFR Part 1944, Subpart N:

- **Structural repairs:** Roof replacement and repair, foundation stabilization, exterior wall repair, window and door replacement.
- **Health and safety systems:** Plumbing repair and replacement, electrical system upgrades, HVAC installation and repair, mold and moisture remediation.
- **Accessibility modifications:** Ramp installation, bathroom accessibility upgrades, doorway widening for homeowners with disabilities or service-connected injuries, particularly veterans.
- **Energy efficiency improvements:** Insulation installation, weatherization, energy-efficient window replacement — improvements that reduce ongoing utility cost burden for very low-income households.
- **Code compliance:** Repairs required to bring units into compliance with local building and safety codes.

**Target Population**

FAITH Foundation will specifically prioritize HPG assistance for:

- Very low-income homeowners (at or below 50% of Area Median Income) in eligible rural Texas communities
- Low-income homeowners (at or below 80% of AMI) in eligible rural Texas communities
- Military veterans and their family members
- Individuals who are formerly incarcerated and have achieved homeownership or stable housing
- Individuals in addiction recovery who are homeowners or transitional housing occupants eligible under HPG guidelines
- Single-parent families headed by women
- Elderly homeowners on fixed incomes

[NEEDS INPUT: specific USDA-designated rural community names or counties to be served]

**Participant Recruitment and Enrollment**

FAITH Foundation's participant recruitment plan draws on our established partnership network across South and Central Texas. Referrals will be received through:

- County social services agencies and local housing authorities, which currently collaborate with FAITH Foundation on benefits enrollment and case management
- Veterans service organizations that refer military veterans experiencing housing insecurity
- Recovery program partners who refer individuals in active recovery
- Reentry service partners coordinating housing for formerly incarcerated individuals
- Church partners providing community outreach, volunteer labor, and referral networks
- Direct community outreach through FAITH Foundation's case management staff

Upon referral, prospective participants will complete an intake screening to verify income eligibility (very low- or low-income as defined by HUD Area Median Income limits for the applicable rural county), rural area residency, and homeownership status. Screening will document household income through pay stubs, tax returns, or Social Security award letters; homeownership through deed or title documentation; and repair needs through a structured property assessment conducted by qualified personnel.

Intake screening will be completed within [NEEDS INPUT: target intake completion timeframe] of referral. All income eligibility determinations will follow USDA RHS guidelines for HPG program participants.

**Inspection and Scope of Work Development**

Given the construction expertise on FAITH Foundation's board — Scott Ellis's 15-plus years leading E4 Roofing & Construction, and Reid Whitesides's 20-plus years in construction, roofing, and project management — the Foundation is uniquely positioned to conduct professional-quality property assessments and develop accurate, cost-controlled scopes of work at minimal administrative cost. Property inspections will be conducted by or under the supervision of qualified construction professionals, with scopes of work developed to address health, safety, and structural priorities first, followed by energy efficiency and code compliance improvements.

All repair projects exceeding applicable procurement thresholds will be competitively bid in accordance with federal procurement standards (2 CFR §§ 200.317–200.327). Micro-purchases under $10,000 may be made without competitive bidding; purchases between $10,000 and $250,000 will require price or rate quotes from an adequate number of qualified sources. Conflicts of interest will be documented and avoided in all procurement decisions.

**Repair Delivery**

FAITH Foundation will deliver repairs through a combination of:

- **Contracted licensed contractors:** Selected through documented competitive bidding, ensuring quality, code compliance, and cost control.
- **Volunteer construction labor:** Coordinated through church partners and community volunteers, reducing labor costs and increasing households served per program dollar.
- **In-kind material donations:** FAITH Foundation actively recruits donations of building materials from suppliers and manufacturers. All in-kind contributions will be documented at fair market value.
- **Board-supervised construction oversight:** Scott Ellis and Reid Whitesides will provide direct construction oversight, contractor management, and quality assurance at no cost to the program, ensuring repair quality and budget discipline.

**Program Timeline**

[NEEDS INPUT: specific program start date pending award notification]

Consistent with USDA grant administration timelines and to maximize the probability of successful program launch, FAITH Foundation will incorporate a 60-day post-award mobilization period into program planning, during which intake protocols, contractor procurement procedures, and participant referral pipelines will be fully activated before the first repair contracts are executed.

## SECTION IV: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY

### Demonstrated Capacity to Administer HPG Funds

FAITH Foundation brings a leadership team whose combined professional expertise is directly and specifically aligned with the technical, financial, and administrative demands of the Housing Preservation Grant program.

**Executive Leadership**

*Reid Whitesides, Founder & President* brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, and housing-related industries. His construction background is not administrative — it is hands-on, field-level expertise in the exact trades most commonly required for home preservation repair: roofing, structural assessment, project coordination, and contractor management. His personal experience navigating housing insecurity, addiction recovery, and reentry — including nearly 20 years of incarceration in Texas, followed by more than 15 years of sustained sobriety — gives him firsthand insight into the barriers facing the very homeowners the HPG program is designed to serve. He leads the Foundation with the credibility of lived experience and the competence of professional expertise.

*Scott Ellis, Treasurer & Board Chair* is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based construction company he has operated successfully for more than 15 years. His expertise encompasses residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, building systems, cost estimation, and long-term asset stewardship. His 15-plus years leading a construction business translate directly into the Foundation's capacity to manage repair scopes, oversee contractor performance, control costs, and ensure that every HPG dollar produces documented, high-quality preservation outcomes. His financial management experience as a business owner directly supports the Foundation's bookkeeping and grant compliance functions, supported by QuickBooks financial management software.

*Pastor Juan Valdez, Secretary & Protector* brings nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience and more than 40 years of Christian faith leadership to the Foundation's governance team. His background includes 34 years of community business ownership in San Antonio and ministry leadership extending across the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. As governance accountability officer, Pastor Valdez provides the ethical oversight, mission stewardship, and community trust necessary for effective faith-based community organization administration.

**Construction and Housing Rehabilitation Expertise**

The combined construction expertise of Reid Whitesides and Scott Ellis represents a significant organizational asset for HPG program administration. Together, they bring direct experience in:

- Roofing systems, replacement, and repair
- Residential construction project coordination and contractor management
- Budget development, cost estimation, and financial control
- Building code compliance and quality assurance
- Procurement of materials and subcontractor services
- Property assessment and scope of work development

This expertise is available to the program at no additional cost, as both leaders serve in volunteer governance capacity. The result is a program that can conduct professional-quality property assessments, develop accurate repair scopes, supervise contractor performance, and ensure quality outcomes without the overhead of outside consultants or contracted inspection services.

**Partnership Network**

FAITH Foundation maintains active partnerships across multiple sectors that directly support HPG program delivery:

- **Church partners** provide volunteer labor, community outreach, and meeting space for participant programming — reducing administrative overhead and expanding community reach.
- **Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers** provide discounted or donated materials, reducing per-unit repair costs.
- **County social services agencies and local housing authorities** refer eligible families, coordinate benefits enrollment, and provide case management collaboration.
- **Recovery program partners** refer individuals completing treatment who need housing stability support.
- **Reentry service partners** coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals and connect them with employment services.
- **Veterans service organizations** refer military veterans experiencing housing insecurity and coordinate VA benefits enrollment.

**Financial Management Systems**

FAITH Foundation maintains financial records using QuickBooks accounting software. The Foundation is committed to maintaining a financial management system compliant with 2 CFR § 200.302, providing accurate, current, and complete disclosures of financial results; adequate records identifying source and application of funds; effective internal controls; and written procedures for cost allowability determination. Indirect costs will be maintained below 15% of total program budget, consistent with the Foundation's established budget framework.

FAITH Foundation is in its inaugural funding cycle. Initial operations have been funded through founder investment and church community support. The organization has not previously received federal financial assistance. As a result:

- If total federal expenditures in any fiscal year reach or exceed $750,000, FAITH Foundation will engage an independent auditor to conduct a Single Audit in compliance with 2 CFR § 200.501 and submit results to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end.
- FAITH Foundation will apply the de minimis indirect cost rate of 10% of modified total direct costs (MTDC) in the absence of a previously negotiated indirect cost rate agreement (NICRA), consistent with 2 CFR § 200.414.

[NEEDS INPUT: confirmation of active SAM.gov registration and UEI number for inclusion in application]

**Volunteer and In-Kind Resource Leverage**

FAITH Foundation actively recruits and accepts in-kind donations of land, building materials, modular and manufactured housing units, construction equipment and labor, furnishings, appliances, and professional services including legal, architectural, surveying, and construction management. All in-kind contributions are documented at fair market value, providing matching fund capacity that extends the reach of each federal dollar invested. Volunteer construction labor coordinated through church partners and the broader FAITH Foundation network is a direct force multiplier for HPG repair delivery.

---

## SECTION V: BUDGET NARRATIVE AND FUND UTILIZATION

### Budget Framework

FAITH Foundation's budget allocation for HPG program administration prioritizes direct repair delivery over administrative overhead. The Foundation's established budget framework maintains indirect costs below 15% of total program budget, with the maximum available indirect cost recovery applied at the de minimis rate of 10% of MTDC.

**Direct Program Costs**

*Personnel:* Case manager and housing navigator staff will coordinate participant intake, eligibility screening, property assessment scheduling, contractor management, and 12-month post-repair follow-up. Personnel costs are documented by function, allocated to the HPG award based on actual time spent on program activities, and supported by time-and-effort records consistent with 2 CFR § 200.430. [NEEDS INPUT: specific staffing positions, FTE allocations, and salary figures]

*Property Assessments and Inspections:* Initial property assessments will be conducted by or under direct supervision of Reid Whitesides and Scott Ellis, whose construction expertise provides this function at minimal cost. Final inspection services will be documented and charged at actual cost.

*Repair Contracts:* The majority of HPG funds will be deployed as direct repair payments to licensed contractors selected through documented competitive procurement. Repair scopes will prioritize health, safety, and structural integrity, followed by energy efficiency and code compliance. Average repair cost per unit is estimated at [NEEDS INPUT: average estimated repair cost per household based on local contractor data].

*Materials:* Building materials not covered by in-kind donations will be procured through competitive purchasing consistent with federal procurement standards. FAITH Foundation's existing relationships with building material suppliers provide access to discounted pricing that reduces per-unit material cost.

*Volunteer Labor (In-Kind):* Church partner volunteer construction labor will be documented at fair market value and reported as in-kind match. [NEEDS INPUT: estimated volunteer labor hours and fair market value for matching documentation]

*Transportation:* Rural case management outreach requires dedicated transportation capacity. Program vehicle operating costs for rural site visits, property assessments, and contractor coordination will be charged at actual cost.

**Administrative and Indirect Costs**

Administrative costs include organizational administration, accounting, financial reporting, grant compliance, and audit preparation. QuickBooks is used for all financial management. Indirect costs will be recovered at the de minimis rate of 10% of MTDC. All costs charged to this award will be allowable, allocable, and reasonable in compliance with 2 CFR Part 200 Subpart E. Unallowable costs — including lobbying, entertainment, alcoholic beverages, and penalties — will not be charged to this award under any circumstances.

**Property Management**

All equipment and real property acquired with HPG funds will be managed in compliance with 2 CFR §§ 200.310–200.316, including maintenance of a current property inventory, physical inventories at minimum every two years, proper depreciation calculation, and federal approval obtained prior to any disposal. Property records will be maintained for a minimum of three years following award closeout.

## SECTION VI: INTENDED IMPACT AND EVALUATION

### Projected Program Outcomes

FAITH Foundation will track and report on the following performance indicators for this HPG program award:

**Housing Preservation Metrics**

- Number of very low-income homeowner households assisted with repair and rehabilitation
- Number of low-income homeowner households assisted with repair and rehabilitation
- Number of housing units brought into safe, habitable condition
- Number of housing units brought into compliance with applicable building codes
- Dollar value of repairs completed per household served
- Average cost per household served (measuring program efficiency)

**Population-Specific Outcomes**

- Number of veteran homeowner households served
- Number of formerly incarcerated homeowner households served
- Number of single-parent homeowner households served
- Number of individuals in recovery whose homeownership stability was preserved through repair assistance
- Number of elderly homeowners on fixed incomes assisted

**Housing Stability Outcomes**

- 12-month housing retention rate: percentage of assisted homeowners remaining stably housed 12 months post-repair
- Reduction in housing cost burden: documentation of reduced utility or maintenance cost burden following energy efficiency improvements

**Program Efficiency Metrics**

- Ratio of direct repair expenditure to total program cost
- Value of in-kind contributions and volunteer labor leveraged per federal dollar invested
- Average time from referral to repair completion

### Data Collection and Reporting

All program data will be collected through FAITH Foundation's case management system and reported quarterly to USDA Rural Housing Service in compliance with 2 CFR Part 200 Subpart D administrative requirements. Participant records will be maintained with a minimum three-year retention period following award closeout. Annual program data will be published in FAITH Foundation's annual impact report and made available to all funders, donors, and stakeholders.

FAITH Foundation will coordinate fully with any USDA monitoring visits, program reviews, or data requests during the award period. Financial reports will be prepared using QuickBooks and reviewed by Scott Ellis as Treasurer and Board Chair prior to submission, ensuring accuracy and completeness.

FAITH Foundation measures impact across five documented domains: housing placement, financial stability, reentry success, recovery outcomes, and community development. For this HPG award, housing placement and financial stability metrics are primary, tracking the number of households transitioned from unsafe or deteriorating conditions to stable, preserved homeownership, and the degree to which repair assistance reduces ongoing cost burden for very low-income families. All outcomes are tracked longitudinally with quarterly reporting and annual program evaluation.

---

## SECTION VII: SUSTAINABILITY

### Long-Term Program Sustainability

FAITH Foundation's sustainability model is not dependent on any single funding source. The Foundation actively pursues diversified revenue across government grants, private foundations, corporate giving programs, faith-based funders, community development financial institutions, church partnerships, and individual donors. This diversification protects program continuity across funding cycles and ensures that families enrolled in HPG-supported repair programs are not exposed to service interruption.

The Foundation's Cornerstone Communities model — which deploys modular and manufactured housing units on donated or acquired land in rural South Texas — generates long-term sustainability through a rotating housing asset model: as residents transition to permanent housing, units become available for new participants, reducing ongoing capital expenditure and creating self-sustaining community impact. Physical assets including land and modular housing units appreciate over time, building organizational balance sheet strength.

For housing preservation activities specifically, sustainability is built through:

- **Volunteer labor infrastructure:** Church partner networks provide ongoing volunteer construction labor that continues beyond any single grant period, reducing per-unit repair costs for future homeowners.
- **Materials donation relationships:** Established relationships with building material suppliers and manufacturers generate recurring in-kind contributions that extend program capacity.
- **Case management integration:** HPG repair participants are integrated into FAITH Foundation's broader case management network, connecting them with financial literacy programming, down payment assistance, and ongoing housing stability support that reduces future repair delinquency.
- **Board expertise retention:** The construction expertise of Reid Whitesides and Scott Ellis represents a durable organizational asset that supports program quality without recurring cost.

FAITH Foundation is committed to pursuing follow-on HPG funding and complementary USDA Rural Development resources to sustain and expand housing preservation capacity in rural South Texas beyond the initial award period.

---

## SECTION VIII: ORGANIZATIONAL HISTORY AND MISSION ALIGNMENT

### About FAITH Foundation

FAITH Foundation was established by Reid Whitesides to address the critical shortage of affordable and transitional housing options in rural South Texas communities. The organization was founded on the conviction that stable housing is the essential foundation for recovery from addiction, successful reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. The Foundation's name reflects its founding purpose: the Foundation for Affordable Instruction and Tenancy Hope.

Drawing on Reid's background in construction, roofing, and housing, the organization developed the Cornerstone Communities model — an innovative approach to deploying affordable housing at scale in rural areas where traditional development is cost-prohibitive. The model uses modular and manufactured housing units sited on acquired or donated land to create purpose-built transitional micro-communities.

FAITH Foundation is a faith-based and community organization, grounding its mission in Christian principles of grace, redemption, and service while maintaining open enrollment for all individuals regardless of faith background. The Foundation's work is guided by the principle that every person — regardless of economic hardship, reentry status, or recovery journey — deserves the dignity of a stable home and a genuine pathway to permanent housing.

### Mission Alignment with HPG Program Priorities

The HPG program exists to assist very low- and low-income homeowners in rural areas in repairing and rehabilitating their homes. FAITH Foundation exists to break the cycle of housing insecurity for exactly these households — veterans, individuals in recovery, formerly incarcerated persons, single parents, and economically disadvantaged families concentrated in rural South Texas. The alignment is not incidental. It is structural.

FAITH Foundation is a qualified faith-based and community organization within the meaning of the HPG Notice of Funding Availability. We serve the income populations the program prioritizes, in the rural geographic areas the program targets, through a model that combines direct repair delivery with case management, financial literacy, and housing stability programming that extends the impact of each preservation investment far beyond the physical repair itself.

Our leadership team brings the construction expertise to manage repair programs competently, the financial management systems to administer federal funds compliantly, and the community relationships to identify and enroll eligible households efficiently. We are prepared to be responsible stewards of HPG resources and to deliver measurable housing preservation outcomes for the rural Texas families who need them most.
