Key Performance Indicators

FAITH Foundation will track and report on the following metrics across all program components. Housing Placement Rate measures units occupied against referrals received and is reported quarterly. Housing Retention Rate tracks the percentage of participants stably housed at 6 and 12 months post, placement and is reported semi, annually. Homeownership Conversion Rate measures the percentage who transition to homeownership within 24 months and is reported annually. Financial Readiness Score captures measured improvement in credit score, debt, to, income ratio, and savings rate among financial literacy program completers and is reported quarterly. Employment Placement Rate tracks the percentage of reentry and recovery participants placed within 90 days of enrollment and is reported quarterly. Recidivism Prevention Rate measures the percentage of reentry participants avoiding reincarceration within 24 months and is reported annually. Recovery Stability Rate tracks the percentage of recovery housing participants maintaining sobriety and stable housing at 12 months and is reported annually. Cornerstone Communities Occupancy measures units built, occupied, and progressing toward permanent housing and is reported quarterly.

All program data will be collected through FAITH Foundation's case management system and reported quarterly to the board of directors. Annual impact reports will be published and made available to all funders and stakeholders. Third, party outcome verification will be pursued beginning in Year 2.

Between 23.1% and 47.8% of annual homeless shelter admissions are formerly incarcerated individuals. (Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019.) Nationally, 82% of individuals released from prison across 24 states were re-arrested within ten years of release, and housing instability is a leading predictor of reincarceration through supervision violations and increased law enforcement contact. (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024; CSG Justice Center, 2025.)

The national shortage of 7.3 million rental units affordable and available to extremely low-income households compounds this crisis for people with criminal records, who are routinely excluded from private rental markets. (National Low Income Housing Coalition.) In Texas, this exclusion lands hardest in rural communities, where the private rental inventory is thinner, landlord screening more restrictive, and nonprofit alternatives nearly nonexistent.

**Single-Parent Households**

The homeownership rate among single mothers is approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples without children. (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024.) Single-parent households face estimated home prices approaching five times their income, indicating severe housing cost burden. (NAHB Eye on Housing, 2024.) These families are disproportionately renters in cost-burdened situations, with 74.2% of homeowner households with incomes below $30,000 cost-burdened — paying more than 30% of income on housing, the highest rate in over 20 years. (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University, 2023 data.)

**The Down Payment and Wealth-Building Gap**

First-time homebuyers now make up just 21% of the market — the lowest share since NAR began tracking in 1981, when they consistently accounted for approximately 40%. (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers.) The median age of first-time buyers has climbed to a record 40 years old, up from the late 20s in the 1980s. (NAR 2025 Profile.) 67% of millennials have no savings for a home down payment. (REsimpli 2025 Market Survey.) The racial homeownership gap persists: the Black homeownership rate stands at 46.6% and the Hispanic homeownership rate at 49.9%, compared to 74.0% for white households as of Q1 2024. (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University.) For the populations FAITH Foundation serves — veterans, reentry individuals, single parents, people in recovery — these systemic barriers are layered on top of discrimination, criminal record exclusions, addiction histories, and service-connected disabilities.

**Rural Texas: The Infrastructure Gap**

Rural South and Central Texas faces an acute affordable housing shortage compounded by limited nonprofit infrastructure. Traditional multifamily housing development is cost-prohibitive in rural markets where land values do not support conventional financing. The populations FAITH Foundation serves are concentrated precisely in these underserved rural corridors. Modular and manufactured housing deployment offers the only scalable, cost-effective solution for bringing new rental units online in communities where traditional construction timelines and costs preclude conventional multifamily development.

The Ida Renters Resilient Housing Incentive program, implemented through FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities model, directly addresses this rural inventory gap.

> **[REQUIRED — COMPLIANCE FLAG]:** FAITH Foundation will coordinate with the responsible entity (the local government grantee) to ensure completion of HUD Environmental Review under 24 CFR Part 58 prior to any choice-limiting actions, including property acquisition, lease execution, or commencement of construction. No funds will be committed or expended on site-specific activities until environmental clearance is received and documented. FAITH Foundation will maintain all required environmental review records and make them available to HUD and the grantee upon request.

---

## SECTION 3: PROJECT DESIGN AND HOUSING STRATEGY

### Overview of the Ida Renters Resilient Housing Incentive Program Implementation

FAITH Foundation will implement the Ida Renters Resilient Housing Incentive program through its Cornerstone Communities model — purpose-built modular micro-communities designed specifically for low-to-moderate income renters in rural and underserved South and Central Texas. The program design integrates three interconnected components: (1) modular multifamily housing unit acquisition and siting, (2) structured transitional tenancy with case management and wraparound services, and (3) a permanent housing pathway through down payment assistance and homeownership counseling.

### Housing Unit Type and Capacity

FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities deploy modular and manufactured housing units sourced through its strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes. These units are move-in-ready, durable, and can be sited on acquired or donated land without the delays and costs of site-built construction. This approach is particularly suited to rural Texas communities where traditional multifamily construction is economically infeasible.

[NEEDS INPUT: Specific unit count committed under this NOFA application — e.g., number of multifamily units proposed for funding, specific Cornerstone Community site(s), and unit mix (bedroom counts, square footage)]

Each Cornerstone Community is designed to include:
- Individual residential units for program participants
- Shared community spaces supporting wraparound programming
- On-site access to case management, peer mentorship, financial literacy, and recovery programming
- Remote work and learning infrastructure
- Community laundry facilities
- Transportation coordination for rural outreach and employment access

Modular housing unit costs range from $30,000 to $60,000 per unit, inclusive of site preparation and utility infrastructure. This cost-per-unit is significantly below market-rate multifamily construction costs in Texas, reflecting the efficiency advantage of the Cornerstone Communities model.

### Site Control and Acquisition

FAITH Foundation acquires land through donations from private landowners, churches, municipalities, and developers, or through reduced-cost purchases in rural South Texas communities. Land owners in rural South Texas communities donate or sell land at reduced cost for community development sites, and the Foundation actively cultivates these relationships through its church partnership network and county social services agency collaborations.

[NEEDS INPUT: Documentation of specific site control for this application — e.g., executed option agreement, deed, letter of intent from landowner, or parcel address and county for the proposed Cornerstone Community site to be funded under this NOFA]

> **[REQUIRED — COMPLIANCE FLAG]:** All property acquisition and site preparation activities are subject to HUD Environmental Review requirements under 24 CFR Part 58. FAITH Foundation will not execute any purchase agreements, leases, or begin site preparation until the responsible entity completes and certifies the required environmental review and HUD approval is obtained. Documentation of environmental clearance will be maintained in the project file.

### Program Intake and Affirmative Marketing

FAITH Foundation conducts affirmative outreach to ensure that program benefits reach the low-to-moderate income populations most in need. Referral and intake channels include:

- **Veterans service organizations:** Referring military veterans experiencing housing insecurity and coordinating VA benefits enrollment
- **Recovery program partners:** Referring individuals completing addiction treatment who need stable transitional housing
- **Reentry service partners:** Coordinating placement of formerly incarcerated individuals upon release, connecting them with employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support
- **County social services agencies and local housing authorities:** Referring eligible families and individuals, coordinating benefits enrollment, and providing case management collaboration
- **Church partners:** Providing volunteer labor, mentorship, and congregational outreach to underserved community members

Affirmative marketing materials will be distributed in English and Spanish to reflect the demographic composition of rural South and Central Texas communities, with outreach prioritizing populations protected under the Fair Housing Act.

> **[REQUIRED — COMPLIANCE FLAG — Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity]:** FAITH Foundation is committed to affirmatively furthering fair housing as required under the Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 3601–3619) and 24 CFR Parts 100, 107, and 110. All program participants will be served without discrimination on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, religion, disability, or familial status. FAITH Foundation will maintain written non-discrimination policies, conduct affirmative marketing to underserved and minority populations, and comply with all Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act requirements. Documentation of affirmative marketing efforts will be maintained and made available to the responsible entity upon request.

[NEEDS INPUT: Written Affirmative Fair Housing Marketing Plan — a formal document describing specific outreach strategies, materials, languages, and target populations must be developed and attached to this application. FAITH Foundation should also document its approach to ADA accessibility compliance for proposed housing units, including physical accessibility features planned for Cornerstone Community units and common areas.]

### Tenancy Structure and Transition Pathway

Participants enter Cornerstone Communities as transitional renters. The program structure includes:

- **Months 1–6 (Stabilization Phase):** Participants receive case management, financial literacy instruction, and connection to employment and benefits. Housing is stable, and case managers operating at a maximum 15-to-1 client ratio monitor progress and address barriers.
- **Months 7–18 (Advancement Phase):** Participants engage in homeownership counseling, credit building, and savings programming. Employment is stabilized; reentry and recovery milestones are documented.
- **Months 19–24 (Transition Phase):** Participants who achieve mortgage readiness receive down payment assistance vouchers ($2,500 per household, funded through the Bright Box Homes partnership) and are connected to homeownership opportunities. Participants who need additional time continue in stabilization with an individualized housing plan.

As residents successfully transition to permanent housing, their units become available for new program participants, creating a self-sustaining cycle of community impact and maximizing the long-term utility of each housing unit funded under this program.

### Lead-Based Paint Compliance

> **[REQUIRED — COMPLIANCE FLAG — Lead-Based Paint]:** Because FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities are developed using new modular and manufactured housing units, lead-based paint hazards associated with pre-1978 construction are not anticipated to be applicable. However, if any rehabilitation of existing structures is involved in site preparation or community common space construction, FAITH Foundation will comply fully with 24 CFR Part 35, the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act of 1992 (Title X), and EPA RRP Rule (40 CFR Part 745), including required notification, inspection, assessment, and lead-safe work practices. Documentation will be maintained in the project file and made available to HUD and the responsible entity upon request.

### Davis-Bacon and Section 3 Compliance

> **[REQUIRED — COMPLIANCE FLAG — Davis-Bacon Prevailing Wage]:** If construction or rehabilitation activities funded under this award involve 8 or more units, FAITH Foundation will comply fully with Davis-Bacon Act prevailing wage requirements (40 U.S.C. §§ 3141–3148; 29 CFR Part 5; HUD Handbook 1344.1). All contractors and subcontractors will be required to pay workers no less than locally prevailing wages as determined by the U.S. Department of Labor. FAITH Foundation will obtain certified payrolls from all contractors and conduct required on-site interviews. Any violations will be addressed with back-pay restitution. Davis-Bacon wage requirements will be incorporated into all construction contracts.

> **[REQUIRED — COMPLIANCE FLAG — Section 3 Hiring]:** For HUD-funded construction contracts exceeding $200,000 or professional services contracts exceeding $100,000, FAITH Foundation will implement a Section 3 hiring plan prioritizing employment of low-income persons and Section 3 businesses as defined under Section 3 of the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1968 (12 U.S.C. § 1701u; 24 CFR Part 135). Outreach efforts will be documented, and FAITH Foundation will submit annual Section 3 Summary Reports (HUD-60002) as required, with a target of 25% of new hires being Section 3 workers. FAITH Foundation will develop a written Section 3 Plan prior to construction commencement.

## SECTION 4: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY AND EXPERIENCE

### Leadership Qualifications

FAITH Foundation's leadership team brings together direct lived experience with the populations served, construction and housing industry expertise, financial stewardship capacity, and decades of governance and ministry experience. This combination is directly relevant to the implementation of a multifamily housing program in rural Texas.

**Reid Whitesides — Founder & President**

Reid Whitesides brings more than 20 years of experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries to the Foundation's leadership. His background in residential construction and project management provides operational grounding for the Cornerstone Communities development model. His commitment to this work is inseparable from his lived experience: during a long struggle with addiction, Reid spent nearly twenty years incarcerated in the State of Texas. Those experiences gave him firsthand, irreplaceable insight into the barriers that veterans, reentry individuals, and people in recovery face when attempting to secure stable housing. Today, he has been sober for more than fifteen years. Reid leads FAITH Foundation with direct understanding of every population the Ida Renters Resilient Housing Incentive program will serve, and with the construction, project management, and organizational skills to execute a modular multifamily housing initiative in rural Texas.

**Scott Ellis — Treasurer & Board Chair**

Scott Ellis is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based construction company he has led successfully for more than 15 years. Scott's expertise encompasses residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, building systems, construction costs, property improvement, and long-term asset stewardship. This expertise directly supports FAITH Foundation's ability to evaluate, procure, site, and manage modular housing units cost-effectively and in compliance with applicable construction standards. As Treasurer, Scott provides financial oversight ensuring responsible stewardship of all grant resources. His 24 years as a Georgetown resident and his direct construction industry experience make him an authoritative voice in the Foundation's housing development decisions.

**Pastor Juan Valdez — Secretary & Protector**

Pastor Juan Valdez brings nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience and more than 40 years of faith leadership to the Foundation's governance. His role as Secretary and Protector ensures mission integrity, ethics oversight, and governance accountability. His ministry experience spans the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and Africa. He and his wife, Martha, operated a successful business in San Antonio for 34 years — a record of community consistency, reliability, and stewardship that reflects the values governing FAITH Foundation's operations. Pastor Valdez currently serves as an Associate Pastor at Temple of Praise in Texas.

### Relevant Experience and Model Design

FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities model was specifically designed to address the conditions that define rural Texas's housing crisis: limited existing inventory, cost-prohibitive traditional construction, thin nonprofit infrastructure, and populations excluded from private rental markets. The modular and manufactured housing approach allows FAITH Foundation to bring new rental units online in rural communities on timelines and at per-unit costs that conventional multifamily development cannot match.

The Foundation's multi-sector partnership network — spanning church partners, recovery programs, reentry service providers, county social services agencies, housing authorities, and building material suppliers — provides the referral pipelines, case management collaboration, and in-kind resource support that are essential for a rural housing program to function efficiently.

FAITH Foundation maintains financial records using QuickBooks and operates with financial oversight by a Treasurer with 15+ years of construction business ownership experience. The Foundation's budget allocation prioritizes direct program delivery, with indirect costs maintained below 15 percent of total program budget.

**Organizational Stage Disclosure:** FAITH Foundation is in its inaugural funding cycle, established to address critical gaps in rural South Texas housing infrastructure. Initial operations have been funded through founder investment and church community support. The organization has not yet produced completed program outcome data. All projected outcomes stated in this proposal are based on evidence-based models documented by HUD, the VA, and peer organizations operating comparable housing voucher and community development programs. The Foundation's leadership team brings the construction expertise, lived-experience credibility, governance accountability, and community partnership network necessary to execute this program successfully in its first funded implementation cycle.

> **[REQUIRED — COMPLIANCE FLAG — State Single Audit]:** FAITH Foundation will comply with all applicable Texas state audit requirements governing organizations receiving state grant funds, including Texas Government Code § 783 and relevant state agency grant requirements. If award amounts trigger federal single audit thresholds under 2 CFR § 200.512, FAITH Foundation will engage a qualified independent auditor and submit required Single Audit reports within required timeframes. The Foundation currently uses QuickBooks for financial management and will implement additional financial controls as required by the grant agreement.

## SECTION 5: EQUITY, FAIR HOUSING, AND LOW-TO-MODERATE INCOME BENEFIT

### Priority Population Alignment

Every population FAITH Foundation serves is a priority population under fair housing principles and CDBG national objectives. Veterans, formerly incarcerated individuals, people in addiction recovery, single parents, and individuals experiencing homelessness are disproportionately low-to-moderate income households, and they face intersecting systemic barriers — criminal records, addiction histories, service-connected disabilities, single-income constraints — that exclude them from conventional rental and homeownership markets even when units are nominally available.

FAITH Foundation's program design ensures that 100% of Ida Renters Resilient Housing Incentive program participants will be low-to-moderate income households as defined under CDBG national objectives. Income eligibility will be verified at intake using HUD income limits applicable to the county of service. Documentation of LMI status will be maintained in participant files and made available to the responsible entity upon request.

### Racial and Ethnic Equity

The housing crisis falls with particular force on communities of color. African Americans represent 32.7% of the homeless population while comprising 14.4% of the U.S. population. (HUD 2025 AHAR.) The Black homeownership rate (46.6%) and Hispanic homeownership rate (49.9%) remain dramatically below the white homeownership rate (74.0%). (Joint Center for Housing Studies, Harvard University, Q1 2024.) Black veterans represent 31% of homeless veterans while comprising only 14% of the veteran population. (Mission Roll Call, 2024.) In rural South and Central Texas, Hispanic households represent a significant share of the low-income renter population.

FAITH Foundation's affirmative marketing plan targets these communities specifically, with outreach materials in English and Spanish, partnerships with faith communities serving Hispanic and African American populations, and intake practices designed to remove barriers for individuals with criminal records, addiction histories, and limited credit histories.

### ADA Accessibility

[NEEDS INPUT: Specific description of ADA accessibility features planned for Cornerstone Community housing units and common areas — e.g., accessible unit percentage, door width standards, accessible bathrooms, ramp access, etc. — required for compliance with Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and Fair Housing Act accessibility requirements]

FAITH Foundation is committed to ensuring that a portion of Cornerstone Community units are designed to meet or exceed ADA and Fair Housing Act physical accessibility standards. All common areas will be accessible to individuals with disabilities. The Foundation will consult with an accessibility specialist during unit design and site preparation to ensure compliance.

---

## SECTION 6: SUSTAINABILITY AND LONG-TERM IMPACT

### Rotating Housing Asset Model

FAITH Foundation's long-term sustainability is built on a structural advantage that distinguishes the Cornerstone Communities model from conventional rental assistance programs: physical housing assets. Unlike voucher-only programs that depend on perpetual funding to maintain participant stability, each modular housing unit acquired through FAITH Foundation becomes a permanent organizational asset. As residents successfully transition to permanent housing, their units become available for new program participants — creating ongoing program capacity without requiring proportional increases in capital expenditure.

This rotating asset model means that each dollar invested in a Cornerstone Community housing unit generates impact across multiple program cycles, not just one participant cohort. The per-unit cost of $30,000 to $60,000, amortized across successive participant cohorts, represents exceptional cost-effectiveness relative to the lifetime social cost of chronic homelessness, reincarceration, or sustained housing instability.

### Diversified Revenue Streams

FAITH Foundation's sustainability plan encompasses the following revenue streams, each independently operational:

- **Bright Box Homes Partnership:** Bright Box Homes donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold, providing a recurring, renewable revenue stream tied to new home construction activity. This partnership converts private market activity into down payment assistance vouchers for program participants.
- **Program Fees:** Assessed on a sliding scale based on participant income, ensuring affordability while contributing to operational sustainability.
- **Rental Income:** From stabilized housing units occupied by program participants, contributing to property operating costs.
- **Recurring Grant Funding:** Federal, state, and private foundation grants, actively pursued through a diversified grant development strategy.
- **Corporate Sponsorships and In-Kind Donations:** Including donated land, building materials, modular housing units, construction equipment and labor, furnishings, appliances, and professional services including legal, architectural, surveying, and construction management.
- **Church Partnerships and Congregational Giving:** Church partners provide volunteer labor, congregational fundraising, mentorship volunteers, and meeting space for participant programming.
- **Individual Donor Cultivation:** Annual giving and major donor development to support operational and capital needs.

Physical assets — land and modular housing units — appreciate over time and reduce ongoing capital expenditure requirements. The Foundation actively pursues diversified funding across government grants, private foundations, corporate giving programs, faith-based funders, and community development financial institutions to avoid dependency on any single source.

### Affordability Restrictions and Long-Term Covenants

[NEEDS INPUT: Description of any long-term affordability restrictions or covenants that will be recorded against properties developed under this program — e.g., deed restrictions, land use restrictions, ground leases, or other mechanisms ensuring continued affordability beyond the grant period. This is required to demonstrate long-term affordability commitment to the funder.]

FAITH Foundation is prepared to execute appropriate long-term affordability agreements as required by the RSHI NOFA and the responsible entity, including recorded deed restrictions or covenants maintaining units as affordable rental housing for a specified restriction period.

### Partnership Sustainability

FAITH Foundation's network of cross-sector partnerships provides sustainable referral pipelines, case management collaboration, and in-kind resource support that reduce the Foundation's dependence on any single funding source:

- Church partners provide ongoing volunteer labor, mentorship, and congregational fundraising independent of grant funding cycles.
- Recovery program partners and reentry service providers maintain active referral relationships that sustain program enrollment.
- County social services agencies and local housing authorities provide case management collaboration and benefits coordination that extend program capacity.
- Veterans service organizations coordinate VA benefits enrollment for veteran participants, connecting them to federal entitlements that supplement program resources.
- Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers provide discounted or donated materials and units, reducing per-unit capital costs.

---

## SECTION 7: INTENDED IMPACT AND EVALUATION

### Theory of Change

Stable housing is the prerequisite for sustained recovery from addiction, successful community reentry after incarceration, and long-term economic self-sufficiency. FAITH Foundation's model addresses the root cause of cyclical homelessness — the absence of affordable transitional housing in rural communities. By deploying modular housing units in purpose-built Cornerstone Communities, paired with case management, peer mentorship, financial literacy, and down payment assistance, individuals progress through a structured pathway from crisis to stability to permanent housing. Each successful transition frees capacity for the next participant, creating a self-sustaining cycle of community impact.

### Intended Outcomes — Program Year Targets

**Year 1:**
- Distribute 10 down payment assistance vouchers ($2,500 each) to qualifying families, totaling $25,000 in direct housing assistance
- Enroll 25 families in homeownership counseling and financial literacy programming
- Provide emergency bridge housing assistance to 15 families facing immediate housing crises
- Establish partnerships with a minimum of 3 local employers for reentry and recovery program participants
- Secure the first donated land parcel for Cornerstone Communities development
- Recruit and train 20 volunteers for mentorship, financial literacy instruction, and community outreach

**Year 2:**
- Distribute 40 housing vouchers totaling $100,000 in direct assistance
- Graduate 20 families from homeownership counseling into active homebuyers
- Begin construction on the first Cornerstone Community with on-site programming
- Expand recovery housing partnerships to serve 30 individuals annually
- Place 15 reentry participants into stable employment within 90 days of program enrollment
- Achieve a 90% housing retention rate among voucher recipients at the 12-month mark

**Year 3:**
- Distribute 100 housing vouchers totaling $250,000 in direct assistance
- Complete and occupy the first Cornerstone Community with a minimum of 20 residential units
- Achieve a homeownership conversion rate of 30% among program participants who entered in Year 1
- Publish the first annual impact report with independently verified outcome data

### Key Performance Indicators

FAITH Foundation will track and report on the following KPIs across all program components:

| Metric | Measurement Method | Reporting Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Housing Placement Rate | Units occupied / referrals received | Quarterly |
| Housing Retention Rate | % stably housed at 6 and 12 months post-placement | Semi-annual |
| Homeownership Conversion Rate | % transitioned to homeownership within 24 months | Annual |
| Financial Readiness Score | Credit score, debt-to-income ratio, savings rate improvement | Quarterly |
| Employment Placement Rate | % placed within 90 days of enrollment (reentry/recovery) | Quarterly |
| Recidivism Prevention Rate | % avoiding reincarceration within 24 months | Annual |
| Recovery Stability Rate | % maintaining sobriety and stable housing at 12 months | Annual |
| Cornerstone Communities Occupancy | Units built, occupied, and progressing to permanent housing | Quarterly |

All program data will be collected through FAITH Foundation's case management system and reported quarterly to the board of directors. Annual impact reports will be published and made available to all funders and stakeholders. Third-party outcome verification will be pursued beginning in Year 2.

---

## SECTION 8: BUDGET JUSTIFICATION AND COST EFFECTIVENESS

### Budget Philosophy

FAITH Foundation's budget allocation prioritizes direct program delivery over administrative overhead. Indirect costs are maintained below 15 percent of total program budget. The modular housing deployment model reduces capital costs substantially relative to traditional multifamily construction, and in-kind donations of building materials, volunteer labor, and professional services further reduce cash outlays while being documented at fair market value for matching fund requirements.

### Cost-Effectiveness

The Cornerstone Communities model achieves cost-effectiveness through three structural mechanisms:

1. **Modular Unit Economics:** Per-unit costs of $30,000–$60,000 represent a fraction of site-built multifamily construction costs in Texas, enabling more units to be deployed per dollar of capital investment.

2. **Rotating Asset Utilization:** Each unit serves multiple program participants across successive cohorts, reducing the effective per-household cost of housing assistance over time.

3. **In-Kind Resource Integration:** FAITH Foundation actively accepts and documents donations of land, building materials, modular housing units, construction equipment and labor, furnishings, appliances, and professional services. These in-kind contributions reduce cash expenditure requirements and constitute leveraged matching resources.

This section is required by the funder for budget scoring and cannot be completed without specific dollar figures tied to the scope of this application.]

FAITH Foundation brings to the Ida Renters Resilient Housing Incentive program a model that is purpose-built for the problem this NOFA is designed to solve: the shortage of affordable, resilient rental housing for low-to-moderate income households in rural and underserved Texas communities.

SECTION I: STATEMENT OF NEED

The Housing Crisis in Rural Texas

Rural South Texas communities are dealing with a housing crisis that isn't one problem - it's three at once. There's a shortage of affordable inventory. There's a near, total absence of wraparound services for vulnerable populations. And there's almost no transitional housing infrastructure for the people most likely to cycle endlessly through homelessness, incarceration, and addiction without a structured way out. FAITH Foundation was established because no other organization in our service area runs an integrated, supply, and, demand housing solution designed specifically for the populations this grant program prioritizes: individuals in reentry, those in addiction recovery, and veterans experiencing housing insecurity.

The data supporting this need isn't anecdotal. It's documented, verified, and getting worse.

Statewide Housing Instability

Nearly 28,000 Texans were experiencing homelessness during the 2024 Point, in, Time count, including 1,837 veterans. (HUD 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report, cited in Texas HB 158.) What's particularly striking is that 44% of those Texans were completely unsheltered - no emergency shelter, no transitional housing, nothing. (HUD 2024 AHAR.) That unsheltered rate tells you something specific about rural Texas: emergency shelter beds are scarce, and the geographic distances involved make urban shelter access practically unreachable for people living in the communities we serve.

Chronic homelessness in Texas isn't holding steady. It's accelerating. The Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network identified 2,594 chronically homeless individuals in 2023, up sharply from 1,949 in 2022 - a 33% increase in a single year. That trajectory reflects a system that's failing its most vulnerable members faster than the current nonprofit and governmental response can keep up with.

Texas is one of seven states that together account for 64% of all homelessness in the United States. (HUD 2024 AHAR.) This isn't a local anomaly. It's a national crisis, and it's concentrated here.

Veterans Experiencing Housing Insecurity

Texas has among the highest concentrations of homeless veterans in the country. In the 2024 Point, in, Time count, 1,837 Texas veterans were experiencing homelessness. By December 2023, 4,085 veterans were being served by Texas Continuums of Care, up from 3,962 in 2022. (Texas Homeless Data Sharing Network.) Nationally, 13,851 veterans were living completely unsheltered in 2024. (VA 2024 PIT Count.) These are people who served their country and came home to communities that don't have the housing infrastructure to support their transition to civilian stability.

FAITH Foundation's Veterans Path Home program is designed to address this gap head, on, connecting veterans experiencing housing insecurity with transitional housing placement, VA benefits navigation, rental assistance, and dedicated case management focused on permanent housing.

Reentry Populations and the Homelessness, Recidivism Cycle

Formerly incarcerated individuals face the steepest housing barriers of anyone we serve. Formerly incarcerated people are roughly 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population. (National Low Income Housing Coalition, 2018; Prison Policy Initiative.) They account for between 23.1% and 47.8% of annual homeless shelter admissions nationally. (Community Solutions / CSG Justice Center, 2019.)

The consequences of housing failure after release are well, documented and severe. Eighty, two percent of individuals released from prison across 24 states were re, arrested within 10 years of release. (UNLV Reentry Research Brief, 2024.) People experiencing homelessness after release face a heightened risk of reincarceration because of increased law enforcement contact and supervision violations tied directly to their housing status. (CSG Justice Center, 2025.) Stable transitional housing isn't a social service amenity for this population. It's the single most important recidivism prevention intervention available.

The national shortage of 7.3 million rental units affordable and available to extremely low, income households makes all of this worse, particularly for individuals with criminal records who are already excluded from most private market rental housing. (National Low Income Housing Coalition.) In rural South Texas, where private market rental inventory is limited even for households without criminal history, a formerly incarcerated person returning to their community of origin has essentially no housing options without an organization like FAITH Foundation stepping in.

Recovery Populations

Individuals completing addiction treatment face a parallel crisis. Without stable, sober housing, recovery outcomes fall apart quickly. FAITH Foundation's Recovery Housing program provides a structured continuum from sober living through transitional housing to permanent independent housing, with on, site support groups and accountability built into every stage. Without that continuum in rural South Texas, people completing treatment get pushed back into the same unstable environments that contributed to their addiction in the first place. The relapse and homelessness cycles that follow impose enormous costs on individuals, families, and public systems alike.

The Down Payment and Homeownership Gap

Even for people who've achieved employment stability after reentry or recovery, the path to homeownership stays blocked. First, time homebuyers now make up just 21% of the housing market, the lowest share since the National Association of Realtors began tracking in 1981, compared to roughly 40% before 2008. (NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers.) The median age of first, time homebuyers has hit a record 40 years old. (NAR 2025 Profile.) For the populations FAITH Foundation serves, people whose economic trajectories have been interrupted by incarceration, addiction, or military service, these barriers are compounded by criminal records, broken employment histories, and damaged credit.

The homeownership rate among single mothers, a core population we serve, is approximately 34%, compared to 84% for married couples without children. (U.S. Census Bureau ACS / LendingTree, 2024.) Single, parent households face estimated home prices approaching five times their income. (NAHB Eye on Housing, 2024.) Direct down payment assistance isn't a supplement to these families' housing strategies. It's the bridge between indefinite rental instability and the wealth, building stability that homeownership provides.

The Rural Infrastructure Gap

Rural South Texas deals with acute housing shortages and very limited nonprofit and governmental housing infrastructure at the same time. Traditional affordable housing development - site, built construction with lengthy permitting, general contractors, and large capital outlays - is cost, prohibitive in communities where land values don't support conventional development economics. The result is a near, complete absence of affordable housing inventory in the exact communities where FAITH Foundation's target populations are concentrated.

FAITH Foundation addresses this rural infrastructure gap through a modular housing deployment model. Units supplied through our strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes can be sited on donated or acquired rural land without the delays and costs of traditional construction. That brings housing solutions directly to underserved rural communities rather than concentrating resources in urban centers that our target populations can't easily reach.

Activity 1: Modular Housing Unit Acquisition - Cornerstone Communities Initiative

SECTION V: SUSTAINABILITY AND LONG, TERM IMPACT

The Rotating Housing Asset Model

FAITH Foundation's sustainability is structurally built into the program design. Cornerstone Communities don't create permanent dependency on grant funding. They create permanent assets.

Each modular housing unit acquired through this grant serves transitional residents during the program period, then generates rental income as units stabilize, contributing to operational sustainability. As residents transition to permanent housing, those units open up for new participants - rotating capacity without additional capital expenditure. And the units appreciate in value over time, reducing the ongoing capital investment required to sustain program capacity.

That rotating housing asset model means every dollar invested in modular unit acquisition generates value across multiple participant cohorts over the life of the asset. The cost, per, household, served decreases with each successive program cycle. The initial capital investment becomes more cost, effective with each person housed.

FAITH Foundation pursues diversified funding to avoid dependence on any single revenue source. Program fees are assessed on a sliding scale based on participant income. Rental income from stabilized housing units contributes to operations. The Foundation pursues recurring grant funding from federal, state, and private sources. Our existing partnership with Bright Box Homes, which donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold, generates a renewable voucher funding stream tied directly to new home construction activity. Church partnerships and congregational giving from our existing faith community network provide additional support. Individual donor cultivation, in, kind donations of land, building materials, modular housing units, construction labor, furnishings, and professional services round out the picture.

**The Rural Infrastructure Gap**

Rural South Texas faces the compounding challenge of acute housing shortages with limited nonprofit and governmental housing infrastructure. Traditional affordable housing development — site-built construction requiring lengthy permitting, general contractors, and large capital outlays — is cost-prohibitive in rural communities where land values do not support conventional development economics. The result is a near-complete absence of affordable housing inventory in the communities where FAITH Foundation's target populations are concentrated.

FAITH Foundation addresses this rural infrastructure gap through a modular housing deployment model — units supplied through our strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes can be sited on donated or acquired rural land without the delays and costs of traditional construction. This approach brings housing solutions directly to underserved rural communities rather than concentrating resources in urban centers where our target populations cannot access them.

---

## SECTION II: PROJECT DESIGN AND HOUSING STRATEGY

### Program Overview

FAITH Foundation requests CDBG Housing funding to support three interconnected, CDBG-eligible activities: (1) acquisition of modular housing units for Cornerstone Communities development; (2) direct down payment assistance for qualifying low-income families; and (3) transitional housing placement with case management support for reentry, recovery, and veteran populations in rural South Texas. These activities directly advance the Texas CDBG national objective of providing benefit to low- and moderate-income persons, with all program participants qualifying at or below 80% of Area Median Income.

### Activity 1: Modular Housing Unit Acquisition — Cornerstone Communities Initiative

The Cornerstone Communities Initiative is FAITH Foundation's flagship housing development program. The model acquires donated or low-cost land parcels in rural South Texas communities and deploys modular and manufactured housing units — supplied through our strategic partnership with Bright Box Homes — to create purpose-built transitional micro-communities. Each Cornerstone Community is designed as a self-contained residential campus with individual housing units, shared community spaces, on-site case management, recovery programming, remote work and learning centers, community laundry facilities, and shuttle transportation for rural mobility.

**Why Modular Housing:** Modular and manufactured housing units are the only cost-effective approach to affordable housing development at scale in rural South Texas communities. Unit costs of $30,000–$60,000 per unit are a fraction of site-built construction costs, units can be deployed on donated or acquired land without lengthy construction timelines, and the modular format allows communities to be expanded incrementally as funding and land become available. This is not an experimental model — it is a field-tested approach to rural affordable housing that FAITH Foundation has specifically designed its organizational infrastructure to deploy.

**Unit Targets:** [NEEDS INPUT: specific number of modular units to be acquired with this grant funding and at what cost per unit, based on the funding amount requested]

**Site Control:** [NEEDS INPUT: identify whether a specific land parcel has been identified or is under negotiation for the Cornerstone Communities site to be funded through this grant. If a parcel has been identified, provide location (county/community), acreage, ownership status, and estimated acquisition cost or donation status.]

**Housing Type and Capacity:** Each Cornerstone Community is designed as a transitional micro-community. Residents enter as transitional housing participants — exiting homelessness, incarceration, or addiction treatment — and progress through a structured pathway toward permanent housing. As residents achieve stability and transition to permanent housing, their units become available for new participants, creating a rotating capacity that maximizes the long-term value of each housing unit acquired.

**Timeline:** [NEEDS INPUT: provide a project implementation timeline including land acquisition milestones, unit procurement, site preparation, utility installation, and first occupancy target dates.]

**CDBG Eligibility:** Acquisition of modular housing units and site development for affordable housing serving low- and moderate-income households is an eligible CDBG activity under 570.201(a) (acquisition) and 570.201(b) (disposition) and 570.201(c) (public facilities and improvements). All participants will be income-qualified at or below 80% AMI consistent with CDBG low-to-moderate income benefit requirements.

> **[REQUIRED — HUD Environmental Review (24 CFR Part 58)]:** FAITH Foundation acknowledges that all HUD-assisted activities require a completed Environmental Review before funds may be committed or expended and before any choice-limiting actions — including signing leases, purchasing property, or beginning construction — may be taken. FAITH Foundation will coordinate with the responsible entity (the local government grantee administering CDBG funds) to ensure that the required environmental review is completed and HUD approval is obtained prior to any project activity. No site acquisition, construction contracts, or lease commitments will be executed until environmental clearance is confirmed.

> **[REQUIRED — Davis-Bacon Prevailing Wage Requirements]:** If construction or rehabilitation activities funded under this grant involve 8 or more units, FAITH Foundation will comply with Davis-Bacon Act prevailing wage requirements, including obtaining certified payrolls from all contractors and subcontractors and conducting required on-site worker interviews. Contractors will be selected through a competitive procurement process consistent with federal procurement standards, and all construction contracts will include Davis-Bacon wage determination language. FAITH Foundation will maintain complete certified payroll records and make them available to the responsible entity upon request.

> **[REQUIRED — Lead-Based Paint Regulations (24 CFR Part 35)]:** Because FAITH Foundation's housing development activities involve the acquisition and occupancy of residential units, FAITH Foundation will comply with all applicable lead-based paint regulations. All modular and manufactured housing units to be acquired through this grant will be confirmed to be post-1978 construction. For any units or properties that may involve pre-1978 construction, FAITH Foundation will conduct required notification, inspection, risk assessment, and abatement activities consistent with 24 CFR Part 35 and the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act of 1992 prior to occupancy. Blood lead level testing requirements for children under 6 residing in covered housing will be addressed in coordination with county health authorities.

### Activity 2: Down Payment Assistance Program

FAITH Foundation's Down Payment Assistance Program provides direct financial awards to qualifying low-income individuals and families to secure permanent housing. Awards of $2,500 are provided as down payment assistance vouchers to households that are employment-stable but lack savings for upfront housing costs — the single most common barrier to homeownership for the populations we serve.

All down payment assistance recipients will be income-qualified at or below 80% AMI. Recipients will complete FAITH Foundation's homeownership counseling and financial literacy programming prior to award disbursement, ensuring that households receiving assistance are prepared for the financial responsibilities of homeownership. Case managers will conduct 6-month and 12-month housing retention check-ins to document ongoing housing stability.

**Estimated Award Activity:** [NEEDS INPUT: number of down payment assistance awards to be funded through this specific grant, total dollar value of awards, and source of match or leveraged funds if applicable.]

**CDBG Eligibility:** Direct down payment assistance to low- and moderate-income homebuyers is an eligible CDBG activity under 570.201(n) (direct homeownership assistance).

### Activity 3: Transitional Housing Placement with Case Management

FAITH Foundation's Transitional Housing Program places individuals exiting homelessness, incarceration, or addiction treatment into stable transitional housing units for periods of up to 24 months. Each participant receives individualized case management, financial literacy training, peer mentorship, and connections to employment services, legal aid, and family support. Case managers maintain a maximum 15-to-1 client ratio to ensure meaningful, consistent support for each participant.

Priority placement is given to:
- Military veterans experiencing housing insecurity
- Formerly incarcerated individuals in reentry
- Individuals in active addiction recovery
- Single-parent families with dependent children

Participants are connected to the full FAITH Foundation program ecosystem: homeownership counseling, financial literacy education, Veterans Path Home benefits navigation, Second Chance Reentry employment support, and recovery support groups. The goal of every transitional housing placement is progression toward permanent, independent housing — not indefinite transitional residency.

## SECTION III: COMMUNITY NEED AND TARGET POPULATION

### Who We Serve

FAITH Foundation serves the populations that are simultaneously most in need of affordable housing and most systematically excluded from the private housing market: military veterans, individuals in addiction recovery, formerly incarcerated individuals reentering society, single-parent families, and individuals experiencing or at risk of homelessness in rural and underserved South Texas communities.

These populations are not peripheral to the affordable housing crisis — they are at its epicenter. As documented in Section I, veterans represent 1,837 of Texas's nearly 28,000 homeless individuals. Formerly incarcerated individuals are 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population and account for up to 47.8% of shelter admissions nationally. Individuals completing addiction treatment without access to stable sober housing face near-certain relapse and homelessness without structured transitional housing. Single mothers face a homeownership rate of only 34% nationally, and in rural communities with limited rental inventory, housing instability for this population is both severe and persistent.

FAITH Foundation's geographic focus on rural South and Central Texas and the Texas Gulf Coast region reflects the specific communities where these populations are concentrated and where nonprofit housing infrastructure is most absent. The rural communities we serve do not have the density of services available in San Antonio, Austin, or Houston. They have limited or no emergency shelter capacity, no transitional housing programs designed for reentry or recovery populations, and no organizations providing down payment assistance to low-income families working toward homeownership. FAITH Foundation exists to fill this gap.

### Income Qualification and LMI Documentation

All FAITH Foundation program participants will be income-qualified at or below 80% of Area Median Income consistent with CDBG low-to-moderate income benefit requirements. Income documentation will be collected at program intake using HUD-defined income calculation methodologies, including review of recent pay stubs, tax returns, benefit award letters, and self-certification where required. Income qualification records will be maintained in FAITH Foundation's case management system and made available to the responsible entity for monitoring and reporting purposes.

## SECTION IV: ORGANIZATIONAL CAPACITY AND EXPERIENCE

### Leadership Qualifications

FAITH Foundation's leadership team brings a distinctive combination of lived experience with the populations we serve, professional expertise in construction and housing, and demonstrated financial stewardship — precisely the profile required to manage a housing development and direct assistance program in rural Texas.

**Reid Whitesides, Founder and President:** Reid Whitesides brings more than 20 years of professional experience in construction, roofing, project management, sales, consulting, and housing-related industries. His qualifications to lead this work are both professional and deeply personal. During a long struggle with addiction, Reid spent nearly 20 years incarcerated in the State of Texas. Those experiences gave him firsthand insight into the barriers that formerly incarcerated individuals and those in recovery face when rebuilding their lives. Today, more than 15 years sober, he leads FAITH Foundation with the conviction that stable housing is the essential first step toward lasting change. His background in construction and project management directly supports the Foundation's capacity to evaluate modular housing procurement, manage site development, and oversee Cornerstone Communities development.

**Scott Ellis, Treasurer and Board Chair:** Scott Ellis is the owner of E4 Roofing & Construction, a Georgetown, Texas-based company he has led for more than 15 years. His background in residential and commercial construction, project coordination, budgeting, contractor management, and building systems provides the Foundation with direct, applicable expertise in housing development. Scott's professional experience in construction cost estimation, building practices, property improvement, and long-term asset stewardship is directly applied to FAITH Foundation's modular housing acquisition and Cornerstone Communities development activities. His financial oversight role ensures that all grant funds are managed with the accountability and transparency required for federal compliance.

**Pastor Juan Valdez, Secretary and Protector:** Pastor Valdez brings more than 40 years of Christian faith and nearly 30 years of ordained ministry experience to the Foundation's governance structure. Beyond his ministry credentials, Pastor Valdez and his wife, Martha, operated a successful business in the same San Antonio location for 34 years — a track record of organizational consistency, community reliability, and long-term stewardship that directly informs his governance role. As Secretary and Protector, he provides mission accountability, ethical oversight, and governance integrity for the Foundation.

### Financial Management Capacity

FAITH Foundation maintains its financial records using QuickBooks accounting software. The Foundation's Treasurer, Scott Ellis, provides professional financial oversight consistent with his background as a business owner with 15 years of operational experience. All grant funds will be maintained in segregated accounts with transaction-level documentation, and financial reports will be provided to the responsible entity on the schedule required by the grant agreement.

FAITH Foundation acknowledges that it is in its inaugural funding cycle. Initial operations have been funded through founder investment and church community support. The Foundation's annual operating budget is $75,000. While FAITH Foundation has not yet completed a funded housing project cycle, the organization's leadership team brings the construction expertise, financial management experience, and lived knowledge of the populations served that position it to deploy these funds effectively and accountably.

### Partnership Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation does not operate in isolation. The Foundation maintains active partnerships across multiple sectors that extend its organizational capacity and reduce duplication of services:

- **Church partners** provide volunteer labor, congregational fundraising, mentorship volunteers, and meeting space for participant programming
- **Recovery program partners** refer individuals completing treatment who need stable transitional housing and provide ongoing support services for residents in active recovery
- **Reentry service partners** coordinate placement of formerly incarcerated individuals into transitional housing upon release, connecting them with employment services, legal aid, and family reunification support
- **County social services agencies and local housing authorities** refer eligible families and individuals, coordinate benefits enrollment, and provide case management collaboration
- **Building material suppliers and modular housing manufacturers** — including Bright Box Homes — provide discounted or donated materials and units, significantly reducing per-unit capital costs
- **Land owners in rural South Texas** donate or sell land at reduced cost for Cornerstone Communities development sites
- **Veterans service organizations** refer military veterans experiencing housing insecurity and coordinate VA benefits enrollment

This partnership infrastructure reduces FAITH Foundation's cost per participant, extends its referral reach into populations that would not otherwise self-identify for services, and creates accountability relationships that strengthen program quality.

> **[REQUIRED — Section 3 Hiring Requirements]:** FAITH Foundation acknowledges that HUD-funded construction projects above $200,000 require best-faith efforts to hire Section 3 workers — low-income persons, including those in public housing — and to engage Section 3 businesses. For any construction activities funded through this grant that meet the applicable thresholds, FAITH Foundation will implement a Section 3 hiring plan, document all outreach efforts, and submit required annual Section 3 Summary Reports (HUD-60002) targeting at least 25% of new hires from Section 3 worker categories consistent with 24 CFR Part 135. Given FAITH Foundation's service to reentry and recovery populations — populations that overlap substantially with Section 3 worker eligibility — the Foundation is uniquely positioned to demonstrate meaningful Section 3 compliance.

---

## SECTION V: SUSTAINABILITY AND LONG-TERM IMPACT

### The Rotating Housing Asset Model

FAITH Foundation's sustainability is structurally built into its program design. Cornerstone Communities do not create permanent dependency on grant funding — they create permanent assets. Each modular housing unit acquired through this grant becomes a long-term organizational asset that:

1. Serves transitional residents during the program period
2. Generates rental income as units stabilize, contributing to operational sustainability
3. Becomes available for new participants as residents transition to permanent housing, creating rotating capacity without additional capital expenditure
4. Appreciates in value over time, reducing the ongoing capital investment required to sustain program capacity

This rotating housing asset model means that every dollar invested in modular unit acquisition generates value across multiple participant cohorts over the life of the asset. The cost-per-household-served decreases with each successive program cycle, making the initial capital investment increasingly cost-effective over time.

### Diversified Revenue Strategy

FAITH Foundation actively pursues diversified funding to avoid dependence on any single revenue source:

- **Program fees** assessed on a sliding scale based on participant income
- **Rental income** from stabilized housing units
- **Recurring grant funding** from federal, state, and private sources
- **Corporate partnerships** — including our existing partnership with Bright Box Homes, which donates $2,500 to FAITH Foundation for every home sold, generating a renewable voucher funding stream tied to new home construction activity
- **Church partnerships and congregational giving** from our existing faith community network
- **Individual donor cultivation**
- **In-kind donations** of land, building materials, modular housing units, construction labor, furnishings, and professional services

### Long-Term Affordability

[NEEDS INPUT: specify whether FAITH Foundation will record long-term affordability restrictions or covenants (e.g., deed restrictions, land use agreements) on Cornerstone Communities properties to ensure continued affordable use. If so, describe the mechanism and duration. This is important for CDBG compliance and scoring.]

### Community Partnerships as Sustainability Infrastructure

FAITH Foundation's partnership network — with recovery programs, reentry service providers, veterans service organizations, county social services agencies, and church communities — creates a referral and support infrastructure that sustains program operations independently of any single funding source. These partnerships generate participant referrals, volunteer labor, donated materials, and co-located services that reduce FAITH Foundation's direct cost per participant and ensure that residents have access to the full continuum of services needed to achieve and maintain housing stability.

### Outcomes We Intend to Achieve

FAITH Foundation tracks and reports on five outcome domains:

1. **Housing Placement:** Number of individuals and families transitioned from homelessness or unstable housing into transitional units and permanent housing, tracked at 30-, 60-, and 90-day retention intervals
2. **Financial Stability:** Number of down payment assistance awards disbursed, average award amount, and percentage of recipients maintaining housing at 12 months
3. **Reentry Success:** Number of formerly incarcerated individuals housed, employment placement rates, and recidivism reduction compared to regional averages
4. **Recovery Outcomes:** Number of individuals in active recovery housed, sobriety milestones maintained, and connection rates to ongoing treatment and support services
5. **Community Development:** Number of Cornerstone Communities sites developed, total modular housing units acquired and placed, occupancy rates, and successful transitions from transitional to permanent housing

All outcomes will be tracked longitudinally through FAITH Foundation's case management system, reported quarterly to the board of directors, and made available to the responsible entity for monitoring and compliance reporting. Annual impact reports will be published and made available to all funders and stakeholders.

### Leveraged Funds and In-Kind Support

FAITH Foundation's cost-effectiveness is significantly enhanced by the leveraged resources the organization brings to every project. In-kind donations of building materials, volunteer labor, and professional services (legal, architectural, surveying, construction management) reduce cash outlays and are documented at fair market value. The Bright Box Homes partnership generates renewable voucher funding at no cost to the grant budget. Church partner volunteers reduce staffing costs for mentorship and programming delivery. Land donations eliminate or reduce the largest single cost in rural housing development.

[NEEDS INPUT: provide specific dollar values for leveraged or in-kind resources to be applied to this project, if known, to document cost-effectiveness and non-duplication of funding.]

### Cost-Effectiveness

At $30,000–$60,000 per modular housing unit, FAITH Foundation's Cornerstone Communities model delivers housing at a fraction of the cost of site-built affordable housing construction. Each unit serves multiple participant cohorts over its useful life, reducing the effective cost-per-household served with each successive cycle. Down payment assistance at $2,500 per household is a highly cost-effective intervention — the return on investment is the lifetime housing stability, wealth accumulation, and reduced public system utilization of a family that transitions from rental instability to homeownership.

---

## SECTION VII: EQUITY, FAIR HOUSING, AND COMPLIANCE

### Affirmative Furthering of Fair Housing

FAITH Foundation is committed to affirmatively furthering fair housing in all program activities. The Foundation's programs are explicitly designed to serve populations that have been systematically excluded from housing opportunity: individuals with criminal records excluded from private market rentals, veterans experiencing service-connected housing instability, individuals whose addiction histories create landlord discrimination, and single-parent families facing income-to-price ratios that foreclose homeownership. Serving these populations is not incidental to FAITH Foundation's mission — it is the mission.

FAITH Foundation's programs are open to all individuals regardless of race, color, national origin, sex, religion, disability, familial status, or any other protected class under the Fair Housing Act. Affirmative marketing to underserved populations will be conducted through partnerships with veterans service organizations, reentry service providers, recovery program partners, and county social services agencies — organizations that have direct relationships with the communities experiencing the greatest housing barriers.

> **[REQUIRED — Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity Compliance (24 CFR Parts 100, 107, 110)]:** FAITH Foundation will maintain written non-discrimination policies consistent with the Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 3601–3619), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. FAITH Foundation will cooperate with the responsible entity's Analysis of Impediments to Fair Housing Choice and will document all affirmative marketing efforts and outreach activities. Annual fair housing certifications will be completed as required by the grant agreement.

FAITH Foundation will document income qualification for all program participants using HUD-approved income calculation methodologies and will maintain income certification records consistent with CDBG recordkeeping requirements. The responsible entity will be provided with full access to participant income documentation for monitoring purposes.

A gift at this level would be allocated as follows: the majority directed toward the acquisition of modular housing units and site preparation infrastructure for our first Cornerstone Community development in [NEEDS INPUT: specific rural Texas community or county name]; a portion toward down payment assistance vouchers ($2,500 each) for qualifying veterans, reentry, and recovery program participants; and the remainder toward case management operational support ensuring residents have sustained access to wraparound services. Every dollar of this investment will be tracked across five measurable outcome domains — housing placement and retention rates, financial stability milestones, reentry success, recovery outcomes, and community development progress — with quarterly reporting provided directly to [NEEDS INPUT: Company name].

- **[REQUIRED] HUD Environmental Review (24 CFR Part 58):** All HUD-assisted activities require a completed environmental review before funds are committed or any choice-limiting actions — including land purchase or construction — are taken. The responsible entity (typically the local government grantee) must certify the review prior to project launch.
